abstract: The potential for presynaptic information processing within the arbor of a single axon will be discussed in this paper. Current knowledge about the activity dependence of the firing threshold, the conditions required for conduction failure, and the similarity of nodes along a single axon will be reviewed. An electronic circuit model for a site of low conduction safety in an axon will be presented. In response to single frequency stimulation the electronic circuit acts as a lowpass filter.
originalAbstract: The potential for presynaptic information processing within the arbor of a single axon will be discussed in this paper. Current knowledge about the activity dependence of the firing threshold, the conditions required for conduction failure, and the similarity of nodes along a single axon will be reviewed. An electronic circuit model for a site of low conduction safety in an axon will be presented. In response to single frequency stimulation the electronic circuit acts as a lowpass filter.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether information processing can occur inside the branching structure of a single axon, before signals reach synapses. Its central question concerns signal propagation itself: an axon’s response to incoming activity may shape which signals continue through it, giving transmission a computational role.

The discussion reviews three relevant biological issues: how firing threshold depends on prior activity, when a signal fails to propagate, and how similar different nodes along one axon are. These issues connect the history of stimulation and local axonal properties to the reliability of signal transmission through the same cell.

The paper also presents an electronic model of an axonal location where propagation has a low safety margin. Under stimulation at a single frequency, the circuit behaves as a low-pass filter, preferentially passing lower-frequency activity over higher-frequency activity. This provides a concrete circuit example of the proposed processing role: a vulnerable transmission site can select among temporal inputs. The stated result concerns this circuit model and stimulation condition.
summary.tldr: An electronic model shows how an axonal site with unreliable conduction can filter activity before it reaches a synapse.

title: Presynaptic Neural Information Processing

abstract: We propose an optimality principle for training an unsu(cid:173) pervised feedforward neural network based upon maximal ability to reconstruct the input data from the network out(cid:173) puts. We describe an algorithm which can be used to train either linear or nonlinear networks with certain types of nonlinearity. Examples of applications to the problems of image coding, feature detection, and analysis of random(cid:173) dot stereograms are presented.
originalAbstract: We propose an optimality principle for training an unsu(cid:173) pervised feedforward neural network based upon maximal ability to reconstruct the input data from the network out(cid:173) puts. We describe an algorithm which can be used to train either linear or nonlinear networks with certain types of nonlinearity. Examples of applications to the problems of image coding, feature detection, and analysis of random(cid:173) dot stereograms are presented.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to decide what an unsupervised feedforward network should learn: its outputs should preserve the information needed to reconstruct its inputs as well as possible. This turns reconstruction into a training objective. A useful output representation is therefore one from which the original data can be recovered effectively.

This principle gives learning a target without requiring externally supplied category labels. The input data themselves provide the reference against which the representation is judged. The authors describe a training algorithm for linear networks and for nonlinear networks with certain types of nonlinearity. That qualification matters because the stated algorithm does not cover every possible nonlinear network.

Applications are presented in image coding, feature detection, and the analysis of random-dot stereograms. These examples connect the reconstruction principle to several visual processing tasks. The shared idea is that preserving recoverable information can guide the formation of useful outputs, providing one objective that can organize learning across different applications.
summary.tldr: The paper trains unsupervised networks to produce representations that preserve the ability to reconstruct their inputs.

title: An Optimality Principle for Unsupervised Learning

abstract: We have created a radial basis function network that allocates a new computational unit whenever an unusual pattern is presented to the network. The network learns by allocating new units and adjusting the parameters of existing units. If the network performs poorly on a presented pattern, then a new unit is allocated which memorizes the response to the presented pattern. If the network performs well on a presented pattern, then the network parameters are updated using standard LMS gradient descent. For predicting the Mackey Glass chaotic time series, our network learns much faster than do those using back-propagation and uses a comparable number of synapses.
originalAbstract: We have created a radial basis function network that allocates a new computational unit whenever an unusual pattern is presented to the network. The network learns by allocating new units and adjusting the parameters of existing units. If the network performs poorly on a presented pattern, then a new unit is allocated which memorizes the response to the presented pattern. If the network performs well on a presented pattern, then the network parameters are updated using standard LMS gradient descent. For predicting the Mackey Glass chaotic time series, our network learns much faster than do those using back-propagation and uses a comparable number of synapses.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a radial basis function network that learns through both memorization and parameter adjustment. Its structure can grow as training proceeds. When the network encounters a pattern it handles poorly, it adds a computational unit that memorizes the desired response to that pattern, giving the difficult example a new place in the representation.

When the network already performs well on an example, it updates existing parameters using least-mean-squares gradient descent. Performance on the current pattern therefore determines which learning operation is used. The method combines a direct response to poorly represented cases with gradual refinement of knowledge already captured by the network.

The authors evaluate the approach on prediction of the Mackey–Glass chaotic time series. They report much faster learning than networks trained by backpropagation while using a comparable number of synapses. In that task, the speed advantage accompanies similar connection counts. The finding supports combining selective network growth with gradient-based adjustment as a way to make learning more efficient.
summary.tldr: A radial basis function network adds units for poorly handled patterns and refines familiar ones, learning a chaotic prediction task faster than backpropagation.

title: Leaning by Combining Memorization and Gradient Descent

abstract: Harmonic grammar (Legendre, et al., 1990) is a connectionist theory of lin(cid:173) guistic well-formed ness based on the assumption that the well-formedness of a sentence can be measured by the harmony (negative energy) of the corresponding connectionist state. Assuming a lower-level connectionist network that obeys a few general connectionist principles but is otherwise unspecified, we construct a higher-level network with an equivalent har(cid:173) mony function that captures the most linguistically relevant global aspects of the lower level network. In this paper, we extend the tensor product representation (Smolensky 1990) to fully recursive representations of re(cid:173) cursively structured objects like sentences in the lower-level network. We show theoretically and with an example the power of the new technique for parallel distributed structure processing.

In this paper, we extend the tensor product representation (Smolensky 1990) to fully recursive representations of re(cid:173) cursively structured objects like sentences in the lower-level network. paragraphs: The paper develops a neural representation for recursively structured objects such as sentences. It works within harmonic grammar, which assumes that a sentence's linguistic well-formedness can be measured by the harmony, or negative energy, of its network state. This makes a numerical property of a connectionist representation stand for a linguistic judgment.

Starting from a lower-level network that satisfies a few general principles, the authors construct a higher-level network with an equivalent harmony function. The higher-level account captures global properties that matter linguistically while leaving much of the lower-level implementation unspecified. Preserving harmony connects the two descriptions through the quantity used to assess well-formedness.

The technical contribution extends tensor product representations so that they can represent fully recursive structures in the lower-level network. Recursive representation allows structured parts to contain further structured parts, as sentences do. The authors support the technique with theory and an example, demonstrating its use for parallel distributed structure processing and linking nested linguistic organization to connectionist computation.
summary.tldr: An extension of tensor product representations lets connectionist networks process recursive structures while preserving a harmony-based account of linguistic well-formedness.

title: Distributed Recursive Structure Processing

abstract: Simplified models of the lateral geniculate nucles (LGN) and stri(cid:173) ate cortex illustrate the possibility that feedback to the LG N may be used for robust, low-level pattern analysis. The information fed back to the LG N is rebroadcast to cortex using the LG N 's full fan-out, so the cortex-LGN-cortex pathway mediates extensive cortico-cortical communication while keeping the number of neces(cid:173) sary connections small.
originalAbstract: Simplified models of the lateral geniculate nucles (LGN) and stri(cid:173) ate cortex illustrate the possibility that feedback to the LG N may be used for robust, low-level pattern analysis. The information fed back to the LG N is rebroadcast to cortex using the LG N 's full fan-out, so the cortex-LGN-cortex pathway mediates extensive cortico-cortical communication while keeping the number of neces(cid:173) sary connections small.

paragraphs: The paper explores a possible computational role for feedback from visual cortex to the lateral geniculate nucleus, or LGN. Using simplified models of the LGN and striate cortex, it asks how this returning information could support robust analysis of basic visual patterns. The focus is on what the feedback pathway makes possible for communication.

In the proposed arrangement, information sent from cortex back to the LGN is distributed outward again through the LGN's full set of projections to cortex. A message can therefore influence a broad cortical population through the cortex-to-LGN-to-cortex route. This makes the return pathway useful for sharing information across cortex.

The models illustrate how extensive communication can be supported while keeping the number of required connections small. The significance is architectural: the distribution of feedback provides a way to combine broad information sharing with economical wiring. The paper presents this as a possible mechanism for robust low-level pattern analysis within the simplified systems it studies.
summary.tldr: Simplified visual-system models suggest that LGN feedback can distribute cortical information widely with relatively few connections.

title: A Model of Feedback to the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus

abstract: This paper describes a neural network classifier for the 11000 chip, which optically reads the E13B font characters at the bottom of checks. The first layer of the neural network is a hardware linear classifier which recognizes the characters in this font . A second software neural layer is implemented on an inexpensive microprocessor to clean up the re(cid:173) sults of the first layer. The hardware linear classifier is mathematically specified using constraints and an optimization principle. The weights of the classifier are found using the active set method, similar to Vap(cid:173) nik's separating hyperplane algorithm. In 7.5 minutes ofSPARC 2 time, the method solves for 1523 Lagrange mUltipliers, which is equivalent to training on a data set of approximately 128,000 examples. The result(cid:173) ing network performs quite well: when tested on a test set of 1500 real checks, it has a 99.995% character accuracy rate. 1 A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE 11000 CHIP At Synaptics, we have created the 11000, an analog VLSI chip that, when combined with associated software, optically reads the E13B font from the bottom of checks. This E13B font is shown in figure 1. The overall architecture of the 11000 chip is shown in figure 2. The 11000 recognizes checks hand-swiped through a slot. A lens focuses the image of the bottom of the check onto the retina. The retina has circuitry which locates the vertical position of the characters on the check . The retina then sends an image vertically centered around a possible character to the classifier. The classifier in the nooo has a tough job. It must be very accurate and immune to noise and ink scribbles in the input . Therefore , we decided to use an integrated segmentation and recognition approach (Martin & Pittman, 1992)(Platt, et al., 1992). When the classifier produces a strong response, we know that a character is horizontally centered in the retina. paragraphs: The paper describes a neural classifier for reading the E13B characters printed along the bottom of checks. Recognition is divided between a hardware linear classifier and a second neural layer running in software on an inexpensive microprocessor. The software layer refines the hardware layer's output, giving the system two stages for reaching a character decision.

The hardware classifier is designed through mathematical constraints and an optimization objective. An active set method determines its weights, using an approach related to separating hyperplanes. The reported optimization solves for 1,523 Lagrange multipliers in 7.5 minutes on a SPARC 2, described as equivalent to training with approximately 128,000 examples.

The system also connects recognition with character positioning: a strong classifier response indicates that a character is horizontally centered. This integrates segmentation with recognition in a setting that includes noise and ink marks. On 1,500 real checks, the resulting network achieves 99.995% character accuracy. That figure describes individual character recognition, rather than the proportion of entire checks read without error.
summary.tldr: A hardware classifier paired with a software neural layer reads check characters with a reported 99.995% character accuracy.

title: A Neural Network Classifier for the I100 OCR Chip

abstract: Coarse codes are widely used throughout the brain to encode sen(cid:173) sory and motor variables. Methods designed to interpret these codes, such as population vector analysis, are either inefficient, i.e., the variance of the estimate is much larger than the smallest possi(cid:173) ble variance, or biologically implausible, like maximum likelihood. Moreover, these methods attempt to compute a scalar or vector estimate of the encoded variable. Neurons are faced with a simi(cid:173) lar estimation problem . They must read out the responses of the presynaptic neurons, but, by contrast, they typically encode the variable with a further population code rather than as a scalar. We show how a non-linear recurrent network can be used to per(cid:173) form these estimation in an optimal way while keeping the estimate in a coarse code format. This work suggests that lateral connec(cid:173) tions in the cortex may be involved in cleaning up uncorrelated noise among neurons representing similar variables.

paragraphs: Sensory and motor variables are often represented across populations of broadly responsive neurons. Reading such a coarse code requires extracting a reliable estimate from noisy activity. The paper points out that conventional methods can either have unnecessarily high estimation variance or require computations regarded as biologically implausible.

It also changes the desired output of the estimation process. A receiving neural population typically represents information through another population code, rather than converting everything into a single scalar or vector. The authors show how a nonlinear recurrent network can perform optimal estimation while preserving that distributed, coarse-code format.

The result connects statistical efficiency with the form in which neurons actually pass information onward. Recurrent interactions do the estimation work without requiring the final representation to leave the population-code setting. The paper consequently proposes that cortical lateral connections may help remove uncorrelated noise among neurons representing similar variables, giving those connections a possible role in improving the reliability of neural representations.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear recurrent network performs optimal estimation while retaining a population code, suggesting a noise-cleaning role for cortical lateral connections.

title: Statistically Efficient Estimations Using Cortical Lateral Connections

abstract: Belief propagation on cyclic graphs is an efﬁcient algorithm for comput- ing approximate marginal probability distributions over single nodes and neighboring nodes in the graph. In this paper we propose two new al- gorithms for approximating joint probabilities of arbitrary pairs of nodes and prove a number of desirable properties that these estimates fulﬁll. The ﬁrst algorithm is a propagation algorithm which is shown to con- verge if belief propagation converges to a stable ﬁxed point. The second algorithm is based on matrix inversion. Experiments compare a number of competing methods.
originalAbstract: Belief propagation on cyclic graphs is an efﬁcient algorithm for comput- ing approximate marginal probability distributions over single nodes and neighboring nodes in the graph. In this paper we propose two new al- gorithms for approximating joint probabilities of arbitrary pairs of nodes and prove a number of desirable properties that these estimates fulﬁll. The ﬁrst algorithm is a propagation algorithm which is shown to con- verge if belief propagation converges to a stable ﬁxed point. The second algorithm is based on matrix inversion. Experiments compare a number of competing methods.

paragraphs: Belief propagation provides an efficient way to approximate probabilities in graphs containing cycles. The paper starts from its estimates for individual nodes and neighboring pairs, then addresses a broader question: how to estimate joint probabilities for any pair of nodes, including nodes that are not directly connected.

The authors propose two algorithms for this purpose. One uses propagation, while the other uses matrix inversion. Both aim to recover information about pairs that goes beyond knowing each node's probability separately. Joint probabilities matter because they describe how two variables behave together, which individual-node estimates alone do not determine.

The paper proves several desirable properties of the resulting estimates. For the propagation algorithm, it establishes convergence when belief propagation converges to a stable fixed point. This is a conditional guarantee tied to the behavior of the underlying belief-propagation procedure. Experiments compare competing methods, complementing the theoretical analysis with an empirical examination of approaches to arbitrary-pair inference.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms extend approximate inference to arbitrary node pairs, with a conditional convergence guarantee for the propagation-based method.

title: Linear Response for Approximate Inference

abstract: In this paper we present a framework for using multi-layer per- ceptron (MLP) networks in nonlinear generative models trained by variational Bayesian learning. The nonlinearity is handled by linearizing it using a Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the hidden neu- rons. This yields an accurate approximation for cases of large pos- terior variance. The method can be used to derive nonlinear coun- terparts for linear algorithms such as factor analysis, independent component/factor analysis and state-space models. This is demon- strated with a nonlinear factor analysis experiment in which even 20 sources can be estimated from a real world speech data set.
originalAbstract: In this paper we present a framework for using multi-layer per- ceptron (MLP) networks in nonlinear generative models trained by variational Bayesian learning. The nonlinearity is handled by linearizing it using a Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the hidden neu- rons. This yields an accurate approximation for cases of large pos- terior variance. The method can be used to derive nonlinear coun- terparts for linear algorithms such as factor analysis, independent component/factor analysis and state-space models. This is demon- strated with a nonlinear factor analysis experiment in which even 20 sources can be estimated from a real world speech data set.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for placing multilayer perceptron networks inside nonlinear generative models trained with variational Bayesian learning. Such models use hidden quantities to explain observed data, with the network providing a nonlinear relationship. The computational challenge addressed here is handling that nonlinearity during Bayesian learning.

The authors linearize the nonlinear behavior using Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the hidden neurons. They report that this produces an accurate approximation in cases with large posterior variance. That qualification matters because posterior variance represents uncertainty in the inferred quantities, and the approximation is intended to remain useful in the stated high-uncertainty setting.

The framework can produce nonlinear counterparts of linear approaches including factor analysis, independent component or factor analysis, and state-space models. A nonlinear factor-analysis experiment on real speech data demonstrates estimation of as many as 20 sources. The contribution combines an approximation method for nonlinear Bayesian learning with a route for extending several established model families and a concrete speech-data demonstration.
summary.tldr: A quadrature-based approximation enables variational Bayesian learning in nonlinear generative models, demonstrated by estimating 20 sources from speech data.

title: Unsupervised Variational Bayesian Learning of Nonlinear Models

abstract: We develop a family of upper and lower bounds on the worst-case ex- pected KL loss for estimating a discrete distribution on a finite number m of points, given N i.i.d. samples. Our upper bounds are approximation- theoretic, similar to recent bounds for estimating discrete entropy; the lower bounds are Bayesian, based on averages of the KL loss under Dirichlet distributions. The upper bounds are convex in their parameters and thus can be minimized by descent methods to provide estimators with low worst-case error; the lower bounds are indexed by a one-dimensional parameter and are thus easily maximized. Asymptotic analysis of the bounds demonstrates the uniform KL-consistency of a wide class of es- timators as c = N/m (no matter how slowly), and shows that no estimator is consistent for c bounded (in contrast to entropy estima- tion). Moreover, the bounds are asymptotically tight as c 0 or , and are shown numerically to be tight within a factor of two for all c. Finally, in the sparse-data limit c 0, we find that the Dirichlet-Bayes (add-constant) estimator with parameter scaling like -c log(c) optimizes both the upper and lower bounds, suggesting an optimal choice of the "add-constant" parameter in this regime.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating a distribution over m outcomes from N independent, identically distributed observations. Accuracy is measured through expected Kullback-Leibler loss in the worst case. The authors develop upper bounds using approximation theory and lower bounds using Bayesian averages under Dirichlet distributions, approaching the estimation problem from both sides.

The upper bounds are convex in their parameters and can be minimized through descent methods to construct estimators with low worst-case error. The lower bounds depend on one parameter, making maximization straightforward. The analysis identifies the sample-to-outcome ratio c = N/m as central: uniform KL consistency is possible as this ratio grows without bound, whereas a bounded ratio prevents consistency.

The bounds become asymptotically tight in both sparse-data and large-ratio regimes, and numerical results place them within a factor of two across ratios. In the sparse regime, an add-constant Dirichlet-Bayes estimator with its parameter scaling as -c log(c) optimizes both bounds. This agreement suggests an optimal smoothing choice in that regime.
summary.tldr: Upper and lower KL-loss bounds characterize discrete-distribution estimation and suggest an optimal add-constant smoothing scale for sparse data.

title: Variational Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under KL Loss

abstract: The concept of surprise is central to sensory processing, adaptation, learning, and attention. Yet, no widely-accepted mathematical theory currently exists to quantitatively characterize surprise elicited by a stimulus or event, for observers that range from single neurons to complex natural or engineered systems. We describe a formal Bayesian definition of surprise that is the only consistent formulation under minimal axiomatic assumptions. Surprise quantifies how data affects a natural or artificial observer, by measuring the difference between posterior and prior beliefs of the observer. Using this framework we measure the extent to which humans direct their gaze towards surprising items while watching television and video games. We find that subjects are strongly attracted towards surprising locations, with 72% of all human gaze shifts directed towards locations more surprising than the average, a figure which rises to 84% when considering only gaze targets simultaneously selected by all subjects. The resulting theory of surprise is applicable across different spatio-temporal scales, modalities, and levels of abstraction.

paragraphs: This paper defines surprise in terms of how an observation changes an observer’s beliefs. The quantity compares beliefs before and after receiving data, making surprise depend on the effect of the data on the observer. The authors characterize this Bayesian definition as the only consistent formulation under their minimal axiomatic assumptions.

They use the framework to investigate where people look while watching television and video games. Across the measured gaze shifts, seventy-two percent go toward locations whose surprise exceeds the average. When considering gaze targets selected simultaneously by all subjects, the proportion rises to eighty-four percent.

These findings show a strong relationship between the proposed surprise measure and gaze allocation in the studied viewing conditions. The mathematical definition also offers a common way to describe surprise across spatial and temporal scales, sensory modalities, and levels of abstraction. The paper connects that broad formulation to observed attention by testing whether changes in modeled beliefs correspond to the places that attract viewers’ eyes.
summary.tldr: Bayesian surprise measures belief change, and the study finds that human gaze shifts strongly favor locations scored as more surprising.

title: Bayesian Surprise Attracts Human Attention

abstract: Reinforcement learning by direct policy gradient estimation is attractive in theory but in practice leads to notoriously ill-behaved optimization problems. We improve its robustness and speed of convergence with stochastic meta-descent, a gain vector adaptation method that employs fast Hessian-vector products. In our experiments the resulting algorithms outperform previously employed online stochastic, ofﬂine conjugate, and natural policy gradient methods.
originalAbstract: Reinforcement learning by direct policy gradient estimation is attractive in theory but in practice leads to notoriously ill-behaved optimization problems. We improve its robustness and speed of convergence with stochastic meta-descent, a gain vector adaptation method that employs fast Hessian-vector products. In our experiments the resulting algorithms outperform previously employed online stochastic, ofﬂine conjugate, and natural policy gradient methods.

paragraphs: Direct policy gradient estimation provides an appealing way to learn behavior in reinforcement learning, but the resulting optimization can be difficult to control in practice. This paper targets that optimization difficulty. Its aim is to make policy gradient learning more robust and to improve how quickly the learning process converges.

The proposed approach uses stochastic meta-descent to adapt a gain vector, adjusting the scales of the optimization updates. The adaptation employs fast Hessian-vector products, which bring information about the curvature of the optimization problem into the update procedure. The method therefore acts on how policy learning proceeds, using an adaptive mechanism to address poorly behaved optimization.

In the reported experiments, the resulting algorithms outperform previously used online stochastic, offline conjugate, and natural policy gradient methods. These findings support the authors' claim that gain adaptation can improve robustness and convergence speed. The comparison is an experimental result for the studied algorithms and problems, providing evidence for the approach's practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: Stochastic meta-descent adapts policy gradient update gains, improving robustness and convergence speed in the reported experiments.

title: Fast Online Policy Gradient Learning with SMD Gain Vector Adaptation

abstract: We present a non-linear, simple, yet effective, feature subset selection method for regression and use it in analyzing cortical neural activity. Our algorithm involves a feature-weighted version of the k-nearest-neighbor algorithm. It is able to capture complex dependency of the target func- tion on its input and makes use of the leave-one-out error as a natural regularization. We explain the characteristics of our algorithm on syn- thetic problems and use it in the context of predicting hand velocity from spikes recorded in motor cortex of a behaving monkey. By applying fea- ture selection we are able to improve prediction quality and suggest a novel way of exploring neural data.

Our algorithm involves a feature-weighted version of the k-nearest-neighbor algorithm. It is able to capture complex dependency of the target func- tion on its input and makes use of the leave-one-out error as a natural regularization. We explain the characteristics of our algorithm on syn- thetic problems and use it in the context of predicting hand velocity from spikes recorded in motor cortex of a behaving monkey. paragraphs: This paper proposes a feature-selection method for regression, where the goal is to predict a numerical target. It uses a feature-weighted version of k-nearest-neighbor prediction. Weighting the inputs changes which examples count as neighbors, allowing the method to identify a useful subset of features while capturing nonlinear relationships between inputs and the target.

The algorithm uses leave-one-out prediction error as a natural form of regularization. In this assessment, each example is predicted without using that example itself as training evidence. The authors explain the method's behavior on synthetic problems, connecting its feature choices to its ability to represent complex dependencies.

They then apply it to predicting hand velocity from spikes recorded in a behaving monkey's motor cortex. Feature selection improves prediction quality in that application. This result supports the method as a practical regression tool and suggests a way to explore neural data through the inputs useful for prediction. The stated finding concerns predictive improvement, rather than a causal explanation of how particular neurons control movement.
summary.tldr: Feature-weighted nearest-neighbor regression selects useful inputs and improves hand-velocity prediction from motor-cortex spikes.

title: Nearest Neighbor Based Feature Selection for Regression and its Application to Neural Activity

abstract: We study the problem of an apprentice learning to behave in an environment with an unknown reward function by observing the behavior of an expert. We follow on the work of Abbeel and Ng [1] who considered a framework in which the true reward function is assumed to be a linear combination of a set of known and observable features. We give a new algorithm that, like theirs, is guaranteed to learn a policy that is nearly as good as the expert's, given enough examples. However, unlike their algorithm, we show that ours may produce a policy that is substantially better than the expert's. Moreover, our algorithm is computationally faster, is easier to implement, and can be applied even in the absence of an expert. The method is based on a game-theoretic view of the problem, which leads naturally to a direct application of the multiplicative-weights algorithm of Freund and Schapire [2] for playing repeated matrix games. In addition to our formal presentation and analysis of the new algorithm, we sketch how the method can be applied when the transition function itself is unknown, and we provide an experimental demonstration of the algorithm on a toy video-game environment.

We give a new algorithm that, like theirs, is guaranteed to learn a policy that is nearly as good as the expert's, given enough examples. However, unlike their algorithm, we show that ours may produce a policy that is substantially better than the expert's. Moreover, our algorithm is computationally faster, is easier to implement, and can be applied even in the absence of an expert. The method is based on a game-theoretic view of the problem, which leads naturally to a direct application of the multiplicative-weights algorithm of Freund and Schapire [2] for playing repeated matrix games. In addition to our formal presentation and analysis of the new algorithm, we sketch how the method can be applied when the transition function itself is unknown, and we provide an experimental demonstration of the algorithm on a toy video-game environment.

paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning asks how an agent can learn useful behavior by watching an expert when the reward for its actions is unknown. This paper assumes that the true reward is a linear combination of known, observable features. That assumption gives the learner a structured family of possible rewards to work with.

The authors frame the learning problem as a game and apply a multiplicative-weights algorithm for repeated matrix games. Given enough examples, their method is guaranteed to learn a policy nearly as good as the expert’s. It may also produce a substantially better policy, although improvement beyond the expert is a possibility rather than the guarantee.

Compared with the earlier approach discussed in the abstract, the algorithm is faster computationally and easier to implement. The authors also describe applicability without an expert, sketch an extension for unknown environment transitions, and demonstrate the method in a toy video game. The contribution connects a formal performance guarantee with a simpler computational approach to learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic apprenticeship algorithm can learn near-expert behavior under a structured reward assumption and may outperform its teacher.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Apprenticeship Learning

abstract: We consider a global optimization problem of a deterministic function f in a semimetric space, given a finite budget of n evaluations. The function f is assumed to be locally smooth (around one of its global maxima) with respect to a semi-metric . We describe two algorithms based on optimistic exploration that use a hierarchical partitioning of the space at all scales. A first contribution is an algorithm, DOO, that requires the knowledge of . We report a finite-sample performance bound in terms of a measure of the quantity of near-optimal states. We then define a second algorithm, SOO, which does not require the knowledge of the semimetric under which f is smooth, and whose performance is almost as good as DOO optimally-fitted.

paragraphs: The paper studies global optimization of a deterministic function with a fixed budget of evaluations. It assumes the function is locally smooth around at least one global maximum with respect to a semimetric. The question is how to search effectively, especially when the optimizer does not know the semimetric that expresses this smoothness.

Both proposed algorithms use optimistic exploration over a hierarchy of partitions at different scales. The first, DOO, requires knowledge of the semimetric. Its finite-sample performance bound depends on a measure of how many near-optimal states the problem contains, connecting search difficulty to the extent of the promising region.

The second algorithm, SOO, does not need to know the semimetric under which the function is smooth. Its performance is almost as good as that of optimally fitted DOO. The significance is that the algorithm can operate without being given the relevant smoothness geometry. The underlying local-smoothness assumption remains part of the problem setting even though SOO does not require that geometry as an input.
summary.tldr: SOO nearly matches optimally fitted DOO without knowing the semimetric governing local smoothness near a global maximum.

title: Optimistic Optimization of a Deterministic Function without the Knowledge of its Smoothness

abstract: An effective strategy to exploit the supervising side information for discovering predictive topic representations is to impose discriminative constraints induced by such information on the posterior distributions under a topic model. This strategy has been adopted by a number of supervised topic models, such as MedLDA, which employs max-margin posterior constraints. However, unlike the likelihood-based supervised topic models, of which posterior inference can be carried out using the Bayes' rule, the max-margin posterior constraints have made Monte Carlo methods infeasible or at least not directly applicable, thereby limited the choice of inference algorithms to be based on variational approximation with strict mean field assumptions. In this paper, we develop two efficient Monte Carlo methods under much weaker assumptions for max-margin supervised topic models based on an importance sampler and a collapsed Gibbs sampler, respectively, in a convex dual formulation. We report thorough experimental results that compare our approach favorably against existing alternatives in both accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models use side information to learn topic representations that help prediction. One approach imposes maximum-margin constraints on the posterior distribution, as in MedLDA. Those constraints complicate inference: ordinary Bayesian sampling methods are not directly applicable, leaving earlier approaches dependent on variational approximations with strict mean-field assumptions.

The paper develops two Monte Carlo methods through a convex dual formulation. One uses importance sampling, while the other uses collapsed Gibbs sampling. Both operate under much weaker assumptions than the previous mean-field approach. The reformulation provides the route for applying sampling methods to a posterior-learning problem shaped by discriminative constraints.

The authors report extensive experiments comparing the methods favorably with existing alternatives in both accuracy and efficiency. The contribution therefore combines a broader choice of inference techniques with evidence of practical benefits. It shows that maximum-margin supervision and Monte Carlo inference can work together when the problem is formulated appropriately, allowing predictive topic representations to be learned without relying on the same strict approximation structure.
summary.tldr: A convex dual formulation enables two efficient Monte Carlo inference methods for maximum-margin supervised topic models under weaker assumptions.

title: Monte Carlo Methods for Maximum Margin Supervised Topic Models

abstract: Ideas from the image processing literature have recently motivated a new set of clustering algorithms that rely on the concept of total variation. While these algorithms perform well for bi-partitioning tasks, their recursive extensions yield unimpressive results for multiclass clustering tasks. This paper presents a general framework for multiclass total variation clustering that does not rely on recursion. The results greatly outperform previous total variation algorithms and compare well with state-of-the-art NMF approaches.
originalAbstract: Ideas from the image processing literature have recently motivated a new set of clustering algorithms that rely on the concept of total variation. This paper presents a general framework for multiclass total variation clustering that does not rely on recursion. The results greatly outperform previous total variation algorithms and compare well with state-of-the-art NMF approaches.

paragraphs: Total variation ideas from image processing have inspired clustering methods that work well when separating data into two groups. Extending that success to several groups is less straightforward. The paper identifies a weakness in recursive extensions: repeatedly applying a two-way clustering method has produced unimpressive results for multiclass clustering.

The authors introduce a general framework that addresses multiclass total variation clustering without recursion. Its central contribution is to formulate the several-group task directly, rather than obtain it through a succession of binary partitions. This makes the multiclass problem itself the focus of the method and preserves total variation as the organizing idea behind the clustering framework.

The reported results substantially outperform previous total variation algorithms and compare favorably with leading nonnegative matrix factorization approaches. The second comparison places the method alongside a different family of clustering techniques, beyond improvements within total variation alone. These findings support the usefulness of a nonrecursive multiclass formulation in the reported evaluation; the abstract does not claim superiority over every competing clustering approach.
summary.tldr: A direct multiclass total variation framework avoids recursive binary splitting and substantially improves on earlier total variation clustering methods.

title: Multiclass Total Variation Clustering

abstract: We consider the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with a prior distribution on the reward distributions. We are interested in studying prior-free and prior-dependent regret bounds, very much in the same spirit than the usual distribution-free and distribution-dependent bounds for the non-Bayesian stochastic bandit. We first show that Thompson Sampling attains an optimal prior-free bound in the sense that for any prior distribution its Bayesian regret is bounded from above by $14 \sqrt{n K}$. This result is unimprovable in the sense that there exists a prior distribution such that any algorithm has a Bayesian regret bounded from below by $\frac{1}{20} \sqrt{n K}$. We also study the case of priors for the setting of Bubeck et al. [2013] (where the optimal mean is known as well as a lower bound on the smallest gap) and we show that in this case the regret of Thompson Sampling is in fact uniformly bounded over time, thus showing that Thompson Sampling can greatly take advantage of the nice properties of these priors.

paragraphs: This paper studies Thompson sampling for stochastic multi-armed bandits with a prior over reward distributions. It examines both guarantees that hold regardless of the prior and guarantees that exploit particular prior information. The relevant performance quantity is Bayesian regret, which averages the cost of imperfect decisions under the prior.

For any prior, the authors bound Thompson sampling's Bayesian regret by 14 sqrt(nK), with n representing the horizon and K the number of arms. They also show that some prior forces every algorithm to incur Bayesian regret of at least sqrt(nK)/20. Together, the bounds establish the optimal order of the prior-free guarantee, up to constants.

The paper then considers priors for a setting where the optimal reward mean and a lower bound on the smallest gap are known. Under those conditions, Thompson sampling's regret is uniformly bounded over time. This demonstrates how useful prior structure can strengthen the guarantee considerably beyond the general square-root growth bound, while keeping that improvement tied to the specified information.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling has an order-optimal prior-free Bayesian regret bound and time-uniform regret bounds for the specified informative-prior setting.

title: Prior-free and prior-dependent regret bounds for Thompson Sampling

abstract: Infinite mixture models are commonly used for clustering. One can sample from the posterior of mixture assignments by Monte Carlo methods or find its maximum a posteriori solution by optimization. However, in some problems the posterior is diffuse and it is hard to interpret the sampled partitionings. In this paper, we introduce novel statistics based on block sizes for representing sample sets of partitionings and feature allocations. We develop an element-based definition of entropy to quantify segmentation among their elements. Then we propose a simple algorithm called entropy agglomeration (EA) to summarize and visualize this information. Experiments on various infinite mixture posteriors as well as a feature allocation dataset demonstrate that the proposed statistics are useful in practice.

We develop an element-based definition of entropy to quantify segmentation among their elements. Then we propose a simple algorithm called entropy agglomeration (EA) to summarize and visualize this information. Experiments on various infinite mixture posteriors as well as a feature allocation dataset demonstrate that the proposed statistics are useful in practice.

paragraphs: Clustering models can produce many plausible groupings rather than one clear answer. When a mixture model's posterior is diffuse, inspecting sampled partitions can be difficult, and a single most-probable solution may not convey the broader collection. This paper develops statistics for summarizing sets of partitionings and feature allocations.

The proposed statistics are based on block sizes. The authors also introduce an element-based definition of entropy to quantify how elements are segmented. These choices provide a way to describe the information in a collection of groupings, making the sampled results more accessible than a list of separate assignments.

A simple algorithm called entropy agglomeration uses this information to create summaries and visualizations. Experiments examine several infinite-mixture posteriors and a feature-allocation dataset, showing that the statistics are useful in practice. The contribution focuses on interpreting uncertain grouping results after inference: it supplies tools for communicating the structure in a sample set when no single partition provides an easy account of the posterior.
summary.tldr: Block-size statistics and entropy agglomeration summarize and visualize uncertain collections of partitions and feature allocations.

title: Summary Statistics for Partitionings and Feature Allocations

abstract: Runge-Kutta methods are the classic family of solvers for ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and the basis for the state of the art. Like most numerical methods, they return point estimates. We construct a family of probabilistic numerical methods that instead return a Gauss-Markov process defining a probability distribution over the ODE solution. In contrast to prior work, we construct this family such that posterior means match the outputs of the Runge-Kutta family exactly, thus inheriting their proven good properties. Remaining degrees of freedom not identified by the match to Runge-Kutta are chosen such that the posterior probability measure fits the observed structure of the ODE. Our results shed light on the structure of Runge-Kutta solvers from a new direction, provide a richer, probabilistic output, have low computational cost, and raise new research questions.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers for ordinary differential equations commonly return a single estimated solution. This paper constructs solvers that instead return a probability distribution over the solution, represented by a Gauss-Markov process. The aim is to provide a richer numerical output while retaining a close connection to established Runge-Kutta methods.

The construction makes the posterior mean agree exactly with the output of a corresponding Runge-Kutta method. This agreement preserves the proven properties of that numerical estimate within the probabilistic formulation. Matching the mean does not determine every aspect of the distribution, so the authors choose the remaining degrees of freedom to fit the observed structure of the differential equation.

The resulting family combines familiar solution estimates with an additional probabilistic description and is reported to have low computational cost. It also offers a new perspective on the structure of Runge-Kutta solvers. The central contribution is the exact connection between classical numerical outputs and posterior means, together with a way to use the remaining freedom to characterize the solution probabilistically.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic ODE solvers return solution distributions whose posterior means exactly reproduce Runge-Kutta outputs.

title: Probabilistic ODE Solvers with Runge-Kutta Means

abstract: An important problem for both graphics and vision is to synthesize novel views of a 3D object from a single image. This is in particular challenging due to the partial observability inherent in projecting a 3D object onto the image space, and the ill-posedness of inferring object shape and pose. However, we can train a neural network to address the problem if we restrict our attention to specific object classes (in our case faces and chairs) for which we can gather ample training data. In this paper, we propose a novel recurrent convolutional encoder-decoder network that is trained end-to-end on the task of rendering rotated objects starting from a single image. The recurrent structure allows our model to capture long- term dependencies along a sequence of transformations, and we demonstrate the quality of its predictions for human faces on the Multi-PIE dataset and for a dataset of 3D chair models, and also show its ability of disentangling latent data factors without using object class labels.

paragraphs: Inferring an object’s appearance from a new viewpoint is ambiguous because a single image hides parts of its three-dimensional shape. This paper tackles the problem within object classes for which ample training data are available, specifically faces and chairs, rather than claiming unrestricted reconstruction from any photograph.

The proposed model is a recurrent convolutional encoder-decoder trained end to end to render rotated objects starting from one image. Its recurrent structure represents sequences of transformations and captures dependencies across those transformations. The learning setup also aims to separate underlying factors in its latent representation.

The authors demonstrate generated views on human faces from Multi-PIE and on a dataset of three-dimensional chair models. They additionally report disentangling latent factors without object-class labels. The abstract offers qualitative claims about prediction quality but no numerical comparison. The work connects view synthesis with learning representations whose factors can support controlled changes in appearance.
summary.tldr: A recurrent encoder-decoder generates rotated object views from a single image.

title: Weakly-supervised Disentangling with Recurrent Transformations for 3D View Synthesis

abstract: Submodular and supermodular functions have found wide applicability in machine learning, capturing notions such as diversity and regularity, respectively. These notions have deep consequences for optimization, and the problem of (approximately) optimizing submodular functions has received much attention. However, beyond optimization, these notions allow specifying expressive probabilistic models that can be used to quantify predictive uncertainty via marginal inference. Prominent, well-studied special cases include Ising models and determinantal point processes, but the general class of log-submodular and log-supermodular models is much richer and little studied. In this paper, we investigate the use of Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to perform approximate inference in general log-submodular and log-supermodular models. In particular, we consider a simple Gibbs sampling procedure, and establish two sufficient conditions, the first guaranteeing polynomial-time, and the second fast (O(nlogn)) mixing. We also evaluate the efficiency of the Gibbs sampler on three examples of such models, and compare against a recently proposed variational approach.

paragraphs: Submodular and supermodular functions capture ideas such as diversity and regularity. Although they are often studied as optimization objectives, they can also define probability distributions. This paper examines that probabilistic use, where inference can describe predictive uncertainty rather than only return an optimized solution.

The authors study Markov chain Monte Carlo inference for general log-submodular and log-supermodular models, a class extending beyond familiar examples such as Ising models and determinantal point processes. They focus on a simple Gibbs sampler and establish two sufficient conditions for its convergence behavior. One guarantees polynomial-time mixing; the other guarantees the faster O(n log n) mixing rate.

Mixing guarantees explain how quickly sampling approaches the model's target distribution, which matters when samples are used for approximate marginal inference. The conditions therefore identify cases where this straightforward sampler has a computational guarantee, without claiming that all models in the class mix quickly. The authors also evaluate the sampler on three example models and compare it with a recently proposed variational approach.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for efficient Gibbs sampling in general log-submodular and log-supermodular probabilistic models.

title: Sampling from Probabilistic Submodular Models

abstract: We introduce a unifying generalization of the Lovász theta function, and the associated geometric embedding, for graphs with weights on both nodes and edges. We show how it can be computed exactly by semidefinite programming, and how to approximate it using SVM computations. We show how the theta function can be interpreted as a measure of diversity in graphs and use this idea, and the graph embedding in algorithms for Max-Cut, correlation clustering and document summarization, all of which are well represented as problems on weighted graphs.

We show how it can be computed exactly by semidefinite programming, and how to approximate it using SVM computations. We show how the theta function can be interpreted as a measure of diversity in graphs and use this idea, and the graph embedding in algorithms for Max-Cut, correlation clustering and document summarization, all of which are well represented as problems on weighted graphs.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes the Lovász theta function and its associated geometric embedding to graphs with weights on both nodes and edges. The aim is a shared mathematical construction for weighted graph problems. Including both kinds of weights allows the formulation to incorporate information attached to individual nodes as well as their connections.

The authors show that the generalized function can be computed exactly with semidefinite programming. They also provide an approximation route using support vector machine computations. These give two computational ways to access the proposed construction, distinguishing an exact optimization formulation from an approximate method.

The paper interprets the theta function as a measure of graph diversity. It uses that interpretation together with the embedding in algorithms for Max-Cut, correlation clustering, and document summarization. All three are represented as weighted graph problems. The contribution is a unifying representation and computational framework that carries a common notion of diversity into several different algorithmic tasks.
summary.tldr: A weighted generalization of the Lovász theta function supplies a diversity measure and embedding for graph optimization and summarization.

title: Weighted Theta Functions and Embeddings with Applications to Max-Cut, Clustering and Summarization

abstract: One approach to improving the running time of kernel-based methods is to build a small sketch of the kernel matrix and use it in lieu of the full matrix in the machine learning task of interest. Here, we describe a version of this approach that comes with running time guarantees as well as improved guarantees on its statistical performance.By extending the notion of \emph{statistical leverage scores} to the setting of kernel ridge regression, we are able to identify a sampling distribution that reduces the size of the sketch (i.e., the required number of columns to be sampled) to the \emph{effective dimensionality} of the problem. This latter quantity is often much smaller than previous bounds that depend on the \emph{maximal degrees of freedom}. We give an empirical evidence supporting this fact. Our second contribution is to present a fast algorithm to quickly compute coarse approximations to thesescores in time linear in the number of samples. More precisely, the running time of the algorithm is $O(np^2)$ with $p$ only depending on the trace of the kernel matrix and the regularization parameter. This is obtained via a variant of squared length sampling that we adapt to the kernel setting. Lastly, we discuss how this new notion of the leverage of a data point captures a fine notion of the difficulty of the learning problem.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can be accelerated by replacing the full kernel matrix with a smaller sketch formed from sampled columns. This paper asks how to choose those columns so that the sketch remains statistically useful while being inexpensive to construct. It supplies both runtime guarantees and improved guarantees on the resulting statistical performance.

The authors extend statistical leverage scores to kernel ridge regression and use them to define a sampling distribution. With this distribution, the required sketch size depends on the problem's effective dimensionality. That quantity is often much smaller than the maximal degrees of freedom used in earlier bounds, and the paper supplies empirical evidence supporting this potential reduction.

Computing the sampling scores must also be affordable. The paper therefore gives an algorithm for coarse score approximations with runtime O(np²), where p depends only on the kernel matrix trace and the regularization parameter. For fixed p, this is linear in the sample count n. An adapted squared-length sampling method provides the construction, connecting computational savings to a more refined measure of learning difficulty.
summary.tldr: Kernel-specific leverage scores enable smaller kernel sketches with statistical guarantees and an efficient procedure for approximating the sampling scores.

title: Fast Randomized Kernel Ridge Regression with Statistical Guarantees

abstract: Contextual bandits have become popular as they offer a middle ground between very simple approaches based on multi-armed bandits and very complex approaches using the full power of reinforcement learning. They have demonstrated success in web applications and have a rich body of associated theoretical guarantees. Linear models are well understood theoretically and preferred by practitioners because they are not only easily interpretable but also simple to implement and debug. Furthermore, if the linear model is true, we get very strong performance guarantees. Unfortunately, in emerging applications in mobile health, the time-invariant linear model assumption is untenable. We provide an extension of the linear model for contextual bandits that has two parts: baseline reward and treatment effect. We allow the former to be complex but keep the latter simple. We argue that this model is plausible for mobile health applications. At the same time, it leads to algorithms with strong performance guarantees as in the linear model setting, while still allowing for complex nonlinear baseline modeling. Our theory is supported by experiments on data gathered in a recently concluded mobile health study.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using information about the current situation, then learn from the resulting rewards. Linear reward models make these systems relatively interpretable and tractable, with strong guarantees when the model is correct. The paper addresses mobile health settings where assuming that rewards follow an unchanging linear relationship is difficult to justify.

The proposed model separates reward into a baseline component and a treatment effect. The baseline can have complex, nonlinear behavior, while the effect associated with treatment retains a simple form. This separation lets the model accommodate complicated background variation without demanding an equally complicated model of how an intervention changes the outcome.

The authors argue that this structure is plausible for mobile health and derive algorithms with strong performance guarantees comparable in character to those available for linear models. Experiments using data from a mobile health study support the theory. The contribution is a way to preserve useful simplicity in the treatment effect while allowing more flexibility in baseline rewards.
summary.tldr: Separating complex baseline rewards from simple treatment effects gives contextual bandits greater flexibility while retaining strong theoretical guarantees.

title: Action Centered Contextual Bandits

abstract: Multi-agent predictive modeling is an essential step for understanding physical, social and team-play systems. Recently, Interaction Networks (INs) were proposed for the task of modeling multi-agent physical systems. One of the drawbacks of INs is scaling with the number of interactions in the system (typically quadratic or higher order in the number of agents). In this paper we introduce VAIN, a novel attentional architecture for multi-agent predictive modeling that scales linearly with the number of agents. We show that VAIN is effective for multi-agent predictive modeling. Our method is evaluated on tasks from challenging multi-agent prediction domains: chess and soccer, and outperforms competing multi-agent approaches.

Recently, Interaction Networks (INs) were proposed for the task of modeling multi-agent physical systems. One of the drawbacks of INs is scaling with the number of interactions in the system (typically quadratic or higher order in the number of agents). In this paper we introduce VAIN, a novel attentional architecture for multi-agent predictive modeling that scales linearly with the number of agents. We show that VAIN is effective for multi-agent predictive modeling. Our method is evaluated on tasks from challenging multi-agent prediction domains: chess and soccer, and outperforms competing multi-agent approaches.

paragraphs: Predicting a system with many agents requires accounting for their interactions. This challenge appears in physical systems, social behavior, and team play. The paper identifies a scaling problem in Interaction Networks: their computational requirements grow with the number of interactions, which is typically quadratic or higher in the number of agents.

The authors introduce VAIN, an attention-based architecture for multi-agent prediction that scales linearly with the number of agents. This changes how computational requirements grow as the system becomes larger. Attention is central to the proposed architecture, providing a different approach to predictive modeling from one whose cost follows the full interaction count.

The method is evaluated on prediction tasks involving chess and soccer, and it outperforms competing multi-agent approaches in those evaluations. These findings support its effectiveness in challenging domains where multiple participants influence the system's behavior. The contribution combines a favorable scaling property with empirical evidence that the architecture remains useful for multi-agent prediction.
summary.tldr: VAIN uses attention for multi-agent prediction with linear scaling and outperforms competing approaches on chess and soccer tasks.

title: VAIN: Attentional Multi-agent Predictive Modeling

abstract: In this paper, we propose a spatial propagation networks for learning affinity matrix. We show that by constructing a row/column linear propagation model, the spatially variant transformation matrix constitutes an affinity matrix that models dense, global pairwise similarities of an image. Specifically, we develop a three-way connection for the linear propagation model, which (a) formulates a sparse transformation matrix where all elements can be the output from a deep CNN, but (b) results in a dense affinity matrix that is effective to model any task-specific pairwise similarity. Instead of designing the similarity kernels according to image features of two points, we can directly output all similarities in a pure data-driven manner. The spatial propagation network is a generic framework that can be applied to numerous tasks, which traditionally benefit from designed affinity, e.g., image matting, colorization, and guided filtering, to name a few. Furthermore, the model can also learn semantic-aware affinity for high-level vision tasks due to the learning capability of the deep model. We validate the proposed framework by refinement of object segmentation. Experiments on the HELEN face parsing and PASCAL VOC-2012 semantic segmentation tasks show that the spatial propagation network provides general, effective and efficient solutions for generating high-quality segmentation results.

summary.tldr: Spatial propagation turns learned sparse transformations into dense image affinities that effectively refine segmentation.

title: Learning Affinity via Spatial Propagation Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of bandit optimization, inspired by stochastic optimization and online learning problems with bandit feedback. In this problem, the objective is to minimize a global loss function of all the actions, not necessarily a cumulative loss. This framework allows us to study a very general class of problems, with applications in statistics, machine learning, and other fields. To solve this problem, we analyze the Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe algorithm, inspired by techniques for bandits and convex optimization. We give theoretical guarantees for the performance of this algorithm over various classes of functions, and discuss the optimality of these results.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization when decisions provide bandit feedback, meaning the learner receives limited information through its actions. The objective is a global loss depending on all the actions and need not be a sum of individual losses. That distinction expands the framework beyond problems whose success is measured solely by accumulated step-by-step loss.

The authors analyze Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe, an algorithm combining ideas from bandit methods and convex optimization. Its motivation is to bring techniques for decision making with incomplete feedback together with techniques for optimizing a global function. The paper establishes performance guarantees across different classes of objective functions and discusses whether those guarantees are optimal.

The contribution is a theoretical treatment of a broad optimization setting, with potential applications in statistics, machine learning, and other fields. Evaluating a global loss makes the collective effect of the actions central to the problem. The guarantees explain the algorithm's behavior for the function classes considered, while the optimality discussion addresses how close those results are to what can be achieved.
summary.tldr: Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe receives theoretical guarantees for bandit optimization of global losses across several function classes.

title: Fast Rates for Bandit Optimization with Upper-Confidence Frank-Wolfe

abstract: Effective implementations of sampling-based probabilistic inference often require manually constructed, model-specific proposals. Inspired by recent progresses in meta-learning for training learning agents that can generalize to unseen environments, we propose a meta-learning approach to building effective and generalizable MCMC proposals. We parametrize the proposal as a neural network to provide fast approximations to block Gibbs conditionals. The learned neural proposals generalize to occurrences of common structural motifs across different models, allowing for the construction of a library of learned inference primitives that can accelerate inference on unseen models with no model-specific training required. We explore several applications including open-universe Gaussian mixture models, in which our learned proposals outperform a hand-tuned sampler, and a real-world named entity recognition task, in which our sampler yields higher final F1 scores than classical single-site Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Sampling-based probabilistic inference often depends on carefully designed proposals for moving between possible model states. Constructing those proposals by hand for each model can require substantial effort. This paper learns proposal mechanisms that can transfer across models, aiming to reuse inference knowledge wherever common structural patterns appear.

The authors parameterize proposals with neural networks that quickly approximate block Gibbs conditional distributions. These proposals operate on groups of variables and generalize across recurring structural motifs. The resulting idea is a library of learned inference primitives: reusable components that can accelerate inference in previously unseen models without training specifically for each new model.

The paper explores several applications. In open-universe Gaussian mixture models, the learned proposals outperform a manually tuned sampler. In a real-world named entity recognition task, the sampler achieves higher final F1 scores than classical single-site Gibbs sampling. These findings support the usefulness of transferring learned sampling behavior across shared model structures, with benefits demonstrated in both probabilistic modeling and a language task.
summary.tldr: Neural MCMC proposals learned for recurring model structures can accelerate inference on unseen models without model-specific training.

title: Meta-Learning MCMC Proposals

abstract: Communication overhead is a major bottleneck hampering the scalability of distributed machine learning systems. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in using gradient compression to improve the communication efficiency of distributed neural network training. Using 1-bit quantization, signSGD with majority vote achieves a 32x reduction in communication cost. However, its convergence is based on unrealistic assumptions and can diverge in practice. In this paper, we propose a general distributed compressed SGD with Nesterov's momentum. We consider two-way compression, which compresses the gradients both to and from workers. Convergence analysis on nonconvex problems for general gradient compressors is provided. By partitioning the gradient into blocks, a blockwise compressor is introduced such that each gradient block is compressed and transmitted in 1-bit format with a scaling factor, leading to a nearly 32x reduction on communication. Experimental results show that the proposed method converges as fast as full-precision distributed momentum SGD and achieves the same testing accuracy. In particular, on distributed ResNet training with 7 workers on the ImageNet, the proposed algorithm achieves the same testing accuracy as momentum SGD using full-precision gradients, but with $46\%$ less wall clock time.

paragraphs: Distributed neural network training can spend substantial time communicating gradients between workers. Compressing these messages reduces traffic, but compression must still support reliable optimization. The paper notes that signSGD with majority vote offers a 32-fold communication reduction, yet its convergence analysis uses unrealistic assumptions and the method can diverge in practice.

The proposed framework combines compressed stochastic gradient descent with Nesterov momentum and considers compression in both communication directions. Its analysis establishes convergence results for nonconvex problems using general gradient compressors. A specific blockwise compressor partitions the gradient, representing each block with one-bit values and a scaling factor. This achieves nearly a 32-fold reduction in communication.

In the reported experiments, the method matches the convergence speed and testing accuracy of full-precision distributed momentum SGD. For ResNet training on ImageNet with seven workers, it reaches the same testing accuracy with 46% less wall-clock time. This separates the reduction in transmitted information from the measured training speedup: the latter reflects the complete distributed training process.
summary.tldr: Two-way blockwise gradient compression supports distributed momentum training with nearly 32-fold less communication and substantial measured training-time savings.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Blockwise Momentum SGD with Error-Feedback

abstract: We study the recovering bandits problem, a variant of the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem where the expected reward of each arm varies according to some unknown function of the time since the arm was last played. While being a natural extension of the classical bandit problem that arises in many real-world settings, this variation is accompanied by significant difficulties. In particular, methods need to plan ahead and estimate many more quantities than in the classical bandit setting. In this work, we explore the use of Gaussian processes to tackle the estimation and planing problem. We also discuss different regret definitions that let us quantify the performance of the methods. To improve computational efficiency of the methods, we provide an optimistic planning approximation. We complement these discussions with regret bounds and empirical studies.

In particular, methods need to plan ahead and estimate many more quantities than in the classical bandit setting. In this work, we explore the use of Gaussian processes to tackle the estimation and planing problem. We also discuss different regret definitions that let us quantify the performance of the methods. paragraphs: In a recovering bandit problem, the expected reward from an option depends on how long it has been since that option was last selected. The relationship between waiting time and reward is unknown and must be learned. This changes the decision problem because choosing an option now also affects the circumstances under which it can be chosen later.

The learner therefore has to estimate more than one fixed reward value per option and plan beyond the immediate next choice. The paper explores Gaussian processes for learning these unknown reward functions and supporting planning. It also examines different definitions of regret, which provide different ways to quantify the performance of a policy in this evolving setting.

To reduce the computational demands of planning, the authors provide an optimistic approximation. Regret bounds and empirical studies complement the modeling and planning discussion. The contribution addresses the linked challenges of learning how rewards depend on time since use and scheduling future actions accordingly, rather than treating each arm as having a constant expected payoff.
summary.tldr: Recovering bandits use Gaussian processes and optimistic planning to handle rewards that depend on the time since an option was last chosen.

title: Recovering Bandits

abstract: We study the problem of fair binary classification using the notion of Equal Opportunity. It requires the true positive rate to distribute equally across the sensitive groups. Within this setting we show that the fair optimal classifier is obtained by recalibrating the Bayes classifier by a group-dependent threshold. We provide a constructive expression for the threshold. This result motivates us to devise a plug-in classification procedure based on both unlabeled and labeled datasets. While the latter is used to learn the output conditional probability, the former is used for calibration. The overall procedure can be computed in polynomial time and it is shown to be statistically consistent both in terms of the classification error and fairness measure. Finally, we present numerical experiments which indicate that our method is often superior or competitive with the state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets.

This result motivates us to devise a plug-in classification procedure based on both unlabeled and labeled datasets.
