paragraphs: Compressed search indexes make retrieval efficient on large collections, but compression can reduce accuracy in high-dimensional spaces. The paper also identifies a training problem: objectives may omit useful interactions between queries and documents. KDindex addresses both concerns by teaching a lightweight index to reproduce ranking information from a more accurate search model.

The teacher can be a high-precision approximate nearest-neighbor or maximum-inner-product search model, such as a graph-based index. The student receives supervision to preserve the teacher's ordering of the top-k relevant results. This supplies information about query-document relationships. Training also includes reconstruction loss and a strategy for balancing posting lists, helping avoid a trivial outcome in which every candidate is assigned to the same centroid.

Experiments show that KDindex outperforms existing learnable quantization-based indexes. The paper also reports an index that is 40 times lighter than the compared state-of-the-art non-exhaustive methods while maintaining comparable recall. The findings support transferring ranking behavior as a way to improve compressed retrieval without requiring the student to retain the teacher's larger index.
summary.tldr: KDindex distills accurate search rankings into compressed indexes, reporting comparable recall with an index 40 times lighter than the compared non-exhaustive methods.

title: Knowledge Distillation for High Dimensional Search Index

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become increasingly popular in modeling graph-structured data due to their ability to learn node representations by aggregating local structure information. However, it is widely acknowledged that the test graph structure may differ from the training graph structure, resulting in a structure shift. In this paper, we experimentally find that the performance of GNNs drops significantly when the structure shift happens, suggesting that the learned models may be biased towards specific structure patterns. To address this challenge, we propose the Cluster Information Transfer (\textbf{CIT}) mechanism, which can learn invariant representations for GNNs, thereby improving their generalization ability to various and unknown test graphs with structure shift. The CIT mechanism achieves this by combining different cluster information with the nodes while preserving their cluster-independent information. By generating nodes across different clusters, the mechanism significantly enhances the diversity of the nodes and helps GNNs learn the invariant representations. We provide a theoretical analysis of the CIT mechanism, showing that the impact of changing clusters during structure shift can be mitigated after transfer. Additionally, the proposed mechanism is a plug-in that can be easily used to improve existing GNNs. We comprehensively evaluate our proposed method on three typical structure shift scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing GNNs' performance.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn node representations by combining information from local graph structure. That makes a change in structure between training and testing consequential. The authors experimentally observe substantial performance drops under such shifts, suggesting that learned representations can depend too heavily on particular structural patterns present during training.

Their Cluster Information Transfer mechanism combines nodes with information from different clusters while preserving information that is independent of cluster membership. Generating nodes across clusters increases the diversity encountered during learning. The aim is to help the network retain useful node information without tying it so tightly to one cluster’s structural context.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing that transfer can mitigate the effects of changing clusters during structure shift. They also design the mechanism as a plug-in for existing graph neural networks. Evaluations covering three typical structure-shift scenarios demonstrate improved performance, supporting cluster transfer as a way to learn representations that generalize better to unfamiliar graph structures.
summary.tldr: Cluster Information Transfer improves graph neural network generalization by varying cluster context while preserving cluster-independent node information.

title: Learning Invariant Representations of Graph Neural Networks via Cluster Generalization

abstract: Diffusion models have been shown to be capable of generating high-quality images, suggesting that they could contain meaningful internal representations. Unfortunately, the feature maps that encode a diffusion model's internal information are spread not only over layers of the network, but also over diffusion timesteps, making it challenging to extract useful descriptors. We propose Diffusion Hyperfeatures, a framework for consolidating multi-scale and multi-timestep feature maps into per-pixel feature descriptors that can be used for downstream tasks. These descriptors can be extracted for both synthetic and real images using the generation and inversion processes. We evaluate the utility of our Diffusion Hyperfeatures on the task of semantic keypoint correspondence: our method achieves superior performance on the SPair-71k real image benchmark. We also demonstrate that our method is flexible and transferable: our feature aggregation network trained on the inversion features of real image pairs can be used on the generation features of synthetic image pairs with unseen objects and compositions. Our code is available at https://diffusion-hyperfeatures.github.io.

Extracting that information is difficult because it is distributed across both network layers and diffusion timesteps. Diffusion Hyperfeatures combines those scattered feature maps into a descriptor for each pixel, making the representations available for downstream tasks.

The framework aggregates features across multiple scales and timesteps. It can obtain descriptors from synthetic images through generation and from real images through inversion. The paper evaluates the descriptors on semantic keypoint correspondence, where the goal is to match corresponding meaningful points between images. It reports superior performance on the SPair-71k benchmark of real images.

The authors also test whether the learned aggregation transfers between these two feature sources. An aggregation network trained on inversion features from real image pairs can be applied to generation features from synthetic pairs containing unseen objects and compositions. This demonstrates useful flexibility in the evaluated setting: information learned from real-image correspondence can support matching within generated imagery.
summary.tldr: Diffusion Hyperfeatures combines features across layers and timesteps into pixel descriptors that support strong semantic correspondence and transfer to generated images.

title: Diffusion Hyperfeatures: Searching Through Time and Space for Semantic Correspondence

abstract: Parallelization techniques have become ubiquitous for accelerating inference and training of deep neural networks. Despite this, several operations are still performed in a sequential manner. For instance, the forward and backward passes are executed layer-by-layer, and the output of diffusion models is produced by applying a sequence of denoising steps. This sequential approach results in a computational cost proportional to the number of steps involved, presenting a potential bottleneck as the number of steps increases. In this work, we introduce DeepPCR, a novel algorithm which parallelizes typically sequential operations in order to speed up inference and training of neural networks. DeepPCR is based on interpreting a sequence of $L$ steps as the solution of a specific system of equations, which we recover using the Parallel Cyclic Reduction algorithm. This reduces the complexity of computing the sequential operations from $\mathcal{O}(L)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log_2L)$, thus yielding a speedup for large $L$. To verify the theoretical lower complexity of the algorithm, and to identify regimes for speedup, we test the effectiveness of DeepPCR in parallelizing the forward and backward pass in multi-layer perceptrons, and reach speedups of up to $30\times$ for the forward and $200\times$ for the backward pass. We additionally showcase the flexibility of DeepPCR by parallelizing training of ResNets with as many as 1024 layers, and generation in diffusion models, enabling up to $7\times$ faster training and $11\times$ faster generation, respectively, when compared to the sequential approach.

summary.tldr: DeepPCR recasts sequential neural computations as equation systems solvable in parallel, yielding substantial speedups in tested training and generation workloads.

title: DeepPCR: Parallelizing Sequential Operations in Neural Networks

abstract: Proteins play a critical role in carrying out biological functions, and their 3D structures are essential in determining their functions. Accurately predicting the conformation of protein side-chains given their backbones is important for applications in protein structure prediction, design and protein-protein interactions. Traditional methods are computationally intensive and have limited accuracy, while existing machine learning methods treat the problem as a regression task and overlook the restrictions imposed by the constant covalent bond lengths and angles. In this work, we present DiffPack, a torsional diffusion model that learns the joint distribution of side-chain torsional angles, the only degrees of freedom in side-chain packing, by diffusing and denoising on the torsional space. To avoid issues arising from simultaneous perturbation of all four torsional angles, we propose autoregressively generating the four torsional angles from $\chi_1$ to $\chi_4$ and training diffusion models for each torsional angle. We evaluate the method on several benchmarks for protein side-chain packing and show that our method achieves improvements of 11.9% and 13.5% in angle accuracy on CASP13 and CASP14, respectively, with a significantly smaller model size ($60\times$ fewer parameters). Additionally, we show the effectiveness of our method in enhancing side-chain predictions in the AlphaFold2 model. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/DiffPack.

paragraphs: DiffPack predicts protein side-chain configurations when the protein backbone is given. The paper emphasizes that this geometry has strong constraints: covalent bond lengths and bond angles are fixed, leaving torsional angles as the adjustable quantities. Learning directly in that space addresses restrictions that existing regression-based machine-learning approaches overlook.

The model learns a joint distribution over side-chain torsional angles through a diffusion process that adds and removes noise in torsional space. Rather than perturbing all four angles simultaneously, it generates them sequentially, from χ1 through χ4. Separate diffusion models for the angles support this autoregressive construction and avoid the issues associated with changing every angle at once.

On side-chain packing benchmarks, the authors report angle-accuracy improvements of 11.9% on CASP13 and 13.5% on CASP14, together with a model using 60 times fewer parameters. They also demonstrate improvements to AlphaFold2 side-chain predictions. These findings support representing the prediction problem through its geometric degrees of freedom and generating their dependencies sequentially.
summary.tldr: DiffPack generates protein side-chain torsional angles sequentially with diffusion, improving benchmark accuracy with substantially fewer model parameters.

title: DiffPack: A Torsional Diffusion Model for Autoregressive Protein Side-Chain Packing

abstract: Finding classifiers robust to adversarial examples is critical for their safedeployment. Determining the robustness of the best possible classifier under agiven threat model for a fixed data distribution and comparing it to thatachieved by state-of-the-art training methods is thus an important diagnostictool. In this paper, we find achievable information-theoretic lower bounds onrobust loss in the presence of a test-time attacker for *multi-classclassifiers on any discrete dataset*. We provide a general framework for findingthe optimal $0-1$ loss that revolves around the construction of a conflicthypergraph from the data and adversarial constraints. The prohibitive cost ofthis formulation in practice leads us to formulate other variants of the attacker-classifiergame that more efficiently determine the range of the optimal loss. Ourvaluation shows, for the first time, an analysis of the gap to optimalrobustness for classifiers in the multi-class setting on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Evaluating adversarial robustness requires knowing how much robustness is possible for the data and allowed attacks. A classifier’s errors may reflect weaknesses in training, but some errors may remain unavoidable even for the best possible classifier. This paper studies that distinction for classification with multiple classes and a test-time attacker.

The authors construct a conflict hypergraph from a discrete dataset and the attacker’s permitted changes. This structure represents conflicts that constrain robust classification and supports a general formulation of the optimal 0–1 loss, which counts incorrect predictions. The framework yields achievable information-theoretic lower bounds for multi-class classifiers on any discrete dataset.

Computing the full formulation is prohibitively expensive in practice. The paper therefore develops alternative attacker–classifier games that more efficiently bound the range containing the optimum. Evaluations on benchmark datasets use these results to analyze the gap between trained classifiers and optimal robustness. This makes the framework a diagnostic tool for separating training shortcomings from limits imposed by the classification problem.
summary.tldr: A conflict-hypergraph framework characterizes optimal adversarial classification loss and helps measure how far trained multi-class classifiers fall short.

title: Characterizing the Optimal $0-1$ Loss for Multi-class Classification with a Test-time Attacker

abstract: For embodied reinforcement learning (RL) agents interacting with the environment, it is desirable to have rapid policy adaptation to unseen visual observations, but achieving zero-shot adaptation capability is considered as a challenging problem in the RL context. To address the problem, we present a novel contrastive prompt ensemble (ConPE) framework which utilizes a pretrained vision-language model and a set of visual prompts, thus enables efficient policy learning and adaptation upon a wide range of environmental and physical changes encountered by embodied agents. Specifically, we devise a guided-attention-based ensemble approach with multiple visual prompts on the vision-language model to construct robust state representations. Each prompt is contrastively learned in terms of an individual domain factors that significantly affects the agent's egocentric perception and observation. For a given task, the attention-based ensemble and policy are jointly learned so that the resulting state representations not only generalize to various domains but are also optimized for learning the task. Through experiments, we show that ConPE outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms for several embodied agent tasks including navigation in AI2THOR, manipulation in Metaworld, and autonomous driving in CARLA, while also improving the sample efficiency of policy learning and adaptation.

paragraphs: An embodied agent must act on what it sees, so environmental or physical changes can alter the observations on which its policy depends. This paper addresses efficient policy learning and adaptation to such changes. Its Contrastive Prompt Ensemble framework, ConPE, combines a pretrained vision-language model with multiple learned visual prompts to construct more robust state representations.

Each prompt is trained contrastively around an individual domain factor that affects the agent's first-person observations. A guided attention mechanism combines the prompts. For a particular task, the attention-based ensemble and the policy are learned together, allowing the representation to reflect both variation across domains and information useful for choosing task-relevant actions.

Experiments cover navigation in AI2THOR, manipulation in Metaworld, and autonomous driving in CARLA. The authors report that ConPE outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms in these settings while improving the sample efficiency of policy learning and adaptation. The findings support combining factor-focused prompts with task-specific attention as a practical route toward adaptation across changing visual conditions.
summary.tldr: ConPE combines contrastively learned visual prompts through task-trained attention to improve embodied agents' policy performance and adaptation efficiency.

title: Efficient Policy Adaptation with Contrastive Prompt Ensemble for Embodied Agents

abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) is sensitive to spurious correlations present in training data, which poses a significant risk when deploying systems trained under this paradigm in high-stake applications. While the existing literature focuses on maximizing group-balanced or worst-group accuracy, estimating these quantities is hindered by costly bias annotations. This study contends that current bias-unsupervised approaches to group robustness continue to rely on group information to achieve optimal performance. Firstly, these methods implicitly assume that all group combinations are represented during training. To illustrate this, we introduce a systematic generalization task on the MPI3D dataset and discover that current algorithms fail to improve the ERM baseline when combinations of observed attribute values are missing. Secondly, bias labels are still crucial for effective model selection, restricting the practicality of these methods in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a revised methodology for training and validating debiased models in an entirely bias-unsupervised manner. We achieve this by employing pretrained self-supervised models to reliably extract bias information, which enables the integration of a logit adjustment training loss with our validation criterion. Our empirical analysis on synthetic and real-world tasks provides evidence that our approach overcomes the identified challenges and consistently enhances robust accuracy, attaining performance which is competitive with or outperforms that of state-of-the-art methods, which, conversely, rely on bias labels for validation.

This study contends that current bias-unsupervised approaches to group robustness continue to rely on group information to achieve optimal performance. Firstly, these methods implicitly assume that all group combinations are represented during training. To illustrate this, we introduce a systematic generalization task on the MPI3D dataset and discover that current algorithms fail to improve the ERM baseline when combinations of observed attribute values are missing. Secondly, bias labels are still crucial for effective model selection, restricting the practicality of these methods in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a revised methodology for training and validating debiased models in an entirely bias-unsupervised manner. We achieve this by employing pretrained self-supervised models to reliably extract bias information, which enables the integration of a logit adjustment training loss with our validation criterion. Our empirical analysis on synthetic and real-world tasks provides evidence that our approach overcomes the identified challenges and consistently enhances robust accuracy, attaining performance which is competitive with or outperforms that of state-of-the-art methods, which, conversely, rely on bias labels for validation.

paragraphs: Classifiers trained to minimize average error can exploit spurious correlations that fail for particular groups. Methods intended to address this without bias annotations may still depend on group information indirectly. This paper identifies two such dependencies: assuming every combination of groups appears during training and using bias labels to select the final model.

The authors introduce a generalization task on MPI3D in which some combinations of observed attribute values are absent. Existing methods fail to improve on ordinary empirical risk minimization in this setting. This test exposes a gap between handling represented groups and generalizing to combinations missing from the training data.

The proposed method uses pretrained self-supervised models to extract bias information without supplied bias labels. That information supports both an adjustment to the training logits and a validation criterion. Experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks show improved robust accuracy and performance competitive with, or better than, methods that use bias labels for validation. The contribution therefore addresses both model training and the often-overlooked process of choosing a model.
summary.tldr: The paper uses self-supervised representations to train and select group-robust classifiers without supplied bias labels, including when attribute combinations are missing.

title: Group Robust Classification Without Any Group Information

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel extra-gradient difference acceleration algorithm for solving constrained nonconvex-nonconcave (NC-NC) minimax problems. In particular, we design a new extra-gradient difference step to obtain an important quasi-cocoercivity property, which plays a key role to significantly improve the convergence rate in the constrained NC-NC setting without additional structural assumption. Then momentum acceleration is also introduced into our dual accelerating update step. Moreover, we prove that, to find an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the function $f$, our algorithm attains the complexity $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ in the constrained NC-NC setting, while the best-known complexity bound is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4})$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic factors compared to $\mathcal{O}(\cdot)$. As the special cases of the constrained NC-NC setting, our algorithm can also obtain the same complexity $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ for both the nonconvex-concave (NC-C) and convex-nonconcave (C-NC) cases, while the best-known complexity bounds are $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2.5})$ for the NC-C case and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4})$ for the C-NC case. For fair comparison with existing algorithms, we also analyze the complexity bound to find $\epsilon$-stationary point of the primal function $\phi$ for the constrained NC-C problem, which shows that our algorithm can improve the complexity bound from $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the proposed algorithm improves the best-known complexity bounds from $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ in both the NC-NC and NC-C settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies constrained minimax optimization, where one set of variables seeks to minimize an objective while another seeks to maximize it. Its main setting allows the objective to be nonconvex in the minimizing variables and nonconcave in the maximizing variables. The goal is to reach an approximately stationary point, rather than establish a globally optimal solution.

The proposed single-loop algorithm combines a new extra-gradient difference step with momentum in its dual update. The difference step establishes a mathematical property called quasi-cocoercivity, which supports the improved convergence analysis. The authors obtain this improvement without adding a structural assumption to the constrained nonconvex-nonconcave setting they consider.

For an epsilon-stationary point of the objective f, the stated complexity improves from roughly epsilon to the power minus four to epsilon to the power minus two. The algorithm also achieves the latter rate in the two partially convex special cases. Separately, for the primal function in the nonconvex-concave setting, it improves the previous roughly inverse-cubic bound to an inverse-square bound. These results distinguish guarantees for two different stationarity targets.
summary.tldr: A single-loop minimax algorithm combines an extra-gradient difference step with momentum to improve stated complexity bounds for approximate stationarity.

title: A Single-Loop Accelerated Extra-Gradient Difference Algorithm with Improved Complexity Bounds for Constrained Minimax Optimization

abstract: The classical analysis of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with polynomially decaying stepsize $\eta_t = \eta/\sqrt{t}$ relies on well-tuned $\eta$ depending on problem parameters such as Lipschitz smoothness constant, which is often unknown in practice. In this work, we prove that SGD with arbitrary $\eta > 0$, referred to as untuned SGD, still attains an order-optimal convergence rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/4})$ in terms of gradient norm for minimizing smooth objectives. Unfortunately, it comes at the expense of a catastrophic exponential dependence on the smoothness constant, which we show is unavoidable for this scheme even in the noiseless setting. We then examine three families of adaptive methods — Normalized SGD (NSGD), AMSGrad, and AdaGrad — unveiling their power in preventing such exponential dependency in the absence of information about the smoothness parameter and boundedness of stochastic gradients. Our results provide theoretical justification for the advantage of adaptive methods over untuned SGD in alleviating the issue with large gradients.

paragraphs: Standard analyses of stochastic gradient descent often assume its learning-rate scale is tuned using properties of the objective, such as a smoothness constant that may be unknown. This paper studies what happens when the stepsize decreases as η divided by the square root of the iteration number, but η is any positive value.

For smooth objectives, the authors prove that this untuned SGD scheme still achieves an order-optimal gradient-norm convergence rate of approximately T to the minus one-quarter, up to logarithmic factors. However, the bound has an exponential dependence on the smoothness constant. They show that this dependence is unavoidable for the scheme, even when gradients contain no stochastic noise.

The paper then analyzes Normalized SGD, AMSGrad, and AdaGrad. These adaptive method families avoid that exponential dependence without requiring knowledge of the smoothness parameter or bounded stochastic gradients. The results explain why an attractive iteration-rate exponent alone can hide severe optimization costs. They also provide theoretical support for using adaptive methods to handle large gradients when the information needed to tune ordinary SGD is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Untuned SGD retains an optimal rate exponent but suffers unavoidable exponential smoothness dependence that the analyzed adaptive methods avoid.

title: Two Sides of One Coin: the Limits of Untuned SGD and the Power of Adaptive Methods

abstract: In recent years, the integration of vision and language understanding has led to significant advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly through Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, existing VLMs face challenges in handling real-world applications with complex scenes and multiple objects, as well as aligning their focus with the diverse attention patterns of human users. In this paper, we introduce gaze information, feasibly collected by ubiquitous wearable devices such as MR glasses, as a proxy for human attention to guide VLMs. We propose a novel approach, Voila-A, for gaze alignment to enhance the effectiveness of these models in real-world applications. First, we collect hundreds of minutes of gaze data to demonstrate that we can mimic human gaze modalities using localized narratives. We then design an automatic data annotation pipeline utilizing GPT-4 to generate the VOILA-COCO dataset. Additionally, we introduce a new model VOILA-A that integrate gaze information into VLMs while maintain pretrained knowledge from webscale dataset. We evaluate Voila-A using a hold-out validation set and a newly collected VOILA-GAZE testset, which features real-life scenarios captured with a gaze-tracking device. Our experimental results demonstrate that Voila-A significantly outperforms several baseline models. By aligning model attention with human gaze patterns, Voila-A paves the way for more intuitive, user-centric VLMs and fosters engaging human-AI interaction across a wide range of applications.

The paper considers gaze collected through wearable devices, including mixed-reality glasses, as a practical source of this guidance.

Voila-A significantly outperforms several baselines in these experiments. The findings support gaze as useful context for aligning model focus with users, making attention-sensitive interaction a concrete modeling and data-construction problem.
summary.tldr: Voila-A incorporates gaze into vision-language models to better align their focus with users and improves performance on the reported evaluations.

title: Voila-A: Aligning Vision-Language Models with User's Gaze Attention

abstract: Leveraging the depth and flexibility of XLand as well as the rapid prototyping features of the Unity engine, we present the United Unity Universe — an open-source toolkit designed to accelerate the creation of innovative reinforcement learning environments. This toolkit includes a robust implementation of XLand 2.0 complemented by a user-friendly interface which allows users to modify the details of procedurally generated terrains and task rules with ease. Additionally, we provide a curated selection of terrains and rule sets, accompanied by implementations of reinforcement learning baselines to facilitate quick experimentation with novel architectural designs for adaptive agents. Furthermore, we illustrate how the United Unity Universe serves as a high-level language that enables researchers to develop diverse and endlessly variable 3D environments within a unified framework. This functionality establishes the United Unity Universe (U3) as an essential tool for advancing the field of reinforcement learning, especially in the development of adaptive and generalizable learning systems.

paragraphs: Developing adaptive reinforcement-learning agents requires environments that can vary in layout and task rules. Building those environments can itself consume substantial research effort. United Unity Universe, or U3, is an open-source toolkit intended to make environment creation and experimentation easier by combining XLand's flexibility with Unity's rapid-prototyping capabilities.

The toolkit includes an implementation of XLand 2.0 and an interface for modifying procedurally generated terrains and rules. It also supplies a curated set of terrains and rule sets, together with reinforcement-learning baseline implementations. These components give researchers starting environments and reference agents so they can move more directly into experiments with new agent architectures.

The authors present U3 as a high-level language for constructing diverse, continually variable three-dimensional environments within one framework. Its contribution is research infrastructure: it makes variation in environments and tasks easier to express and reuse. The intended benefit is faster experimentation on adaptive and generalizable learning systems, with the toolkit supporting the creation of the settings in which those capabilities can be studied.
summary.tldr: U3 combines XLand 2.0 and Unity into an open-source toolkit for rapidly building varied 3D reinforcement-learning environments.

title: Using Unity to Help Solve Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Phenotype imputation plays a crucial role in improving comprehensive and accurate medical evaluation, which in turn can optimize patient treatment and bolster the reliability of clinical research. Despite the adoption of various techniques, multi-modal biological data, which can provide crucial insights into a patient's overall health, is often overlooked. With multi-modal biological data, patient characterization can be enriched from two distinct views: the biological view and the phenotype view. However, the heterogeneity and imprecise nature of the multimodal data still pose challenges in developing an effective method to model from two views. In this paper, we propose a novel framework to incorporate multi-modal biological data via view decoupling. Specifically, we segregate the modeling of biological data from phenotype data in a graph-based learning framework. From the biological view, the latent factors in biological data are discovered to model patient correlation. From the phenotype view, phenotype co-occurrence can be modeled to reveal patterns across patients. Then patients are encoded from these two distinct views. To mitigate the influence of noise and irrelevant information in biological data, we devise a cross-view contrastive knowledge distillation aimed at distilling insights from the biological view to enhance phenotype imputation. We show that phenotype imputation with the proposed model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art models on the real-world biomedical database.

paragraphs: This paper estimates missing phenotype information by incorporating multiple forms of biological data. Such data can enrich patient characterization, but their heterogeneity and imprecision make them difficult to combine effectively. The proposed framework separates biological information and phenotype information into two views instead of treating them as one undifferentiated source.

A graph-based learning framework models each view separately. In the biological view, latent factors reveal relationships among patients. In the phenotype view, patterns of phenotype co-occurrence reveal structure across patients. The model then encodes patients from both perspectives, preserving the distinct kinds of relationships each source contributes.

This transfers useful insights from the biological view to support phenotype imputation. On a real-world biomedical database, the proposed model significantly outperforms leading comparison models. The result supports separating the views during modeling and selectively transferring their information for the specific task of filling in missing phenotypes.
summary.tldr: Separately modeling biological and phenotype relationships, then transferring useful information between them, improves missing-phenotype prediction.

title: Unified Insights: Harnessing Multi-modal Data for Phenotype Imputation via View Decoupling

abstract: Recent advances in data-driven imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning have highlighted the use of expert data for skill acquisition and the development of hierarchical policies based on these skills. However, these approaches have not significantly advanced in adapting these skills to unseen contexts, which may involve changing environmental conditions or different user requirements. In this paper, we present a novel LLM-based policy adaptation framework LDuS which leverages an LLM to guide the generation process of a skill diffusion model upon contexts specified in language, facilitating zero-shot skill-based policy adaptation to different contexts. To implement the skill diffusion model, we adapt the loss-guided diffusion with a sequential in-painting technique, where target trajectories are conditioned by masking them with past state-action sequences, thereby enabling the robust and controlled generation of skill trajectories in test-time. To have a loss function for a given context, we employ the LLM-based code generation with iterative refinement, by which the code and controlled trajectory are validated to align with the context in a closed-loop manner. Through experiments, we demonstrate the zero-shot adaptability of LDuS to various context types including different specification levels, multi-modality, and varied temporal conditions for several robotic manipulation tasks, outperforming other language-conditioned imitation and planning methods.

LDuS addresses this problem by using language descriptions of a new context to guide a skill diffusion model. The approach connects a language-level requirement to trajectory generation through an executable objective, allowing the requested context to influence how an acquired skill is expressed at test time.
summary.tldr: LDuS uses language-model-generated objectives to guide skill diffusion and adapt robotic policies to new contexts at test time.

title: LLM-based Skill Diffusion for Zero-shot Policy Adaptation

abstract: We introduce DataComp for Language Models, a testbed for controlled dataset experiments with the goal of improving language models.As part of DCLM, we provide a standardized corpus of 240T tokens extracted from Common Crawl, effective pretraining recipes based on the OpenLM framework, and a broad suite of 53 downstream evaluations.Participants in the DCLM benchmark can experiment with data curation strategies such as deduplication, filtering, and data mixing atmodel scales ranging from 412M to 7B parameters.As a baseline for DCLM, we conduct extensive experiments and find that model-based filtering is key to assembling a high-quality training set.The resulting dataset, DCLM-Baseline, enables training a 7B parameter language model from scratch to 63% 5-shot accuracy on MMLU with 2T training tokens.Compared to MAP-Neo, the previous state-of-the-art in open-data language models, DCLM-Baseline represents a 6 percentage point improvement on MMLU while being trained with half the compute.Our results highlight the importance of dataset design for training language models and offer a starting point for further research on data curation. We release the \dclm benchmark, framework, models, and datasets at https://www.datacomp.ai/dclm/

paragraphs: DataComp-LM provides a controlled setting for studying how training-data choices affect language models. It supplies a Common Crawl corpus containing 240 trillion tokens, pretraining recipes based on OpenLM, and 53 downstream evaluations. Researchers can investigate deduplication, filtering, and data mixing at model sizes from 412 million to 7 billion parameters.

The shared setup makes dataset curation the central experimental variable. In their baseline experiments, the authors find model-based filtering to be a key ingredient for constructing a high-quality training set. Their resulting DCLM-Baseline dataset supports training a 7-billion-parameter model from scratch with 2 trillion training tokens.

That model reaches 63% accuracy on MMLU in a five-shot evaluation. Compared with MAP-Neo, described in the abstract as the previous leader among open-data language models, this is a six-percentage-point improvement using half the compute. These results support the practical importance of dataset design, while the released benchmark, models, framework, and datasets give subsequent curation research a common starting point.
summary.tldr: DataComp-LM standardizes language-model data experiments and demonstrates strong results from a training set built with model-based filtering.

title: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models

abstract: When applying reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the reward is learned from data and, therefore, always has some error. It is common to mitigate this by regularizing the policy with KL divergence from a base model, with the hope that balancing reward with regularization will achieve desirable outcomes despite this reward misspecification. We show that when the reward function has light-tailed error, optimal policies under less restrictive KL penalties achieve arbitrarily high utility. However, if error is heavy-tailed, some policies obtain arbitrarily high reward despite achieving no more utility than the base model--a phenomenon we call catastrophic Goodhart. We adapt a discrete optimization method to measure the tails of reward models, finding that they are consistent with light-tailed error. However, the pervasiveness of heavy-tailed distributions in many real-world applications indicates that future sources of RL reward could have heavy-tailed error, increasing the likelihood of reward hacking even with KL regularization.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback optimizes a learned reward that inevitably contains some error. A common safeguard penalizes departures from a base model using KL divergence. The hope is that this penalty will keep reward optimization connected to actual utility, even when the reward model is imperfect.

The paper shows that the behavior of rare, extreme reward errors matters. With light-tailed error, optimal policies under progressively less restrictive KL penalties achieve arbitrarily high utility. With heavy-tailed error, however, some policies can achieve arbitrarily high measured reward while delivering no more utility than the base model. The authors call this separation catastrophic Goodhart.

The authors also adapt a discrete optimization method to investigate reward-model tails. Their measurements are consistent with light-tailed error, so the empirical result does not establish the catastrophic case for those models. The broader warning concerns possible future reward sources: heavy-tailed misspecification can permit severe reward hacking despite KL regularization.
summary.tldr: KL regularization can fail to prevent arbitrarily inflated reward without utility gains when reward errors are heavy-tailed.

title: Catastrophic Goodhart: regularizing RLHF with KL divergence does not mitigate heavy-tailed reward misspecification

abstract: The Lion optimizer has been a promising competitor with the AdamW for training large AI models, with advantages in memory, computation, and sample efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Distributed Lion, an innovative adaptation of Lion for distributed training environments. Leveraging the sign operator in Lion, our Distributed Lion only requires to communicate binary or lower-precision vectorsbetween workers to the center server, significantly reducing the communication cost. Our theoretical analysis confirms Distributed Lion's convergence properties. Empirical results demonstrate its robustness across a range of tasks, worker counts, and batch sizes, on both vision and language problems. Notably, Distributed Lion attains comparable performance to standard Lion or AdamW optimizers applied on aggregated gradients, but with significantly reduced communication bandwidth. This feature is particularly advantageous for training large models. In addition, we also demonstrate that \mavolion{} presents a more favorable performance-bandwidth balance compared to existing efficient distributed methods such as deep gradient compression and ternary gradients.

paragraphs: Distributed training requires workers to exchange information so they can jointly update a model. This communication can be expensive for large models. The paper introduces Distributed Lion, an adaptation of the Lion optimizer that reduces the amount of information workers send to a central server. It builds on the sign operation already used by Lion.

Using that operation, workers can communicate binary or other lower-precision vectors. The method therefore targets the communication cost of coordinating updates while retaining an optimizer suitable for distributed training. The authors provide a theoretical analysis establishing convergence properties and empirically examine behavior across different tasks, numbers of workers, and batch sizes.

On the tested vision and language problems, Distributed Lion achieves performance comparable to standard Lion or AdamW operating on aggregated gradients, while requiring substantially less communication bandwidth. The paper also reports a more favorable performance–bandwidth balance than deep gradient compression and ternary-gradient methods. These findings support the usefulness of designing distributed optimization around compact updates.
summary.tldr: Distributed Lion reduces training communication through binary or lower-precision updates while retaining comparable performance in the evaluated vision and language tasks.

title: Communication Efficient Distributed Training with Distributed Lion

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated proficiency in utilizing various tools by coding, yet they face limitations in handling intricate logic and precise control. In embodied tasks, high-level planning is amenable to direct coding, while low-level actions often necessitate task-specific refinement, such as Reinforcement Learning (RL). To seamlessly integrate both modalities, we introduce a two-level hierarchical framework, RL-GPT, comprising a slow agent and a fast agent. The slow agent analyzes actions suitable for coding, while the fast agent executes coding tasks. This decomposition effectively focuses each agent on specific tasks, proving highly efficient within our pipeline. Our approach outperforms traditional RL methods and existing GPT agents, demonstrating superior efficiency. In the Minecraft game, it rapidly obtains diamonds within a single day on an RTX3090. Additionally, it achieves SOTA performance across all designated MineDojo tasks.

The paper’s motivation is that high-level planning lends itself to direct coding, while low-level actions often benefit from task-specific learning.

The framework organizes this combination through two agents operating at different levels. A slow agent analyzes which actions are suitable for coding, and a fast agent carries out the coding tasks. This division gives each agent a more focused responsibility within the overall pipeline, providing a structure for integrating planning through code with refinement through reinforcement learning.

The authors report greater efficiency than traditional reinforcement-learning methods and existing GPT agents. In Minecraft, the system obtains diamonds within a single day using an RTX3090, and it achieves leading performance across all designated MineDojo tasks. These results support the proposed decomposition in the evaluated environments, showing how coded planning and learned control can contribute within one framework.
summary.tldr: RL-GPT combines hierarchical coding agents with reinforcement learning to improve efficiency on embodied tasks, including Minecraft and designated MineDojo evaluations.

title: RL-GPT: Integrating Reinforcement Learning and Code-as-policy

abstract: Detecting Human-Object Interactions (HOI) in zero-shot settings, where models must handle unseen classes, poses significant challenges. Existing methods that rely on aligning visual encoders with large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to tap into the extensive knowledge of VLMs, require large, computationally expensive models and encounter training difficulties. Adapting VLMs with prompt learning offers an alternative to direct alignment. However, fine-tuning on task-specific datasets often leads to overfitting to seen classes and suboptimal performance on unseen classes, due to the absence of unseen class labels. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel prompt learning-based framework for Efficient Zero-Shot HOI detection (EZ-HOI). First, we introduce Large Language Model (LLM) and VLM guidance for learnable prompts, integrating detailed HOI descriptions and visual semantics to adapt VLMs to HOI tasks. However, because training datasets contain seen-class labels alone, fine-tuning VLMs on such datasets tends to optimize learnable prompts for seen classes instead of unseen ones. Therefore, we design prompt learning for unseen classes using information from related seen classes, with LLMs utilized to highlight the differences between unseen and related seen classes. Quantitative evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our EZ-HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance across various zero-shot settings with only 10.35\% to 33.95\% of the trainable parameters compared to existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ChelsieLei/EZ-HOI.

EZ-HOI guides learnable prompts using both language-model descriptions and vision-language-model semantics. Detailed descriptions explain the interactions, while visual semantics help adapt the prompts to the detection task. The framework also explicitly develops prompts for unseen classes by drawing on related seen classes. Language models highlight differences between the related classes so that this transfer preserves distinctions needed for recognition.

Benchmark evaluations report state-of-the-art results across multiple zero-shot settings. EZ-HOI uses between 10.35% and 33.95% of the trainable parameters used by the compared methods. These findings support guided prompt adaptation as an efficient way to transfer vision-language knowledge, with explicit attention to unseen classes helping counter the tendency of task-specific training to favor only labeled interactions.
summary.tldr: EZ-HOI uses guided prompts for seen and unseen interaction classes to improve zero-shot detection with substantially fewer trainable parameters.

title: EZ-HOI: VLM Adaptation via Guided Prompt Learning for Zero-Shot HOI Detection

abstract: Originally proposed for handling time series data, Auto-regressive Decision Trees (ARDTs) have not yet been explored for language modeling. This paper delves into both the theoretical and practical applications of ARDTs in this new context. We theoretically demonstrate that ARDTs can compute complex functions, such as simulating automata, Turing machines, and sparse circuits, by leveraging "chain-of-thought" computations. Our analysis provides bounds on the size, depth, and computational efficiency of ARDTs, highlighting their surprising computational power. Empirically, we train ARDTs on simple language generation tasks, showing that they can learn to generate coherent and grammatically correct text on par with a smaller Transformer model. Additionally, we show that ARDTs can be used on top of transformer representations to solve complex reasoning tasks. This research reveals the unique computational abilities of ARDTs, aiming to broaden the architectural diversity in language model development.

paragraphs: This paper studies autoregressive decision trees as an architecture for language modeling. These trees were originally proposed for time-series problems, but the authors examine both what they can compute through sequential generation and what they can learn in language tasks. The work combines theoretical expressiveness results with practical experiments.

The analysis shows that intermediate chain-of-thought computations allow these models to simulate automata, Turing machines, and sparse circuits. It also bounds the tree size, depth, and computational resources involved. These results explain how sequential computation can give decision-tree models substantial expressive power, even though their building blocks differ from those of transformers.

In experiments on simple language-generation tasks, trained trees produce coherent, grammatically correct text at a level comparable to a smaller transformer. The authors also show that trees placed on top of transformer representations can solve complex reasoning tasks. The empirical comparison is specific to the reported tasks, while the broader contribution is to establish autoregressive trees as a computationally capable alternative worth exploring in language-model architecture.
summary.tldr: Autoregressive decision trees show strong theoretical computational abilities and promising results on simple text generation and reasoning over transformer representations.

title: On the Power of Decision Trees in Auto-Regressive Language Modeling

abstract: In this work, we empirically confirm that the key reason causing such an issue is that the training images are usually paired with short captions, leaving certain tokens easily overshadowed by salient tokens. Towards this problem, our initial attempt is to relabel the data with long captions, however, directly learning with which may lead to performance degradation in understanding short text (e.g., in the image classification task). Then, after incorporating corner tokens to aggregate diverse textual information, we manage to help the model catch up to its original level of short text understanding yet greatly enhance its capability of long text understanding. We further look into whether the model can continuously benefit from longer captions and notice a clear trade-off between the performance and the efficiency. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach using a self-constructed large-scale dataset, which consists of 100M long caption oriented text-image pairs. Our method achieves superior performance in long-text-image retrieval tasks. The project page is available at https://wuw2019.github.io/lot-lip.

paragraphs: LoTLIP studies how language–image pretraining can better handle long descriptions. The authors empirically identify short training captions as a key cause of weak long-text understanding: prominent tokens can overshadow other textual information. Simply replacing short captions with longer ones does not fully solve the problem, because it can reduce performance on short-text tasks such as image classification.

The proposed approach adds corner tokens that aggregate diverse textual information. With these tokens, the model recovers its original short-text understanding while substantially improving its handling of long text. The intervention therefore addresses both the richer training descriptions and the model’s ability to collect information from them.

The authors further examine increasing caption length and observe a clear trade-off between performance and efficiency. They validate the approach on a self-constructed collection of 100 million image–text pairs oriented toward long captions, reporting superior long-text image retrieval performance. The findings show that benefiting from richer descriptions depends on how textual information is aggregated, alongside the amount of text provided during training.
summary.tldr: LoTLIP combines long captions with information-aggregating corner tokens to improve long-text image understanding while recovering short-text performance.

title: LoTLIP: Improving Language-Image Pre-training for Long Text Understanding

abstract: Agda is a dependently-typed programming language and a proof assistant, pivotal in proof formalization and programming language theory.This paper extends the Agda ecosystem into machine learning territory, and, vice versa, makes Agda-related resources available to machine learning practitioners.We introduce and release a novel dataset of Agda program-proofs that is elaborate and extensive enough to support various machine learning applications -- the first of its kind.Leveraging the dataset's ultra-high resolution, which details proof states at the sub-type level, we propose a novel neural architecture targeted at faithfully representing dependently-typed programs on the basis of structural rather than nominal principles.We instantiate and evaluate our architecture in a premise selection setup, where it achieves promising initial results, surpassing strong baselines.

paragraphs: Dependently typed programs encode rich relationships between expressions, types, and proofs. This paper brings Agda program-proofs into machine-learning research through a newly released dataset detailed enough to expose proof states at the subtype level.

The authors use that structure to design a neural architecture representing dependently typed programs through their organization rather than primarily through names. The high-resolution dataset enables learning from fine-grained proof information that would be lost in a coarse text-only description.

An evaluation on premise selection shows promising results that surpass strong baselines. The abstract does not state dataset size, numerical accuracy, or performance on complete automated proof construction. The contribution is both a resource connecting Agda with machine learning and an initial structural modeling method, with evidence on the specific task of choosing useful premises.
summary.tldr: A detailed Agda proof dataset supports structural neural representations and improved premise selection.

title: Learning Structure-Aware Representations of Dependent Types

abstract: Attention, as a core layer of the ubiquitous Transformer architecture, is the bottleneck for large language models and long-context applications. elaborated an approach to speed up attention on GPUs through minimizing memory reads/writes. However, it has yet to take advantage of new capabilities present in recent hardware, with FlashAttention-2 achieving only 35% utilization on the H100 GPU.We develop three main techniques to speed up attention on Hopper GPUs: exploiting asynchrony of the Tensor Cores and TMA to (1) overlap overall computation and data movement via warp-specialization and (2) interleave block-wise matmul and softmax operations, and (3) block quantization and incoherent processing that leverages hardware support for FP8 low-precision. We demonstrate that our method, FlashAttention-3, achieves speedup on H100 GPUs by 1.5-2.0$\times$ with BF16 reaching up to 840 TFLOPs/s (85\% utilization), and with FP8 reaching 1.3 PFLOPs/s. We validate that FP8 FlashAttention-3 achieves 2.6$\times$ lower numerical error than a baseline FP8 attention.

paragraphs: FlashAttention-3 targets the attention computation that can bottleneck large language models and long-context applications. Earlier attention acceleration reduced memory traffic, but the abstract reports that FlashAttention-2 used only 35% of H100 GPU capacity. This work seeks additional performance by organizing computation around capabilities of Hopper GPUs.

Two techniques exploit asynchronous execution. Warp specialization overlaps computation with data movement, while another scheduling strategy interleaves blockwise matrix multiplication and softmax. A third technique combines block quantization with incoherent processing to use FP8 hardware. These changes address both keeping hardware busy and carrying out attention efficiently at lower numerical precision.

On H100 GPUs, the authors report speedups of 1.5–2.0 times, with BF16 reaching up to 840 TFLOPs/s and 85% utilization. FP8 reaches 1.3 PFLOPs/s, and its numerical error is reported as 2.6 times lower than a baseline FP8 attention implementation. The findings demonstrate gains for the attention operation on the evaluated hardware, combining higher throughput with improved accuracy relative to that low-precision baseline.
summary.tldr: FlashAttention-3 accelerates attention on Hopper GPUs through asynchronous scheduling and FP8 processing with improved numerical accuracy.

title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision

abstract: Face feature fusion is indispensable for robust face recognition, particularly in scenarios involving long-range, low-resolution media (unconstrained environments) where not all frames or features are equally informative. Existing methods often rely on large intermediate feature maps or face metadata information, making them incompatible with legacy biometric template databases that store pre-computed features. Additionally, real-time inference and generalization to large probe sets remains challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce a linear time O(N) proxy based sparse expert selection and pooling approach for context driven feature-set attention. Our approach is order invariant on the feature-set, generalizes to large sets, is compatible with legacy template stores, and utilizes significantly less parameters making it suitable real-time inference and edge use-cases. Through qualitative experiments, we demonstrate that ProxyFusion learns discriminative information for importance weighting of face features without relying on intermediate features. Quantitative evaluations on challenging low-resolution face verification datasets such as IARPA BTS3.1 and DroneSURF show the superiority of ProxyFusion in unconstrained long-range face recognition setting. Our code and pretrained models are available at: https://github.com/bhavinjawade/ProxyFusion

paragraphs: Combining multiple face features can improve recognition when images are distant, low-resolution, or otherwise unconstrained. The difficulty is that some frames contain much more useful information than others. Existing fusion methods may require intermediate feature maps or face metadata that legacy databases storing only precomputed features cannot provide.

ProxyFusion uses proxy-based sparse expert selection and pooling to assign context-dependent importance within a feature set. Its computation grows linearly with the number of features, and changing their order does not change the result. The method works with stored features, generalizes to large sets, and uses substantially fewer parameters, supporting real-time and edge applications.

Qualitative experiments show that ProxyFusion learns information useful for weighting face features without accessing intermediate representations. Quantitative evaluations on IARPA BTS3.1 and DroneSURF report superior performance in challenging long-range, low-resolution verification settings. The contribution combines recognition effectiveness with a practical interface: feature aggregation can operate on representations that existing biometric template stores already contain.
summary.tldr: ProxyFusion efficiently combines stored face features using sparse experts, improving recognition in evaluated long-range, low-resolution settings.

title: ProxyFusion: Face Feature Aggregation Through Sparse Experts

abstract: Teaching to improve student models (e.g., knowledge distillation) is an extensively studied methodology in LLMs. However, in human education, teaching enhances not only the students but also the teachers by fostering more rigorous and clearer reasoning, as well as deeper knowledge building. We ask: Can LLMs also learn by teaching (LbT) for better reasoning? If the answer is yes, we can potentially unlock the possibility of continuously advancing the models without solely relying on human-produced data or stronger models. In this paper, we provide a preliminary exploration of this question. We show that LbT ideas can be incorporated into existing LLM training/prompting pipelines and bring improvements. Specifically, we design three methods, each mimicking one of the three levels of LbT: observing students' feedback, learning from the feedback, and learning iteratively, with the goal of improving answer accuracy without training or improving models' inherent capability with fine-tuning. We reveal some findings: (1) Teaching materials that make it easier for students to learn (via in-context learning) have clearer and more accurate logic; (2) Weak-to-strong generalization: LbT might help improve strong models by teaching weak models; (3) Diversity in students might help: teaching multiple students could be better than teaching a single student or the teacher alone. We hope that our exploration can inspire future research on LbT and, more broadly, the adoption of advanced education techniques to improve LLMs. The code and website are at https://github.com/imagination-research/lbt and https://sites.google.com/view/llm-learning-by-teaching.

paragraphs: Teaching can improve a human teacher's own understanding by encouraging clearer explanations and more careful reasoning. This paper investigates whether language models can benefit similarly. Its focus is on improving the model doing the teaching, extending the familiar use of a stronger model to train a student.

The authors design three approaches reflecting different levels of involvement with students: observing their feedback, learning from that feedback, and repeating the learning process iteratively. These ideas fit into existing prompting and training pipelines. Some aim to improve answer accuracy without training, while others use fine-tuning to improve the model's underlying capability. The study reports improvements from incorporating these teaching-based procedures.

Teaching materials that students can learn from through in-context examples exhibit clearer and more accurate logic. The authors also find indications that teaching weaker students might improve stronger models, and that multiple students could help more than one student or the teacher alone. These are preliminary findings, suggesting a possible route toward improvement that depends less exclusively on human-produced data or stronger teachers.
summary.tldr: This preliminary study finds that incorporating student feedback into teaching can improve language-model reasoning.

title: Can LLMs Learn by Teaching for Better Reasoning? A Preliminary Study

abstract: Neural network pruning is a key technique towards engineering large yet scalable, interpretable, and generalizable models. Prior work on the subject has developed largely along two orthogonal directions: (1) differentiable pruning for efficiently and accurately scoring the importance of parameters, and (2) combinatorial optimization for efficiently searching over the space of sparse models. We unite the two approaches, both theoretically and empirically, to produce a coherent framework for structured neural network pruning in which differentiable pruning guides combinatorial optimization algorithms to select the most important sparse set of parameters. Theoretically, we show how many existing differentiable pruning techniques can be understood as nonconvex regularization for group sparse optimization, and prove that for a wide class of nonconvex regularizers, the global optimum is unique, group-sparse, and provably yields an approximate solution to a sparse convex optimization problem. The resulting algorithm that we propose, SequentialAttention++, advances the state of the art in large-scale neural network block-wise pruning tasks on the ImageNet and Criteo datasets.

paragraphs: Structured pruning removes groups of neural-network parameters to obtain a smaller model. Two research directions address different parts of this problem: differentiable pruning estimates which parameters matter, while combinatorial optimization searches for a useful sparse selection. This paper combines them so that learned importance information guides the search over parameter groups.

The theoretical analysis interprets many differentiable pruning techniques as forms of nonconvex regularization for group-sparse optimization. For a broad class of these regularizers, the authors prove that the global optimum is unique and group-sparse, and that it provides an approximate solution to a sparse convex optimization problem. This connects continuous training objectives with discrete decisions about which groups to retain.

The resulting algorithm, SequentialAttention++, applies this combined perspective to block-wise neural-network pruning. It advances the reported state of the art on large-scale pruning tasks using ImageNet and Criteo. The contribution gives both a mathematical connection between previously separate approaches and an algorithm that turns that connection into improved empirical pruning results.
summary.tldr: SequentialAttention++ combines differentiable importance scoring with combinatorial optimization to improve structured neural-network pruning.

title: SequentialAttention++ for Block Sparsification: Differentiable Pruning Meets Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Exploiting symmetry inherent in data can significantly improve the sample efficiency of a learning procedure and the generalization of learned models. When data clearly reveals underlying symmetry, leveraging this symmetry can naturally inform the design of model architectures or learning strategies. Yet, in numerous real-world scenarios, identifying the specific symmetry within a given data distribution often proves ambiguous. To tackle this, some existing works learn symmetry in a data-driven manner, parameterizing and learning expected symmetry through data. However, these methods often rely on explicit knowledge, such as pre-defined Lie groups, which are typically restricted to linear or affine transformations. In this paper, we propose a novel symmetry learning algorithm based on transformations defined with one-parameter groups, continuously parameterized transformations flowing along the directions of vector fields called infinitesimal generators. Our method is built upon minimal inductive biases, encompassing not only commonly utilized symmetries rooted in Lie groups but also extending to symmetries derived from nonlinear generators. To learn these symmetries, we introduce a notion of a validity score that examine whether the transformed data is still valid for the given task. The validity score is designed to be fully differentiable and easily computable, enabling effective searches for transformations that achieve symmetries innate to the data. We apply our method mainly in two domains: image data and partial differential equations, and demonstrate its advantages. Our codes are available at \url{https://github.com/kogyeonghoon/learning-symmetry-from-scratch.git}.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations that preserve what matters for a learning task. Knowing them can improve sample efficiency and generalization, but the relevant transformations are often unclear from real data. Existing methods for learning symmetries can require predefined groups, commonly restricting the search to linear or affine transformations.

This paper learns continuously parameterized transformations through vector fields called infinitesimal generators. A generator specifies the direction of an infinitesimal change, and following that field produces a family of transformations. The approach uses minimal inductive biases and accommodates nonlinear generators, expanding the types of symmetry it can represent beyond the commonly used predefined transformations.

To guide learning, the authors introduce a validity score that checks whether transformed data remains valid for the task. Because the score is differentiable and easy to compute, it supports an effective search for transformations consistent with the data. Applications to image data and partial differential equations demonstrate advantages. The contribution combines a flexible representation of continuous transformations with a task-based criterion for discovering which transformations preserve validity.
summary.tldr: The method learns continuous symmetries, including nonlinear ones, by searching for transformations that preserve task validity.

title: Learning Infinitesimal Generators of Continuous Symmetries from Data

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate surprising capabilities, but we do not understand how they are implemented. One hypothesis suggests that these capabilities are primarily executed by small subnetworks within the LLM, known as circuits. But how can we evaluate this hypothesis?In this paper, we formalize a set of criteria that a circuit is hypothesized to meet and develop a suite of hypothesis tests to evaluate how well circuits satisfy them. abstract: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning (CRL) is an approach to facilitate the learning process of agents by structuring tasks in a sequence of increasing complexity. Despite its potential, many existing CRL methods struggle to efficiently guide agents toward desired outcomes, particularly in the absence of domain knowledge. This paper introduces DiCuRL (Diffusion Curriculum Reinforcement Learning), a novel method that leverages conditional diffusion models to generate curriculum goals. To estimate how close an agent is to achieving its goal, our method uniquely incorporates a $Q$-function and a trainable reward function based on Adversarial Intrinsic Motivation within the diffusion model. Furthermore, it promotes exploration through the inherent noising and denoising mechanism present in the diffusion models and is environment-agnostic. This combination allows for the generation of challenging yet achievable goals, enabling agents to learn effectively without relying on domain knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DiCuRL in three different maze environments and two robotic manipulation tasks simulated in MuJoCo, where it outperforms or matches nine state-of-the-art CRL algorithms from the literature.

DiCuRL addresses this problem by using a conditional diffusion model to generate goals that challenge the agent while remaining achievable.

The results support diffusion-based goal generation as an effective curriculum mechanism in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: DiCuRL uses conditional diffusion to generate achievable but challenging goals and matches or outperforms nine curriculum-learning methods in evaluated tasks.

title: Diffusion-based Curriculum Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Surgical video-language pretraining (VLP) faces unique challenges due to the knowledge domain gap and the scarcity of multi-modal data. This study aims to bridge the gap by addressing issues regarding textual information loss in surgical lecture videos and the spatial-temporal challenges of surgical VLP. To tackle these issues, we propose a hierarchical knowledge augmentation approach and a novel Procedure-Encoded Surgical Knowledge-Augmented Video-Language Pretraining (PeskaVLP) framework. The proposed knowledge augmentation approach uses large language models (LLM) to refine and enrich surgical concepts, thus providing comprehensive language supervision and reducing the risk of overfitting. The PeskaVLP framework combines language supervision with visual self-supervision, constructing hard negative samples and employing a Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) based loss function to effectively comprehend the cross-modal procedural alignment. Extensive experiments on multiple public surgical scene understanding and cross-modal retrieval datasets show that our proposed method significantly improves zero-shot transferring performance and offers a generalist visual repre- sentation for further advancements in surgical scene understanding. The source code will be available at https://github.com/CAMMA-public/PeskaVLP.

Surgical lecture videos can also lose useful textual information, while procedures unfold across space and time. PeskaVLP addresses these connected problems by enriching language supervision and explicitly learning alignment between language and visual procedures.

A hierarchical knowledge augmentation approach uses large language models to refine and expand surgical concepts. This provides richer supervision and reduces overfitting risk. The pretraining framework combines that language information with visual self-supervision, constructs hard negative samples, and uses a Dynamic Time Warping loss to learn cross-modal alignment across procedural sequences.

Experiments on several public datasets for surgical scene understanding and cross-modal retrieval report significant improvements in zero-shot transfer. The resulting visual representation is intended to serve multiple surgical understanding tasks. These findings support using structured domain knowledge together with temporal alignment when learning from surgical video, where understanding the progression of a procedure matters alongside recognizing visual content.
summary.tldr: PeskaVLP enriches surgical language supervision and learns procedural video-language alignment to improve zero-shot transfer.

title: Procedure-Aware Surgical Video-language Pretraining with Hierarchical Knowledge Augmentation

abstract: Video diffusion models have made substantial progress in various video generation applications. However, training models for long video generation tasks require significant computational and data resources, posing a challenge to developing long video diffusion models.This paper investigates a straightforward and training-free approach to extend an existing short video diffusion model (e.g. pre-trained on 16-frame videos) for consistent long video generation (e.g. 128 frames). Our preliminary observation has found that directly applying the short video diffusion model to generate long videos can lead to severe video quality degradation. Further investigation reveals that this degradation is primarily due to the distortion of high-frequency components in long videos, characterized by a decrease in spatial high-frequency components and an increase in temporal high-frequency components. Motivated by this, we propose a novel solution named FreeLong to balance the frequency distribution of long video features during the denoising process. FreeLong blends the low-frequency components of global video features, which encapsulate the entire video sequence, with the high-frequency components of local video features that focus on shorter subsequences of frames. This approach maintains global consistency while incorporating diverse and high-quality spatiotemporal details from local videos, enhancing both the consistency and fidelity of long video generation. We evaluated FreeLong on multiple base video diffusion models and observed significant improvements. Additionally, our method supports coherent multi-prompt generation, ensuring both visual coherence and seamless transitions between scenes. Our project page is at: https://yulu.net.cn/freelong.
