The paper also demonstrates coherent generation from multiple prompts, with smooth transitions between scenes. Examples in the abstract frame the extension as moving from models pretrained on 16-frame clips to 128-frame generation. The contribution is therefore a way to reuse existing short-video models through changes to generation rather than resource-intensive long-video training.
summary.tldr: FreeLong blends global low-frequency and local high-frequency features to generate longer, more coherent videos without retraining short-video diffusion models.

title: FreeLong: Training-Free Long Video Generation with SpectralBlend Temporal Attention

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs), such as DINOv2, achieve strong performance across domains but often repurpose low-informative patch tokens in ways that reduce the interpretability of attention and feature maps. This challenge is especially evident in medical imaging, where domain shifts can degrade both performance and transparency. In this paper, we introduce Randomized-MLP (RMLP) regularization, a contrastive learning-based method that encourages more semantically aligned representations. We apply RMLP when fine-tuning DINOv2 to both medical and natural image modalities, showing that it improves or maintains downstream performance while producing more interpretable attention maps. We also provide a mathematical analysis of RMLPs, offering insights into its role in enhancing ViT-based models and advancing our understanding of contrastive learning in this context.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can repurpose image-patch tokens that carry little useful information, making their attention and feature maps harder to interpret. The paper examines this issue in DINOv2, particularly when adapting to medical images. In that setting, differences between the original and target domains can harm both prediction performance and the transparency of learned representations.

The authors introduce Randomized-MLP regularization, a method based on contrastive learning that encourages representations to align more closely with semantic content. They apply it during DINOv2 fine-tuning on medical and natural images. The intervention therefore targets the representations learned during adaptation, with the aim of improving how meaning is reflected in the model's attention maps.

The reported results show improved or maintained downstream performance alongside more interpretable attention maps. The paper also supplies a mathematical analysis of randomized MLPs to explain their role in this learning setting. Together, the empirical and analytical contributions suggest that regularization during fine-tuning can improve representational interpretability without necessarily sacrificing performance on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Randomized-MLP regularization makes fine-tuned DINOv2 attention maps more interpretable while improving or maintaining downstream performance.

title: Randomized-MLP Regularization Improves Domain Adaptation and Interpretability in DINOv2

abstract: Explaining time series classification models is crucial, particularly in high-stakes applications such as healthcare and finance, where transparency and trust play a critical role. Although numerous time series classification methods have identified key subsequences, known as shapelets, as core features for achieving state-of-the-art performance and validating their pivotal role in classification outcomes, existing post-hoc time series explanation (PHTSE) methods primarily focus on timestep-level feature attribution. These explanation methods overlook the fundamental prior that classification outcomes are predominantly driven by key shapelets. To bridge this gap, we present ShapeX, an innovative framework that segments time series into meaningful shapelet-driven segments and employs Shapley values to assess their saliency. At the core of ShapeX lies the Shapelet Describe-and-Detect (SDD) framework, which effectively learns a diverse set of shapelets essential for classification. We further demonstrate that ShapeX produces explanations which reveal causal relationships instead of just correlations, owing to the atomicity properties of shapelets. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ShapeX outperforms existing methods in identifying the most relevant subsequences, enhancing both the precision and causal fidelity of time series explanations.

paragraphs: Time-series classifiers often depend on meaningful short patterns, called shapelets. Yet many methods for explaining their predictions assign importance to individual timesteps. ShapeX builds explanations around subsequences instead, following the premise that the patterns driving a decision are often more meaningful as complete units than as isolated points.

Its Shapelet Describe-and-Detect framework learns a diverse collection of shapelets important for classification. ShapeX uses these to divide a series into meaningful segments, then applies Shapley values to assess each segment’s contribution. This connects the units used in an explanation with the types of patterns that the paper identifies as central to classification.

The authors further demonstrate causal relationships in the resulting explanations, attributing this property to the atomicity of shapelets. On synthetic and real-world datasets, ShapeX outperforms existing methods in finding the most relevant subsequences, improving precision and causal fidelity. The result supports treating meaningful temporal patterns as the explanatory units when analyzing how a time-series model reaches its decisions.
summary.tldr: ShapeX explains time-series predictions through shapelet-based segments, improving identification of relevant subsequences and reported causal fidelity.

title: ShapeX: Shapelet-Driven Post Hoc Explanations for Time Series Classification Models

abstract: Recent advances in multimodal semantic segmentation show that incorporating auxiliary inputs—such as depth or thermal images—can significantly improve performance over single-modality (RGB-only) approaches. However, most existing solutions rely on parallel backbone networks and complex fusion modules, greatly increasing model size and computational demands. Inspired by prompt tuning in large language models, we introduce \textbf{MixPrompt}: a prompting-based framework that integrates auxiliary modalities into a pretrained RGB segmentation model without modifying its architecture. MixPrompt uses a lightweight prompting module to extract and fuse information from auxiliary inputs into the main RGB backbone. This module is initialized using the early layers of a pretrained RGB feature extractor, ensuring a strong starting point. At each backbone layer, MixPrompt aligns RGB and auxiliary features in multiple low-rank subspaces, maximizing information use with minimal parameter overhead. An information mixing scheme enables cross-subspace interaction for further performance gains. During training, only the prompting module and segmentation head are updated, keeping the RGB backbone frozen for parameter efficiency. Experiments across NYU Depth V2, SUN-RGBD, MFNet, and DELIVER datasets show that MixPrompt achieves improvements of 4.3, 1.1, 0.4, and 1.1 mIoU, respectively, over two-branch baselines, while using nearly half the parameters. MixPrompt also outperforms recent prompting-based methods under similar compute budgets.

title: MixPrompt: Efficient Mixed Prompting for Multimodal Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Crystal structures are defined by the periodic arrangement of atoms in 3D space, inherently making them equivariant to SO(3) group. A fundamental requirement for crystal property prediction is that the model's output should remain invariant to arbitrary rotational transformations of the input structure. One promising strategy to achieve this invariance is to align the given crystal structure into a canonical orientation with appropriately computed rotations, or called frames. However, existing work either only considers a global frame or solely relies on more advanced local frames based on atoms' local structure. A global frame is too coarse to capture the local structure heterogeneity of the crystal, while local frames may inadvertently disrupt crystal symmetry, limiting their expressivity. In this work, we revisit the frame design problem for crystalline materials and propose a novel approach to construct expressive {\bf S}ymmetry Preserving Frames, dubbed as SPFrame, for modeling crystal structures. Specifically, this local-global associative frame constructs invariant local frames rather than equivariant ones, thereby preserving the symmetry of the crystal. In parallel, it integrates global structural information to construct an equivariant global frame to enforce SO(3) invariance. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that SPFrame consistently outperforms traditional frame construction techniques and existing crystal property prediction baselines across multiple benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: A crystal property predictor should give the same result when the input structure is rotated. One way to achieve this is to compute frames that align the structure with a canonical orientation. However, a single global frame can miss local differences, while local frames can inadvertently disrupt the crystal’s symmetry.

SPFrame combines local and global structural information with different roles for each. It constructs invariant local frames to preserve crystal symmetry, while an equivariant global frame enforces rotational invariance of the overall modeling approach. Here, invariance means remaining unchanged under rotation, while equivariance means changing consistently with the rotation applied to the structure.

This design aims to capture local structural heterogeneity without losing the symmetry requirements of crystal modeling. Across multiple benchmark tasks, the authors report consistent improvements over traditional frame-construction techniques and existing crystal property prediction baselines. The results support the paper’s central architectural choice: coordinating local and global frames so that expressivity and symmetry preservation work together.
summary.tldr: SPFrame coordinates invariant local frames with an equivariant global frame to improve crystal property prediction while preserving symmetry.

title: Local-Global Associative Frames for Symmetry-Preserving Crystal Structure Modeling

abstract: Flow matching is an emerging generative modeling framework that learns continuous-time dynamics to map noise into data. To enhance expressiveness and sampling efficiency, recent works have explored incorporating high-order trajectory information. Despite the empirical success, a holistic theoretical foundation is still lacking. We present a unified framework for standard and high-order flow matching that incorporates trajectory derivatives up to an arbitrary order $K$. Our key innovation is establishing the marginalization technique that converts the intractable $K$-order loss into a simple conditional regression with exact gradients and identifying the consistency constraint. We establish sharp statistical rates of the $K$-order flow matching implemented with transformer networks. With $n$ samples, flow matching estimates nonparametric distributions at a rate $\tilde{O}(n^{-\Theta(1/d )})$, matching minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Flow matching learns continuous dynamics that transform noise into data. Recent extensions incorporate higher-order information about these trajectories to improve expressiveness and sampling efficiency. This paper develops a unified theoretical treatment of ordinary flow matching and versions that use trajectory derivatives up to any chosen order K.

Its central construction turns an otherwise intractable higher-order loss into a conditional regression problem through marginalization. The resulting regression supplies exact gradients. The framework also identifies a consistency constraint, making explicit a requirement that accompanies the higher-order formulation. This connects a broad class of trajectory-based objectives to a tractable learning procedure.

The rate has the form n raised to a negative exponent proportional to 1/d, with logarithmic factors suppressed. It matches minimax lower bounds up to those factors. The result gives theoretical support for the framework while retaining an explicit dependence on dimensionality in its sample-efficiency characterization.
summary.tldr: A unified higher-order flow-matching framework yields tractable regression objectives and statistical rates matching minimax bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: High-Order Flow Matching: Unified Framework and Sharp Statistical Rates

abstract: In this position paper we argue that conclusions drawn about relative system safety or attack method efficacy via AI red teaming are often not supported by evidence provided by attack success rate (ASR) comparisons. We show, through conceptual, theoretical, and empirical contributions, that many conclusions are founded on apples-to-oranges comparisons or low-validity measurements. Our arguments are grounded in asking a simple question: When can attack success rates be meaningfully compared? To answer this question, we draw on ideas from social science measurement theory and inferential statistics, which, taken together, provide a conceptual grounding for understanding when numerical values obtained through the quantification of system attributes can be meaningfully compared. Through this lens, we articulate conditions under which ASRs can and cannot be meaningfully compared. Using jailbreaking as a running example, we provide examples and extensive discussion of apples-to-oranges ASR comparisons and measurement validity challenges.

Our arguments are grounded in asking a simple question: When can attack success rates be meaningfully compared? To answer this question, we draw on ideas from social science measurement theory and inferential statistics, which, taken together, provide a conceptual grounding for understanding when numerical values obtained through the quantification of system attributes can be meaningfully compared. Using jailbreaking as a running example, we provide examples and extensive discussion of apples-to-oranges ASR comparisons and measurement validity challenges.

paragraphs: Attack success rates summarize how often attempts to defeat an AI system succeed. They are frequently used to compare system safety or the effectiveness of attack methods. This position paper argues that many such conclusions go beyond what the reported measurements support: two numerical rates can look comparable while measuring different things or measuring the intended attribute poorly.

The authors examine this problem using social science measurement theory and inferential statistics. Their central question is when numerical measurements support a meaningful comparison. They use that perspective to articulate conditions under which attack success rates can and cannot be compared, supported by conceptual arguments, theoretical contributions, and empirical evidence.

Jailbreaking provides the running example for examining mismatched comparisons and problems with measurement validity. The contribution is a framework for interpreting red-teaming evidence, rather than a new attack or defense. Its practical significance is that a difference in reported success rates does not, by itself, establish a corresponding difference in safety or attack effectiveness; that interpretation depends on the validity and comparability of the measurements.
summary.tldr: This position paper explains why attack success rates support safety comparisons only when the underlying measurements are valid and comparable.

title: Comparison requires valid measurement: Rethinking attack success rate comparisons in AI red teaming

abstract: Continual offline reinforcement learning (CORL) has shown impressive ability in diffusion-based continual learning systems by modeling the joint distributions of trajectories. However, most research only focuses on limited continual task settings where the tasks have the same observation and action space, which deviates from the realistic demands of training agents in various environments. In view of this, we propose Vector-Quantized Continual Diffuser, named VQ-CD, to break the barrier of different spaces between various tasks. Specifically, our method contains two complementary sections, where the quantization spaces alignment provides a unified basis for the selective weights activation. In the quantized spaces alignment, we leverage vector quantization to align the different state and action spaces of various tasks, facilitating continual training in the same space. Then, we propose to leverage a unified diffusion model attached by the inverse dynamic model to master all tasks by selectively activating different weights according to the task-related sparse masks. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on 15 continual learning (CL) tasks, including conventional CL task settings (identical state and action spaces) and general CL task settings (various state and action spaces). Compared with 17 baselines, our method reaches the SOTA performance.

Specifically, our method contains two complementary sections, where the quantization spaces alignment provides a unified basis for the selective weights activation. Then, we propose to leverage a unified diffusion model attached by the inverse dynamic model to master all tasks by selectively activating different weights according to the task-related sparse masks. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on 15 continual learning (CL) tasks, including conventional CL task settings (identical state and action spaces) and general CL task settings (various state and action spaces). Compared with 17 baselines, our method reaches the SOTA performance.

paragraphs: Continual offline reinforcement learning seeks to learn successive tasks from recorded experience. Diffusion-based approaches can model trajectories, but much previous work assumes that every task uses the same observation and action spaces. VQ-CD addresses the broader case in which an agent must learn across environments with different representations of states and actions.

The method first uses vector quantization to align these differing spaces into a shared basis. It then combines a unified diffusion model with an inverse dynamics model, selectively activating weights through sparse masks associated with each task. The space alignment makes shared training possible, while the masks determine which weights participate for a particular task.

Experiments cover 15 continual-learning tasks, including both conventional settings with matching spaces and more general settings with different spaces. VQ-CD achieves the best reported performance against 17 baselines. The findings support the combination of representation alignment and selective weight activation as a way to extend continual diffusion-based learning beyond tasks that already share compatible inputs and actions.
summary.tldr: VQ-CD aligns different state and action spaces and selectively activates weights to improve continual offline reinforcement learning.

title: Tackling Continual Offline RL through Selective Weights Activation on Aligned Spaces

abstract: Understanding the remarkable efficacy of Adam when training transformer-based language models has become a central research topic within the optimization community. To gain deeper insights, several simplifications of Adam have been proposed, such as the signed gradient and signed momentum methods. In this work, we conduct an extensive empirical study — training over 1,500 language models across different data configurations and scales — comparing Adam to several known simplified variants. We find that signed momentum methods are faster than SGD, but consistently underperform relative to Adam, even after careful tuning of momentum, clipping setting and learning rates. However, our analysis reveals a compelling option that preserves near-optimal performance while allowing for new insightful reformulations: constraining the Adam momentum parameters to be equal, $\beta_1=\beta_2$. Beyond robust performance, this choice affords new theoretical insights, highlights the "secret sauce" on top of signed momentum, and grants a precise statistical interpretation: we show that Adam in this setting implements a natural online algorithm for estimating the mean and variance of gradients—one that arises from a mean-field Gaussian variational inference perspective.

paragraphs: The paper asks which parts of Adam explain its strong performance when training transformer language models. Simplified methods based on gradient signs or signed momentum offer possible explanations, but their practical behavior must be compared carefully. The authors train more than 1,500 language models across different scales and data configurations to examine these alternatives.

This result indicates that signed momentum alone does not reproduce Adam’s effectiveness in the tested settings. The contribution links an empirically strong simplification to a precise statistical account of what Adam contributes beyond signed momentum.
summary.tldr: Matching Adam’s momentum parameters preserves strong performance and reveals an interpretation based on online gradient mean and variance estimation.

title: In Search of Adam’s Secret Sauce

abstract: Sharpness‐aware minimization (SAM) has emerged as a highly effective technique for improving model generalization, but its underlying principles are not fully understood. We investigated the phenomenon known as m-sharpness, where the performance of SAM improves monotonically as the micro-batch size for computing perturbations decreases. In practice, the empirical m-sharpness effect underpins the deployment of SAM in distributed training, yet a rigorous theoretical account has remained lacking. To provide a theoretical explanation for m-sharpness, we leverage an extended Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) framework and analyze the structure of stochastic gradient noise (SGN) to characterize the dynamics of various SAM variants, including n-SAM and m-SAM. Our findings reveal that the stochastic noise introduced during SAM perturbations inherently induces a variance-based sharpness regularization effect. Motivated by our theoretical insights, we introduce Reweighted SAM (RW-SAM), which employs sharpness-weighted sampling to mimic the generalization benefits of m-SAM while remaining parallelizable. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our theoretical analysis and proposed method.

The contribution is therefore explanatory and algorithmic: it identifies a useful role for perturbation noise and turns that insight into a sampling strategy intended to retain its benefits in parallel training.
summary.tldr: The paper links SAM's micro-batch benefits to noise-induced regularization and proposes parallelizable sharpness-weighted sampling to reproduce them.

title: Unveiling m-Sharpness Through the Structure of Stochastic Gradient Noise

abstract: Semantic retrieval is crucial for modern applications yet remains underexplored in current research. Existing datasets are limited to single languages, single images, or singular retrieval conditions, often failing to fully exploit the expressive capacity of visual information as evidenced by maintained performance when images are replaced with captions. However, practical retrieval scenarios frequently involve interleaved multi-condition queries with multiple images. Hence, this paper introduces MERIT, the first multilingual dataset for interleaved multi-condition semantic retrieval, comprising 320,000 queries with 135,000 products in 5 languages, covering 7 distinct product categories. Extensive experiments on MERIT identify existing models's critical limitation: focusing solely on global semantic information while neglecting specific conditional elements in queries. Consequently, we propose Coral, a novel fine-tuning framework that adapts pre-trained MLLMs by integrating embedding reconstruction to preserve fine-grained conditional elements and contrastive learning to extract comprehensive global semantics. Experiments demonstrate that Coral achieves a 45.9% performance improvement over conventional approaches on MERIT, with strong generalization capabilities validated across 8 established retrieval benchmarks. Collectively, our contributions—a novel dataset, identification of critical limitations in existing approaches, and an innovative fine-tuning framework—establish a foundation for future research in interleaved multi-condition semantic retrieval. **Data & Code**: [MERIT-2025.github.io](https://merit-2025.github.io)

paragraphs: A retrieval query can combine several images and textual conditions, requiring a system to preserve particular details as well as overall meaning. Existing datasets often cover only one language, one image, or one condition. MERIT expands this setting with 320,000 queries and 135,000 products spanning five languages and seven product categories.

Experiments on the dataset identify a recurring weakness: existing models concentrate on global semantics while overlooking individual conditions. The authors propose Coral, a fine-tuning framework for pretrained multimodal language models, to address this. Embedding reconstruction helps preserve fine-grained conditions, while contrastive learning develops a representation of the query’s broader meaning.

Coral achieves a reported 45.9% performance improvement over conventional approaches on MERIT, with generalization assessed on eight established retrieval benchmarks. Together, the dataset and method make it possible to study retrieval that depends on several interleaved requirements. The results suggest that preserving specific conditions and learning overall semantic similarity are complementary needs in this more expressive query setting.
summary.tldr: MERIT benchmarks multilingual retrieval with multiple interleaved conditions, while Coral improves retrieval by preserving both detailed requirements and global meaning.

title: MERIT: Multilingual Semantic Retrieval with Interleaved Multi-Condition Query

abstract: Existing machine unlearning (MU) approaches exhibit significant sensitivity to hyperparameters, requiring meticulous tuning that limits practical deployment. In this work, we first empirically demonstrate the instability and suboptimal performance of existing popular MU methods when deployed in different scenarios. To address this issue, we propose Dual Optimizer (DualOptim), which incorporates adaptive learning rate and decoupled momentum factors. Empirical and theoretical evidence demonstrates that DualOptim contributes to effective and stable unlearning. Through extensive experiments, we show that DualOptim can significantly boost MU efficacy and stability across diverse tasks, including image classification, image generation, and large language models, making it a versatile approach to empower existing MU algorithms.

To address this issue, we propose Dual Optimizer (DualOptim), which incorporates adaptive learning rate and decoupled momentum factors. Empirical and theoretical evidence demonstrates that DualOptim contributes to effective and stable unlearning. paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove learned information from a trained model. Its practical usefulness depends on whether the procedure works reliably across operating conditions. This paper begins by empirically showing that popular unlearning methods can be unstable and perform poorly in different scenarios, with substantial sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

DualOptim addresses the optimization process underlying unlearning. It combines adaptive learning rates with decoupled momentum factors. Learning rates govern update size, while momentum carries information from preceding updates. By adapting the former and separating the latter, the framework changes how unlearning updates are controlled. The proposed contribution is designed to strengthen existing unlearning algorithms.

The authors provide both empirical and theoretical evidence that DualOptim contributes to effective, stable unlearning. Their experiments span image classification, image generation, and large language models, and report substantial improvements in efficacy and stability. This breadth supports its usefulness across different kinds of models and tasks. The stated result is improved robustness of the unlearning process, rather than a claim that hyperparameter choices cease to matter.
summary.tldr: DualOptim uses adaptive learning rates and decoupled momentum to improve the effectiveness and stability of existing machine unlearning algorithms.

title: DualOptim: Enhancing Efficacy and Stability in Machine Unlearning with Dual Optimizers

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, due to their strong instruction-following capabilities. This raised interest in optimizing instructions for black-box LLMs, whose internal parameters are inaccessible but popular for their strong performance and ease of use. Recent approaches leverage white-box LLMs to assist instruction optimization for black-box LLMs by generating instructions from soft prompts. However, white-box LLMs often map different soft prompts to the same instruction, leading to redundant queries to the black-box model. While previous studies regarded this many-to-one mapping as a redundancy to be avoided, we reinterpret it as useful prior knowledge that can enhance the optimization performance. To this end, we introduce PREimage-informed inSTruction Optimization (PRESTO), a novel framework that leverages the preimage structure of soft prompts to improve query efficiency. PRESTO consists of three key components: (1) score sharing, which shares the evaluation score with all soft prompts in a preimage; (2) preimage-based initialization, which select initial data points that maximize search space coverage using preimage information; and (3) score consistency regularization, which enforces prediction consistency within each preimage. By leveraging preimages, PRESTO observes 14 times more scored data under the same query budget, resulting in more efficient optimization. Experimental results on 33 instruction optimization tasks demonstrate the superior performance of PRESTO.

paragraphs: Optimizing instructions for a black-box language model requires evaluating prompts without access to its internal parameters. Some methods use a white-box model to turn adjustable soft prompts into written instructions. Multiple soft prompts can produce the same instruction, leading to repeated black-box evaluations of effectively identical candidates.

PRESTO uses that many-to-one relationship as information about the search space. The set of soft prompts producing one instruction is its preimage. The framework shares an instruction’s evaluation score across its preimage, chooses initial candidates to improve search-space coverage using preimage information, and regularizes score predictions to remain consistent within each preimage.

These components make one evaluation informative about multiple soft prompts and incorporate their equivalence into optimization. Under the same query budget, PRESTO observes 14 times as much scored data, according to the paper. Experiments on 33 instruction-optimization tasks report superior performance. The gain concerns the effective use of evaluations, rather than requiring 14 times as many distinct instructions to be queried.
summary.tldr: PRESTO improves black-box instruction optimization by sharing evaluation information among soft prompts that generate the same instruction.

title: PRESTO: Preimage-Informed Instruction Optimization for Prompting Black-Box LLMs

abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDM) are powerful generative models for discrete data that generate samples by progressively unmasking tokens in a sequence. Each token can take one of two states: masked or unmasked. We observe that token sequences often remain unchanged between consecutive sampling steps; consequently, the model repeatedly processes identical inputs, leading to redundant computation. To address this inefficiency, we propose the Partial masking scheme (Prime), which augments MDM by allowing tokens to take intermediate states interpolated between the masked and unmasked states. This design enables the model to make predictions based on partially observed token information, and facilitates a fine-grained denoising process. We derive a variational training objective and introduce a simple architectural design to accommodate intermediate-state inputs. Our method demonstrates superior performance across a diverse set of generative modeling tasks. On text data, it achieves a perplexity of 15.36 on OpenWebText, outperforming previous MDM (21.52), autoregressive models (17.54), and their hybrid variants (17.58), without relying on an autoregressive formulation. On image data, it attains competitive FID scores of 3.26 on CIFAR-10 and 6.98 on ImageNet-32, comparable to leading continuous generative models.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models generate discrete sequences by gradually revealing hidden tokens. With only two token states, hidden or revealed, consecutive sampling steps can receive exactly the same sequence. The paper identifies this repeated processing as a source of redundant computation and proposes Partial masking, called Prime, to make the generation process more fine-grained.

Prime introduces intermediate token states between fully masked and fully visible. The model can therefore make predictions from partial information instead of waiting for a token to become completely available. The authors derive a variational training objective and add an architectural design that accepts these intermediate inputs. This changes both what the model observes during generation and how it learns to remove uncertainty.

On OpenWebText, Prime achieves perplexity of 15.36, compared with 21.52 for previous masked diffusion models, 17.54 for autoregressive models, and 17.58 for hybrid variants. It does so without an autoregressive formulation. Image results include FID scores of 3.26 on CIFAR-10 and 6.98 on ImageNet-32, which the authors describe as competitive with leading continuous generative models.
summary.tldr: Prime gives diffusion tokens partially visible states, enabling finer-grained generation and strong reported text and image results.

title: Beyond Masked and Unmasked: Discrete Diffusion Models via Partial Masking

abstract: Determining whether an algorithmic decision-making system discriminates against a specific demographic typically involves comparing a single point estimate of a fairness metric against a predefined threshold. This practice is statistically brittle: it ignores sampling error and treats small demographic subgroups the same as large ones. The problem intensifies in intersectional analyses, where multiple sensitive attributes are considered jointly, giving rise to a larger number of smaller groups. As these groups become more granular, the data representing them becomes too sparse for reliable estimation, and fairness metrics yield excessively wide confidence intervals, precluding meaningful conclusions about potential unfair treatments. In this paper, we introduce a unified, size-adaptive, hypothesis‑testing framework that turns fairness assessment into an evidence‑based statistical decision. Our contribution is twofold. (i) For sufficiently large subgroups, we prove a Central‑Limit result for the statistical parity difference, leading to analytic confidence intervals and a Wald test whose type‑I (false positive) error is guaranteed at level $\alpha$. (ii) For the long tail of small intersectional groups, we derive a fully Bayesian Dirichlet–multinomial estimator; Monte-Carlo credible intervals are calibrated for any sample size and naturally converge to Wald intervals as more data becomes available. We validate our approach empirically on benchmark datasets, demonstrating how our tests provide interpretable, statistically rigorous decisions under varying degrees of data availability and intersectionality.

summary.tldr: A size-adaptive fairness framework combines large-sample hypothesis tests with Bayesian estimation for small intersectional groups.

title: Size-adaptive Hypothesis Testing for Fairness

abstract: We introduce *Backward Conformal Prediction*, a method that guarantees conformal coverage while providing flexible control over the size of prediction sets. Unlike standard conformal prediction, which fixes the coverage level and allows the conformal set size to vary, our approach defines a rule that constrains how prediction set sizes behave based on the observed data, and adapts the coverage level accordingly. Our method builds on two key foundations: (i) recent results by Gauthier et al. [2025] on post-hoc validity using e-values, which ensure marginal coverage of the form $\mathbb{P}(Y_{\rm test} \in \hat C_n^{\tilde{\alpha}}(X_{\rm test})) \ge 1 - \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\alpha}]$ up to a first-order Taylor approximation for any data-dependent miscoverage $\tilde{\alpha}$, and (ii) a novel leave-one-out estimator $\hat{\alpha}^{\rm LOO}$ of the marginal miscoverage $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\alpha}]$ based on the calibration set, ensuring that the theoretical guarantees remain computable in practice. This approach is particularly useful in applications where large prediction sets are impractical such as medical diagnosis. We provide theoretical results and empirical evidence supporting the validity of our method, demonstrating that it maintains computable coverage guarantees while ensuring interpretable, well-controlled prediction set sizes.

paragraphs: Prediction sets express uncertainty by returning multiple possible answers. Standard conformal prediction chooses a coverage target first and lets the number of answers vary. Backward Conformal Prediction reverses that arrangement: it specifies a data-dependent rule controlling set sizes, then adapts the coverage level to that rule. This addresses applications where an excessively large set is difficult to use.

The theoretical foundation uses e-values to support validity after choosing a data-dependent miscoverage level. The stated marginal coverage bound is one minus the expected selected miscoverage, up to a first-order Taylor approximation. That qualification matters: the abstract's mathematical guarantee concerns this averaged quantity and includes the approximation, rather than promising an arbitrary fixed coverage level for every selected set.

The paper also introduces a leave-one-out estimator that uses calibration data to estimate the marginal miscoverage. This makes the coverage assessment computable in practice. Theoretical results and experiments support the method's ability to combine interpretable control over set sizes with an accompanying, computable coverage guarantee.
summary.tldr: Backward Conformal Prediction controls prediction-set sizes first and adapts coverage, with a computable marginal guarantee qualified by a first-order approximation.

title: Backward Conformal Prediction

abstract: We introduce the attention-indexed model (AIM), a theoretical framework for analyzing learning in deep attention layers. Inspired by multi-index models, AIM captures how token-level outputs emerge from layered bilinear interactions over high-dimensional embeddings. Unlike prior tractable attention models, AIM allows full-width key and query matrices, aligning more closely with practical transformers. Using tools from statistical mechanics and random matrix theory, we derive closed-form predictions for Bayes-optimal generalization error and identify sharp phase transitions as a function of sample complexity, model width, and sequence length. We propose a matching approximate message passing algorithm and show that gradient descent can reach optimal performance. AIM offers a solvable playground for understanding learning in self-attention layers, that are key components of modern architectures.

paragraphs: Understanding how attention layers learn requires models that are mathematically manageable while retaining relevant architectural features. This paper introduces the attention-indexed model, a theoretical framework describing how token outputs arise from layered bilinear interactions among high-dimensional embeddings. It permits full-width key and query matrices, making its attention structure closer to practical transformers than earlier tractable models.

Using statistical mechanics and random matrix theory, the authors derive closed-form predictions for Bayes-optimal generalization error. These predictions describe the best performance under the framework’s Bayesian formulation. The analysis also identifies sharp changes in learning behavior as sample complexity, model width, and sequence length vary, connecting these quantities to transitions in achievable generalization.

The paper proposes an approximate message passing algorithm that matches the theoretical performance and shows that gradient descent can attain optimal performance. Together, these results provide both a performance characterization and algorithms capable of reaching it within the studied framework. AIM offers a solvable setting for investigating self-attention learning, with conclusions grounded in that theoretical model.
summary.tldr: AIM provides a tractable attention model with explicit optimal-error predictions, learning phase transitions, and algorithms that can attain optimal performance.

title: Bayes optimal learning of attention-indexed models

abstract: Current 3D gaze estimation methods struggle to generalize across diverse data domains, primarily due to $\textbf{i)}$ $\textit{the scarcity of annotated datasets}$, and $\textbf{ii)}$ $\textit{the insufficient diversity of labeled data}$. In this work, we present OmniGaze, a semi-supervised framework for 3D gaze estimation, which utilizes large-scale unlabeled data collected from diverse and unconstrained real-world environments to mitigate domain bias and generalize gaze estimation in the wild. First, we build a diverse collection of unlabeled facial images, varying in facial appearances, background environments, illumination conditions, head poses, and eye occlusions. In order to leverage unlabeled data spanning a broader distribution, OmniGaze adopts a standard pseudo-labeling strategy and devises a reward model to assess the reliability of pseudo labels. Beyond pseudo labels as 3D direction vectors, the reward model also incorporates visual embeddings extracted by an off-the-shelf visual encoder and semantic cues from gaze perspective generated by prompting a Multimodal Large Language Model to compute confidence scores. Then, these scores are utilized to select high-quality pseudo labels and weight them for loss computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniGaze achieves state-of-the-art performance on five datasets under both in-domain and cross-domain settings. Furthermore, we also evaluate the efficacy of OmniGaze as a scalable data engine for gaze estimation, which exhibits robust zero-shot generalization on four unseen datasets.

Furthermore, we also evaluate the efficacy of OmniGaze as a scalable data engine for gaze estimation, which exhibits robust zero-shot generalization on four unseen datasets.

paragraphs: OmniGaze addresses poor transfer in 3D gaze estimation caused by limited and insufficiently diverse labeled data. It uses a large collection of unlabeled face images from unconstrained environments, covering variation in appearance, lighting, backgrounds, head orientation, and eye occlusion. The objective is to make this broader visual diversity useful for learning gaze direction.

The framework assigns pseudo-labels to unlabeled images and uses a reward model to estimate their reliability. That model considers the predicted 3D direction, visual embeddings from an existing encoder, and gaze-related semantic cues produced by a multimodal language model. Its confidence scores determine which pseudo-labels are retained and how strongly they contribute to the training loss.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on five datasets in both in-domain and cross-domain evaluations. They also demonstrate robust zero-shot generalization on four unseen datasets when evaluating the framework as a scalable data engine. These findings support confidence-based selection and weighting as a way to benefit from diverse unlabeled images while accounting for the varying quality of generated gaze labels.
summary.tldr: OmniGaze scores and weights pseudo-labels on diverse unlabeled face images to improve 3D gaze estimation across domains.

title: OmniGaze: Reward-inspired Generalizable Gaze Estimation in the Wild

abstract: Addressing the critical need for robust safety in Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly against adversarial attacks and in-distribution errors, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Backtracking Feedback (RLBF). This framework advances upon prior methods, such as BSAFE, by primarily leveraging a Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage where models learn to dynamically correct their own generation errors. Through RL with critic feedback on the model's live outputs, LLMs are trained to identify and recover from their actual, emergent safety violations by emitting an efficient "backtrack by x tokens" signal, then continuing generation autoregressively. This RL process is crucial for instilling resilience against sophisticated adversarial strategies, including middle filling, Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attacks, and decoding parameter manipulations. To further support the acquisition of this backtracking capability, we also propose an enhanced Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) data generation strategy (BSAFE+). This method improves upon previous data creation techniques by injecting violations into coherent, originally safe text, providing more effective initial training for the backtracking mechanism. Comprehensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that RLBF significantly reduces attack success rates across diverse benchmarks and model scales, achieving superior safety outcomes while critically preserving foundational model utility.

paragraphs: A language model can begin generating unsafe content even after safety training, especially under adversarial prompting. Reinforcement Learning with Backtracking Feedback, or RLBF, trains models to recognize and recover from such mistakes during generation. Its central capability is a signal specifying how many tokens to backtrack before continuing to generate.

The main training stage uses reinforcement learning with critic feedback on the model's live outputs. This exposes the model to its own emerging safety violations and teaches corrective behavior around those errors. The authors also introduce BSAFE+, a supervised training-data strategy that inserts violations into otherwise coherent, safe text to help initialize the backtracking capability.

Evaluations cover multiple benchmarks and model sizes, including attacks involving middle filling, Greedy Coordinate Gradient, and manipulated decoding parameters. The authors report significantly lower attack success rates while preserving foundational model utility. These results support training recovery as part of safe generation: the model learns how to respond when its current output goes wrong, and the reinforcement-learning stage develops that response using feedback on actual generated behavior.
summary.tldr: RLBF trains language models to backtrack over unsafe generated tokens and continue safely, reducing attack success while preserving model utility in evaluations.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Backtracking Feedback

abstract: Vision-Language Foundation Models (VLMs), trained on large-scale multimodal datasets, have driven significant advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) by enabling rich cross-modal reasoning. Despite their success in general domains, applying these models to medical imaging remains challenging due to the limited availability of diverse imaging modalities and multilingual clinical data. Most existing medical VLMs are trained on a subset of imaging modalities and focus primarily on high-resource languages, thus limiting their generalizability and clinical utility. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Vietnamese-language multimodal medical dataset consisting of 2,757 whole-body PET/CT volumes from independent patients and their corresponding full-length clinical reports. This dataset is designed to fill two pressing gaps in medical AI development: (1) the lack of PET/CT imaging data in existing VLMs training corpora, which hinders the development of models capable of handling functional imaging tasks; and (2) the underrepresentation of low-resource languages, particularly the Vietnamese language, in medical vision-language research. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset to provide comprehensive PET/CT-report pairs in Vietnamese. We further introduce a training framework to enhance VLMs' learning, including data augmentation and expert-validated test sets. We conduct comprehensive experiments benchmarking state-of-the-art VLMs on downstream tasks, including medical report generation and visual question answering. The experimental results show that incorporating our dataset significantly improves the performance of existing VLMs. However, despite these advancements, the models still underperform on clinically critical criteria, particularly the diagnosis of lung cancer, indicating substantial room for future improvement. We believe this dataset and benchmark will serve as a pivotal step in advancing the development of more robust VLMs for medical imaging, particularly in low-resource languages, and improving their clinical relevance in Vietnamese healthcare.

title: Toward a Vision-Language Foundation Model for Medical Data: Multimodal Dataset and Benchmarks for Vietnamese PET/CT Report Generation

abstract: Graph condensation (GC) aims to distill the original graph into a small-scale graph, mitigating redundancy and accelerating GNN training. However, conventional GC approaches heavily rely on rigid GNNs and task-specific supervision. Such a dependency severely restricts their reusability and generalization across various tasks and architectures. In this work, we revisit the goal of ideal GC from the perspective of GNN optimization consistency, and then a generalized GC optimization objective is derived, by which those traditional GC methods can be viewed nicely as special cases of this optimization paradigm. Based on this, \textbf{Pre}-trained \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ondensation (\textbf{PreGC}) via optimal transport is proposed to transcend the limitations of task- and architecture-dependent GC methods. Specifically, a hybrid-interval graph diffusion augmentation is presented to suppress the weak generalization ability of the condensed graph on particular architectures by enhancing the uncertainty of node states. Meanwhile, the matching between optimal graph transport plan and representation transport plan is tactfully established to maintain semantic consistencies across source graph and condensed graph spaces, thereby freeing graph condensation from task dependencies. To further facilitate the adaptation of condensed graphs to various downstream tasks, a traceable semantic harmonizer from source nodes to condensed nodes is proposed to bridge semantic associations through the optimized representation transport plan in pre-training. Extensive experiments verify the superiority and versatility of PreGC, demonstrating its task-independent nature and seamless compatibility with arbitrary GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph condensation compresses a graph into a smaller graph intended to accelerate graph neural network training. Existing approaches often tie that compressed result to a particular architecture or supervised task. PreGC aims to produce condensed graphs that can be reused more broadly across downstream tasks and network designs.

The authors derive a generalized condensation objective from consistency in GNN optimization, placing traditional methods within a common framework. Their proposed method combines graph diffusion augmentation with optimal transport. The augmentation increases uncertainty in node states to address architecture-specific generalization, while matching graph and representation transport plans preserves semantic consistency between original and condensed graphs.

A traceable semantic harmonizer then connects source nodes to condensed nodes through the representation transport plan learned during pretraining. This provides a route for adapting the condensed graph to downstream tasks. Extensive experiments support the method’s effectiveness and versatility, including task independence and broad GNN compatibility. The central contribution is making condensed graphs more reusable by preserving semantic relationships without task-specific supervision.
summary.tldr: PreGC uses optimal transport and graph augmentation to create condensed graphs intended for reuse across tasks and GNN architectures.

title: Towards Pre-trained Graph Condensation via Optimal Transport

abstract: This position paper argues that real-time generative AI has the potential to become the next wave of addictive digital media, creating a new class of digital content akin to ``digital heroin'' with severe implications for mental health and youth development. By shortening the content-generation feedback loop to mere seconds, these advanced models will soon be able to hyper-personalize outputs on the fly. When paired with misaligned incentives (e.g., maximizing user engagement), this will fuel unprecedented compulsive consumption patterns with far-reaching consequences for mental health, cognitive development, and social stability. Drawing on interdisciplinary research, from clinical observations of social media addiction to neuroscientific studies of dopamine-driven feedback, we illustrate how real-time tailored content generation may erode user autonomy, foment emotional distress, and disproportionately endanger vulnerable groups, such as adolescents. Due to the rapid advancement of generative AI and its potential to induce severe addiction-like effects, we call for strong government oversight akin to existing controls on addictive substances, particularly for minors. We further urge the machine learning community to act proactively by establishing robust design guidelines, collaborating with public health experts, and supporting targeted policy measures to ensure responsible and ethical deployment, rather than paving the way for another wave of unregulated digital dependence.

The phrase “digital heroin” expresses the authors’ warning about potentially severe dependence-like effects.

The argument draws on interdisciplinary work, including clinical observations of social-media addiction and research on dopamine-related feedback. summary.tldr: This position paper calls for oversight and preventive design measures against addiction-like risks from real-time, engagement-driven personalized generative media.

title: Real-Time Hyper-Personalized Generative AI Should Be Regulated to Prevent the Rise of "Digital Heroin"

abstract: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents have made substantial strides in understanding and executing user instructions across diverse platforms. Yet, grounding these instructions to precise interface elements remains challenging—especially in complex, high-resolution, professional environments. Traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods often require large volumes of diverse data and exhibit weak generalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that incorporates three core strategies: (1) seed data curation to ensure high-quality training samples, (2) a dense policy gradient that provides continuous feedback based on prediction accuracy, and (3) a self-evolutionary reinforcement finetuning mechanism that iteratively refines the model using attention maps. With only 3k training samples, our 7B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among similarly sized models on three grounding benchmarks. Notably, it attains 47.3\% accuracy on the ScreenSpot-Pro dataset—outperforming much larger models, such as UI-TARS-72B, by a margin of 24.2\%. These findings underscore the effectiveness of RL-based approaches in enhancing GUI agent performance, particularly in high-resolution, complex environments.

paragraphs: A GUI agent must connect a user’s instruction to the precise interface element it should act on. This grounding step becomes difficult in dense, high-resolution professional interfaces. SE-GUI addresses it with reinforcement learning, motivated by the large data requirements and weak generalization the authors identify in traditional supervised fine-tuning approaches.

The framework combines three strategies. Carefully curated seed examples provide a high-quality starting point. A dense policy gradient supplies continuous feedback based on prediction accuracy. An iterative reinforcement fine-tuning process then uses attention maps to refine the model. Together, these strategies focus on the quality of training examples, the informativeness of feedback, and repeated model improvement.

With 3,000 training samples, the seven-billion-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among similarly sized models on three grounding benchmarks. It reaches 47.3% accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro and outperforms substantially larger models, including UI-TARS-72B. These results support the effectiveness of the combined reinforcement-learning approach for interface grounding, particularly in the complex, high-resolution environments emphasized by the study.
summary.tldr: SE-GUI combines curated examples, dense accuracy feedback, and attention-guided refinement to improve interface grounding with 3,000 training samples.

title: SE-GUI: Enhancing Visual Grounding for GUI Agents via Self-Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advances in generative models trained on large-scale datasets have enabled high-quality 3D synthesis across various domains. However, these models also raise critical privacy concerns. Unlike 2D image synthesis, where risks typically involve the leakage of visual features or identifiable patterns, 3D generation introduces additional challenges, as reconstructed shapes, textures, and spatial structures may inadvertently expose proprietary designs, biometric data, or other sensitive geometric information. This paper presents the first exploration of machine unlearning in 3D generation tasks. We investigate different unlearning objectives, including re-targeting and partial unlearning, and propose a novel framework that does not require full supervision of the unlearning target. To enable a more efficient unlearning process, we introduce a skip-acceleration mechanism, which leverages the similarity between multi-view generated images to bypass redundant computations. By establishing coherence across viewpoints during acceleration, our framework not only reduces computation but also enhances unlearning effectiveness, outperforming the non-accelerated baseline in both accuracy and efficiency. We conduct extensive experiments on the typical 3D generation models (Zero123 and Zero123XL), demonstrating that our approach achieves a 30\% speedup, while effectively unlearning target concepts without compromising generation quality. Our framework provides a scalable and practical solution for privacy-preserving 3D generation, ensuring responsible AI deployment in real-world applications. The code is available at: https://github.com/sxxsxw/Fast-3D-Unlearn-with-Skip-acceleration

Experiments on Zero123 and Zero123XL show a 30% speedup while removing target concepts without compromising generation quality. The method also outperforms the non-accelerated baseline in accuracy and efficiency. These results support viewpoint-aware computation reuse as a practical component of unlearning for the evaluated 3D generation models.
summary.tldr: A viewpoint-coherent skipping mechanism accelerates targeted unlearning in 3D generators while improving reported unlearning effectiveness.

title: Machine Unlearning in 3D Generation: A Perspective-Coherent Acceleration Framework

abstract: Time series forecasting is a critical and complex task, characterized by diverse temporal patterns, varying statistical properties, and different prediction horizons across datasets and domains. Conventional approaches typically rely on a single, unified model architecture to handle all forecasting scenarios. However, such monolithic models struggle to generalize across dynamically evolving time series with shifting patterns. In reality, different types of time series may require distinct modeling strategies. Some benefit from homogeneous multi-scale forecasting awareness, while others rely on more complex and heterogeneous signal perception. Relying on a single model to capture all temporal diversity and structural variations leads to limited performance and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-Agent Forecasting System (MAFS) that abandons the one-size-fits-all paradigm. MAFS decomposes the forecasting task into multiple sub-tasks, each handled by a dedicated agent trained on specific temporal perspectives (e.g., different forecasting resolutions or signal characteristics). Furthermore, to achieve holistic forecasting, agents share and refine information through different communication topology, enabling cooperative reasoning across different temporal views. A lightweight voting aggregator then integrates their outputs into consistent final predictions. Extensive experiments across 11 benchmarks demonstrate that MAFS significantly outperforms traditional single-model approaches, yielding more robust and adaptable forecasts.

The paper argues that this burden can limit generalization and interpretability, motivating a system in which different components specialize in different temporal perspectives.

summary.tldr: MAFS combines specialized forecasting agents through communication and voting, improving results across 11 time-series benchmarks.

title: Many Minds, One Goal: Time Series Forecasting via Sub-task Specialization and Inter-agent Cooperation

abstract: Nonparametric mixture models based on the Dirichlet process are an elegant alternative to finite models when the number of underlying components is unknown, but inference in such models can be slow. Existing attempts to parallelize inference in such models have relied on introducing approximations, which can lead to inaccuracies in the posterior estimate. In this paper, we describe auxiliary variable representations for the Dirichlet process and the hierarchical Dirichlet process that allow us to perform MCMC using the correct equilibrium distribution, in a distributed manner. We show that our approach allows scalable inference without the deterioration in estimate quality that accompanies existing methods.

paragraphs: Dirichlet-process mixture models are useful when the number of underlying components is unknown, but inference can be slow. Distributing the computation offers a route to larger problems. The difficulty addressed here is that earlier attempts at parallel inference introduced approximations that could reduce the accuracy of the estimated posterior distribution.

The paper develops auxiliary-variable representations for both the Dirichlet process and the hierarchical Dirichlet process. These representations allow Markov chain Monte Carlo computation to be distributed while retaining the correct equilibrium distribution. The key contribution is therefore a way to reorganize inference across computing resources while preserving the distribution that the sampling procedure is intended to target.

The authors report scalable inference without the deterioration in estimate quality associated with the existing approaches they discuss. This matters because computational scale and posterior fidelity are addressed together. The equilibrium-distribution result supports the correctness of the sampling target, while the reported scalability shows why the representation is useful for performing inference in these nonparametric mixture models.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary-variable representations enable distributed MCMC for Dirichlet-process models while preserving the correct equilibrium distribution.

title: Parallel Markov Chain Monte Carlo for Nonparametric Mixture Models

abstract: Max-product (max-sum) message passing algorithms are widely used for MAP inference in MRFs. It has many variants sharing a common flavor of passing "messages" over some graph-object. Recent advances revealed that its convergent versions (such as MPLP, MSD, TRW-S) can be viewed as performing block coordinate descent (BCD) in a dual objective. That is, each BCD step achieves dual-optimal w.r.t. a block of dual variables (messages), thereby decreases the dual objective monotonically. However, most existing algorithms are limited to updating blocks selected in rather restricted ways. In this paper, we show a "unified" message passing algorithm that: (a) subsumes MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S as special cases when applied to their respective choices of dual objective and blocks, and (b) is able to perform BCD under much more flexible choices of blocks (including very large blocks) as well as the dual objective itself (that arise from an arbitrary dual decomposition).

In this paper, we show a "unified" message passing algorithm that: (a) subsumes MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S as special cases when applied to their respective choices of dual objective and blocks, and (b) is able to perform BCD under much more flexible choices of blocks (including very large blocks) as well as the dual objective itself (that arise from an arbitrary dual decomposition).

paragraphs: Max-product and max-sum message passing are widely used to seek the most probable configuration in a Markov random field. Many variants exchange messages over a graph, but their updates can also be understood as optimization steps. Convergent methods such as MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S fit a block coordinate descent interpretation on a dual objective.

In this view, an update optimizes a selected block of message variables while holding the others fixed, monotonically decreasing the dual objective. The paper identifies restrictions in how existing algorithms choose those blocks. Such restrictions limit the ways a larger inference problem can be organized into updates.

The proposed unified algorithm recovers MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S when given their respective objectives and block choices. It also supports much more flexible blocks, including very large ones, and dual objectives arising from arbitrary dual decompositions. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: it places established methods in one framework and expands the choices available for designing message-passing optimization.
summary.tldr: A unified message-passing framework recovers several established algorithms while allowing more flexible update blocks and dual decompositions.

title: Subproblem-Tree Calibration: A Unified Approach to Max-Product Message Passing

abstract: Low-dimensional representations are key to the success of many video classification algorithms. However, the commonly-used dimensionality reduction techniques fail to account for the fact that only part of the signal is shared across all the videos in one class. As a consequence, the resulting representations contain instance-specific information, which introduces noise in the classification process. In this paper, we introduce Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis: A method that overcomes this issue by explicitly separating the stationary parts of the video signal (i.e., the parts shared across all videos in one class), from its non-stationary parts (i.e., specific to individual videos). We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on action recognition, dynamic texture classification and scene recognition.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on action recognition, dynamic texture classification and scene recognition.

paragraphs: Video classification often depends on compressing a complex signal into a lower-dimensional representation. The paper argues that common dimensionality reduction methods overlook an important distinction: some information is shared across videos belonging to the same class, while other information is specific to an individual video. Retaining the latter can introduce noise into classification.

Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis explicitly separates these two components. Here, stationary refers to the parts shared across all videos within a class, and non-stationary refers to parts specific to particular videos. The method therefore makes the relationship between variation and class membership central to how the representation is constructed.

The authors demonstrate the approach on action recognition, dynamic texture classification, and scene recognition. These applications provide evidence that separating shared and instance-specific signal components is useful across several video classification tasks. The contribution is a representation-learning approach that accounts for which information persists across a class, rather than treating all retained variation as equally useful for classification.
summary.tldr: Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis separates class-shared video information from instance-specific variation to improve representations for classification.

title: Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis with Application to Video Classification

abstract: The LDA topic model is being used to model corpora of documents that can be represented by bags of words. Here we extend the LDA model to deal with documents that are represented more naturally by bags of continuous descriptors. Given a finite dictionary of words which are generative models of descriptors, our extended LDA model allows for the soft assignment of descriptors to (many) dictionary words. We derive variational inference and parameter estimation procedures for the extended model, which closely resemble those obtained for the original model, with two important differences: First, the histogram of word counts is replaced by a histogram of pseudo word counts, or sums of responsibilities over all descriptors. Second, parameter estimation now depends on the average covariance matrix between these pseudo-counts, reflecting the fact that with soft assignment words are not independent. We use this approach to address novelty detection, where we seek to identify video events with low posterior probability. Video events are described by a generative dynamic texture model, from which we naturally derive a dictionary of generative words. Using a benchmark dataset for novelty detection, we show a very significant improvement in the detection of novel events when using our extended LDA model with soft assignment to words as against hard assignment (the original model), achieving state of the art novelty detection results.

A finite dictionary supplies generative models for those descriptors, and each descriptor can be assigned softly to several dictionary words. On a benchmark dataset, the soft-assignment model substantially improves novel-event detection over hard-assignment LDA and achieves results reported as state of the art.
summary.tldr: Extending LDA with soft descriptor-to-word assignments and dependent pseudo-counts substantially improves video novelty detection on a benchmark.

title: LDA Topic Model with Soft Assignment of Descriptors to Words

abstract: We present a practical and powerful new framework for both unconstrained and constrained submodular function optimization based on discrete semidifferentials (sub- and super-differentials). The resulting algorithms, which repeatedly compute and then efficiently optimize submodular semigradients, offer new and generalize many old methods for submodular optimization. Our approach, moreover, takes steps towards providing a unifying paradigm applicable to both submodular minimization and maximization, problems that historically have been treated quite distinctly. The practicality of our algorithms is important since interest in submodularity, owing to its natural and wide applicability, has recently been in ascendance within machine learning. We analyze theoretical properties of our algorithms for minimization and maximization, and show that many state-of-the-art maximization algorithms are special cases. Lastly, we complement our theoretical analyses with supporting empirical experiments.

This repeated construction-and-optimization pattern produces new methods and generalizes existing ones, allowing different algorithms to be understood through the same underlying procedure.

They also provide empirical experiments supporting the analysis. The significance is partly organizational and partly computational: the framework moves toward a unified account of submodular optimization while supplying practical algorithms for a class of functions with broad relevance in machine learning.
summary.tldr: A semidifferential framework connects submodular minimization and maximization, yielding practical algorithms and encompassing many existing methods.

title: Fast Semidifferential-based Submodular Function Optimization

abstract: We develop a general framework for margin-based multicategory classification in metric spaces. The basic work-horse is a margin-regularized version of the nearest-neighbor classifier. We prove generalization bounds that match the state of the art in sample size n and significantly improve the dependence on the number of classes k. Our point of departure is a nearly Bayes-optimal finite-sample risk bound independent of k. Although k-free, this bound is unregularized and non-adaptive, which motivates our main result: Rademacher and scale-sensitive margin bounds with a logarithmic dependence on k. As the best previous risk estimates in this setting were of order \sqrt k, our bound is exponentially sharper. From the algorithmic standpoint, in doubling metric spaces our classifier may be trained on n examples in O(n^2\log n) time and evaluated on new points in O(\log n) time.

The theoretical goal is to control generalization error without letting the guarantee deteriorate too quickly as the number of classes grows. This matters when a classification problem has many possible labels.

With n training examples, training takes O(n² log n) time and evaluating a new point takes O(log n) time. Thus, the contribution combines sharper multiclass risk guarantees with efficient prediction in the stated geometric setting.
summary.tldr: Margin-regularized nearest neighbors achieve generalization bounds with logarithmic class-count dependence and efficient prediction in doubling metric spaces.

title: Maximum Margin Multiclass Nearest Neighbors

abstract: We present two computationally inexpensive techniques for estimating the numerical rank of a matrix, combining powerful tools from computational linear algebra. These techniques exploit three key ingredients. The first is to approximate the projector on the non-null invariant subspace of the matrix by using a polynomial filter. Two types of filters are discussed, one based on Hermite interpolation and the other based on Chebyshev expansions. The second ingredient employs stochastic trace estimators to compute the rank of this wanted eigen-projector, which yields the desired rank of the matrix. In order to obtain a good filter, it is necessary to detect a gap between the eigenvalues that correspond to noise and the relevant eigenvalues that correspond to the non-null invariant subspace. The third ingredient of the proposed approaches exploits the idea of spectral density, popular in physics, and the Lanczos spectroscopic method to locate this gap.

paragraphs: Numerical rank concerns the effective non-null part of a matrix when small spectral components may reflect noise. This paper presents two inexpensive estimation techniques built from three computational ingredients. Both aim to count the relevant spectral directions through an approximate projection onto the corresponding invariant subspace.

First, a polynomial filter approximates that projection. The two proposed filter constructions use Hermite interpolation and Chebyshev expansions. Second, stochastic trace estimation approximates the trace of the projector, which gives the rank of the selected subspace. This turns rank estimation into a combination of filtering and randomized estimation of a matrix quantity.

The third ingredient determines where the filter should separate relevant eigenvalues from noise. The authors use spectral density and Lanczos spectroscopy to locate a gap between those groups. Detecting such a gap is necessary for obtaining a good filter in the proposed approach. The method therefore connects the rank estimate directly to a spectral separation that guides which directions should count.
summary.tldr: Two rank-estimation methods combine polynomial filtering, stochastic trace estimation, and spectral-gap detection.

title: Fast methods for estimating the Numerical rank of large matrices

abstract: The partition function is fundamental for probabilistic graphical models—it is required for inference, parameter estimation, and model selection. Evaluating this function corresponds to discrete integration, namely a weighted sum over an exponentially large set. This task quickly becomes intractable as the dimensionality of the problem increases. We propose an approximation scheme that, for any discrete graphical model whose parameter vector has bounded norm, estimates the partition function with arbitrarily small error. Our algorithm relies on a near minimax optimal polynomial approximation to the potential function and a Clenshaw-Curtis style quadrature. Furthermore, we show that this algorithm can be randomized to split the computation into a high-complexity part and a low-complexity part, where the latter may be carried out on small computational devices. Experiments confirm that the new randomized algorithm is highly accurate if the parameter norm is small, and is otherwise comparable to methods with unbounded error.
