summary.tldr: Polynomial approximation and randomized quadrature estimate partition functions with arbitrarily small error under a bounded-parameter-norm condition.

title: Stochastic Discrete Clenshaw-Curtis Quadrature

abstract: Given a non-convex function $f(x)$ that is an average of $n$ smooth functions, we design stochastic first-order methods to find its approximate stationary points. The performance of our new methods depend on the smallest (negative) eigenvalue $-\sigma$ of the Hessian. This parameter $\sigma$ captures how strongly non-convex $f(x)$ is, and is analogous to the strong convexity parameter for convex optimization. At least in theory, our methods outperform known results for a range of parameter $\sigma$, and can also be used to find approximate local minima. Our result implies an interesting dichotomy: there exists a threshold $\sigma_0$ so that the (currently) fastest methods for $\sigma>\sigma_0$ and for $\sigma<\sigma_0$ have different behaviors: the former scales with $n^{2/3}$ and the latter scales with $n^{3/4}$.

The paper develops stochastic first-order methods for finding approximate stationary points, where the gradient is small. Their performance depends on a parameter sigma associated with the smallest negative Hessian eigenvalue, which measures how strongly nonconvex the objective is.

This parameter plays a role analogous to strong convexity in convex optimization. Accounting for it allows the authors to obtain theoretical improvements over known results for a range of sigma values. The methods can also be used to find approximate local minima. The claimed speed advantage is qualified as theoretical and applies within the stated parameter range.

The analysis reveals a threshold separating two regimes among the currently fastest methods. Above that threshold, their dependence on the number of component functions scales as n to the two-thirds power; below it, the scaling is n to the three-quarters power. This highlights how the degree of nonconvexity can change which algorithmic behavior gives the strongest available guarantee.
summary.tldr: Natasha obtains theoretical optimization improvements in certain regimes by making algorithmic performance depend on the objective's degree of nonconvexity.

title: Natasha: Faster Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization via Strongly Non-Convex Parameter

abstract: We study two procedures (reverse-mode and forward-mode) for computing the gradient of the validation error with respect to the hyperparameters of any iterative learning algorithm such as stochastic gradient descent. These procedures mirror two ways of computing gradients for recurrent neural networks and have different trade-offs in terms of running time and space requirements. Our formulation of the reverse-mode procedure is linked to previous work by Maclaurin et al (2015) but does not require reversible dynamics. Additionally, we explore the use of constraints on the hyperparameters. The forward-mode procedure is suitable for real-time hyperparameter updates, which may significantly speedup hyperparameter optimization on large datasets. We present a series of experiments on image and phone classification tasks. In the second task, previous gradient-based approaches are prohibitive. We show that our real-time algorithm yields state-of-the-art results in affordable time.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization asks how choices governing training affect performance on validation data. This paper studies two ways to calculate that relationship through the steps of an iterative learning algorithm. Both compute gradients of validation error with respect to hyperparameters, allowing the validation objective to guide changes to the training setup.

The reverse-mode and forward-mode procedures mirror two gradient-computation approaches used for recurrent neural networks. Their runtime and memory demands differ, making the choice consequential for larger problems. The reverse-mode formulation does not require reversible training dynamics. The paper also explores constraints on hyperparameters, incorporating restrictions on their allowable values into the optimization setting.

Experiments cover image and phone classification; in the latter, previous gradient-based approaches are prohibitively expensive. The authors report state-of-the-art results from their real-time algorithm in affordable time. This supports the practical value of choosing a differentiation procedure that fits the computational demands of training.
summary.tldr: Forward- and reverse-mode differentiation enable gradient-based hyperparameter tuning, with forward mode supporting practical real-time updates.

title: Forward and Reverse Gradient-Based Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: We lay theoretical foundations for new database release mechanisms that allow third-parties to construct consistent estimators of population statistics, while ensuring that the privacy of each individual contributing to the database is protected. The proposed framework rests on two main ideas. First, releasing (an estimate of) the kernel mean embedding of the data generating random variable instead of the database itself still allows third-parties to construct consistent estimators of a wide class of population statistics. Second, the algorithm can satisfy the definition of differential privacy by basing the released kernel mean embedding on entirely synthetic data points, while controlling accuracy through the metric available in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. We describe two instantiations of the proposed framework, suitable under different scenarios, and prove theoretical results guaranteeing differential privacy of the resulting algorithms and the consistency of estimators constructed from their outputs.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for releasing information from a database while protecting each contributor through differential privacy. The intended recipients are third parties who want to estimate population statistics. The central challenge is to provide an output that remains statistically useful without releasing the original database.

The proposed output is an estimate of the data-generating distribution's kernel mean embedding, a representation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The authors show that this representation still permits consistent estimation of a broad class of population statistics. Their release mechanism bases the embedding on entirely synthetic data points and uses the space's metric to control accuracy.

The paper describes two versions of the framework for different scenarios and proves privacy guarantees for the resulting algorithms. It also proves consistency for estimators built from their outputs, connecting the released representation to reliable population estimation as data increases. These results establish a route from private synthetic releases to statistical analysis, with the kernel embedding serving as the common mathematical object linking privacy and accuracy.
summary.tldr: Private releases based on synthetic kernel mean embeddings let third parties consistently estimate a broad class of population statistics.

title: Differentially Private Database Release via Kernel Mean Embeddings

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a low-rank matrix, constrained to lie in a linear subspace, and introduce a novel factorization for modeling such matrices. A salient feature of the proposed factorization scheme is it decouples the low-rank and the structural constraints onto separate factors. We formulate the optimization problem on the Riemannian spectrahedron manifold, where the Riemannian framework allows to develop computationally efficient conjugate gradient and trust-region algorithms. Experiments on problems such as standard/robust/non-negative matrix completion, Hankel matrix learning and multi-task learning demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

Experiments on problems such as standard/robust/non-negative matrix completion, Hankel matrix learning and multi-task learning demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a matrix that must satisfy two requirements simultaneously: it must have low rank, and it must belong to a specified linear subspace. Low rank restricts the number of independent patterns the matrix can express, while the subspace requirement imposes additional structure. The challenge is to handle both requirements within one learning procedure.

The proposed factorization assigns the low-rank requirement and the structural requirement to separate factors. This separation is the central design choice: instead of making the same factor carry both constraints, the representation gives them distinct roles. The authors formulate learning on a Riemannian spectrahedron manifold and use its geometry to develop computationally efficient conjugate-gradient and trust-region algorithms.

Experiments cover standard, robust, and non-negative matrix completion, along with Hankel matrix learning and multi-task learning. These results support the effectiveness of the framework across several structured matrix problems. The contribution is therefore both a representation that separates constraints and an optimization approach that makes that representation usable.
summary.tldr: A new matrix factorization separates low-rank and structural constraints, enabling efficient geometric optimization across several matrix-learning tasks.

title: A Unified Framework for Structured Low-rank Matrix Learning

abstract: Metric learning has the aim to improve classification accuracy by learning a distance measure which brings data points from the same class closer together and pushes data points from different classes further apart. Recent research has demonstrated that metric learning approaches can also be applied to trees, such as molecular structures, abstract syntax trees of computer programs, or syntax trees of natural language, by learning the cost function of an edit distance, i.e. the costs of replacing, deleting, or inserting nodes in a tree. However, learning such costs directly may yield an edit distance which violates metric axioms, is challenging to interpret, and may not generalize well. In this contribution, we propose a novel metric learning approach for trees which we call embedding edit distance learning (BEDL) and which learns an edit distance indirectly by embedding the tree nodes as vectors, such that the Euclidean distance between those vectors supports class discrimination. We learn such embeddings by reducing the distance to prototypical trees from the same class and increasing the distance to prototypical trees from different classes. In our experiments, we show that BEDL improves upon the state-of-the-art in metric learning for trees on six benchmark data sets, ranging from computer science over biomedical data to a natural-language processing data set containing over 300,000 nodes.

paragraphs: Tree edit distance compares structured objects through the costs of inserting, deleting, or replacing nodes. Learning those costs can improve classification by making same-class trees closer and different-class trees farther apart. However, directly learned costs may violate metric axioms, be difficult to interpret, or generalize poorly. This paper proposes an indirect way to learn the distance.

Embedding edit distance learning, or BEDL, represents tree nodes as vectors and uses Euclidean distances between them to support class discrimination. Training pulls trees closer to representative trees from their own class and pushes them away from representatives of other classes. The learned vector representation thus determines how local node differences contribute to comparisons between whole trees.

The authors report improvements over leading tree metric learning methods on six benchmark datasets. The examples span computer science, biomedical data, and natural language processing, including a dataset with more than 300,000 nodes. These results support learning the geometry of node symbols as a useful route to improving distances between structured objects.
summary.tldr: BEDL learns vector embeddings for tree symbols to improve class-sensitive edit distances, with gains on six benchmarks.

title: Tree Edit Distance Learning via Adaptive Symbol Embeddings

abstract: In many applications where collecting data is expensive, for example neuroscience or medical imaging, the sample size is typically small compared to the feature dimension. These datasets call for intelligent regularization that exploits known structure, such as correlations between the features arising from the measurement device. However, existing structured regularizers need specially crafted solvers, which are difficult to apply to complex models. We propose a new regularizer specifically designed to leverage structure in the data in a way that can be applied efficiently to complex models. Our approach relies on feature grouping, using a fast clustering algorithm inside a stochastic gradient descent loop: given a family of feature groupings that capture feature covariations, we randomly select these groups at each iteration. Experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach produces models that generalize better than those trained with conventional regularizers, and also improves convergence speed, and has a linear computational cost.

Regularization can exploit that structure, but existing structured methods often require specialized solvers that are difficult to integrate with complex models.

The proposed regularizer uses feature groupings that capture which measurements vary together. A fast clustering algorithm operates within stochastic gradient descent, with groups randomly selected from a family of groupings at each iteration. This makes the data’s feature relationships part of the training procedure while retaining an approach designed for efficient use in complex models.

These findings support stochastic feature grouping as a practical way to use known structure when examples are scarce, with the performance comparison grounded in the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Randomly selected feature groupings provide efficient structural regularization, improving generalization and convergence on two real-world datasets.

title: Feature Grouping as a Stochastic Regularizer for High-Dimensional Structured Data

abstract: Plug-and-play (PnP) is a non-convex framework that integrates modern denoising priors, such as BM3D or deep learning-based denoisers, into ADMM or other proximal algorithms. An advantage of PnP is that one can use pre-trained denoisers when there is not sufficient data for end-to-end training. Although PnP has been recently studied extensively with great empirical success, theoretical analysis addressing even the most basic question of convergence has been insufficient. In this paper, we theoretically establish convergence of PnP-FBS and PnP-ADMM, without using diminishing stepsizes, under a certain Lipschitz condition on the denoisers. We then propose real spectral normalization, a technique for training deep learning-based denoisers to satisfy the proposed Lipschitz condition. Finally, we present experimental results validating the theory.

An advantage of PnP is that one can use pre-trained denoisers when there is not sufficient data for end-to-end training. Although PnP has been recently studied extensively with great empirical success, theoretical analysis addressing even the most basic question of convergence has been insufficient. paragraphs: Plug-and-play methods place denoisers inside iterative optimization algorithms such as ADMM. This allows a pretrained denoiser to act as a prior, which is useful when there is insufficient data for end-to-end training. Despite strong empirical results, establishing whether the resulting non-convex iterations converge has remained a basic theoretical challenge.

The paper proves convergence for PnP-FBS and PnP-ADMM under a particular Lipschitz condition on the denoiser. Such a condition controls how the denoiser's outputs respond to changes in its inputs. The guarantee does not require diminishing step sizes, connecting convergence to properties of the denoiser rather than to progressively smaller updates.

The authors then propose real spectral normalization, a training technique intended to make deep denoisers satisfy the required condition. Experiments validate the theory. The contribution connects an abstract convergence requirement to a concrete training procedure: the denoiser is designed with the surrounding iterative algorithm in mind. The guarantee remains conditional on the specified Lipschitz property, rather than applying to every pretrained denoiser.
summary.tldr: A Lipschitz condition guarantees convergence of two plug-and-play methods, and real spectral normalization trains denoisers to satisfy it.

title: Plug-and-Play Methods Provably Converge with Properly Trained Denoisers

abstract: The ability to learn disentangled representations that split underlying sources of variation in high dimensional, unstructured data is important for data efficient and robust use of neural networks. While various approaches aiming towards this goal have been proposed in recent times, a commonly accepted definition and validation procedure is missing. We provide a causal perspective on representation learning which covers disentanglement and domain shift robustness as special cases. Our causal framework allows us to introduce a new metric for the quantitative evaluation of deep latent variable models. We show how this metric can be estimated from labeled observational data and further provide an efficient estimation algorithm that scales linearly in the dataset size.

Such separation matters for data efficiency and robustness, but evaluating whether a representation achieves it requires a clear definition. This paper addresses the absence of a commonly accepted definition and validation procedure through a causal perspective on representation learning.

The proposed framework includes disentanglement and robustness to domain shifts as special cases. Bringing them into a common causal formulation supports a new metric for evaluating deep latent-variable models quantitatively. The contribution focuses on making representation quality assessable through that framework, giving a concrete evaluation target to an otherwise broad modeling objective.

The authors show how to estimate the metric from labeled observational data and provide an efficient algorithm whose cost grows linearly with dataset size. This makes the proposed evaluation usable without requiring the estimation procedure to scale superlinearly with the number of examples. Together, the causal formulation and estimator connect a conceptual account of robust representations to a practical validation method.
summary.tldr: A causal framework unifies disentanglement and domain-shift robustness and yields a metric estimable from labeled observational data in linear time.

title: Robustly Disentangled Causal Mechanisms: Validating Deep Representations for Interventional Robustness

abstract: This paper aims to build efficient convolutional neural networks using a set of Lego filters. Many successful building blocks, e.g., inception and residual modules, have been designed to refresh state-of-the-art records of CNNs on visual recognition tasks. Beyond these high-level modules, we suggest that an ordinary filter in the neural network can be upgraded to a sophisticated module as well. Filter modules are established by assembling a shared set of Lego filters that are often of much lower dimensions. Weights in Lego filters and binary masks to stack Lego filters for these filter modules can be simultaneously optimized in an end-to-end manner as usual. Inspired by network engineering, we develop a split-transform-merge strategy for an efficient convolution by exploiting intermediate Lego feature maps. The compression and acceleration achieved by Lego Networks using the proposed Lego filters have been theoretically discussed. Experimental results on benchmark datasets and deep models demonstrate the advantages of the proposed Lego filters and their potential real-world applications on mobile devices.

LegoNet applies a similar idea at the level of individual filters: it constructs filter modules by assembling a shared collection of smaller Lego filters. summary.tldr: LegoNet assembles convolutional filters from shared smaller components and reuses intermediate feature maps to support compression and acceleration.

title: LegoNet: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks with Lego Filters

abstract: Smooth finite-sum optimization has been widely studied in both convex and nonconvex settings. However, existing lower bounds for finite-sum optimization are mostly limited to the setting where each component function is (strongly) convex, while the lower bounds for nonconvex finite-sum optimization remain largely unsolved. In this paper, we study the lower bounds for smooth nonconvex finite-sum optimization, where the objective function is the average of $n$ nonconvex component functions. We prove tight lower bounds for the complexity of finding $\epsilon$-suboptimal point and $\epsilon$-approximate stationary point in different settings, for a wide regime of the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian of the objective function (or each component function). Given our lower bounds, we can show that existing algorithms including {KatyushaX} \citep{allen2018katyushax}, {Natasha} \citep{allen2017natasha} and {StagewiseKatyusha} \citep{yang2018does} have achieved optimal {Incremental First-order Oracle} (IFO) complexity (i.e., number of IFO calls) up to logarithm factors for nonconvex finite-sum optimization. We also point out potential ways to further improve these complexity results, in terms of making stronger assumptions or by a different convergence analysis.

A lower bound establishes a benchmark for judging whether an algorithm's complexity can be improved.

Their analysis covers a broad range of curvature conditions expressed through the smallest Hessian eigenvalue of the objective or its individual components. These settings matter because the allowable curvature helps determine the difficulty of the optimization problem.

This concerns the number of oracle calls, rather than a blanket claim about every aspect of runtime. The paper also identifies possible routes to stronger complexity results through additional assumptions or different convergence analyses, clarifying both established limits and opportunities for further progress.
summary.tldr: Tight lower bounds show that several nonconvex finite-sum algorithms already achieve optimal oracle complexity up to logarithmic factors in the studied settings.

title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Finite-Sum Optimization

abstract: Deep learning models achieve high predictive accuracy across a broad spectrum of tasks, but rigorously quantifying their predictive uncertainty remains challenging. Usable estimates of predictive uncertainty should (1) cover the true prediction targets with high probability, and (2) discriminate between high- and low confidence prediction instances. Existing methods for uncertainty quantification are based predominantly on Bayesian neural networks; these may fall short of (1) and (2) {—} i.e., Bayesian credible intervals do not guarantee frequentist coverage, and approximate posterior inference undermines discriminative accuracy. In this paper, we develop the discriminative jackknife (DJ), a frequentist procedure that utilizes influence functions of a model’s loss functional to construct a jackknife (or leave one-out) estimator of predictive confidence intervals. The DJ satisfies (1) and (2), is applicable to a wide range of deep learning models, is easy to implement, and can be applied in a post-hoc fashion without interfering with model training or compromising its accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that DJ performs competitively compared to existing Bayesian and non-Bayesian regression baselines.

paragraphs: Useful predictive uncertainty should accomplish two things: include the true target with high probability and distinguish predictions deserving high confidence from those deserving less. The paper argues that strong predictive accuracy alone does not supply these properties. It also identifies potential shortcomings of Bayesian credible intervals and approximate posterior inference for these particular goals.

The proposed discriminative jackknife is a frequentist procedure based on leave-one-out reasoning. It uses influence functions of the model's loss functional to construct predictive confidence intervals. This ties uncertainty estimation to how the fitted model responds to changes in its training data, giving the procedure a basis in the variability captured by jackknife estimation.

The authors state that the method provides both coverage and discrimination between confidence levels. It applies to a broad range of deep learning models and can be added after training without changing that training or reducing predictive accuracy. Regression experiments show competitive performance against Bayesian and non-Bayesian alternatives, supporting the practical usefulness of the proposed interval estimates.
summary.tldr: The discriminative jackknife uses influence functions to add predictive confidence intervals with coverage and instance-level discrimination to trained deep models.

title: Discriminative Jackknife: Quantifying Uncertainty in Deep Learning via Higher-Order Influence Functions

abstract: We give strengthened provable guarantees on the performance of widely employed and empirically successful {\sl top-down decision tree learning heuristics}. While prior works have focused on the realizable setting, we consider the more realistic and challenging {\sl agnostic} setting. We show that for all monotone functions $f$ and $s\in \mathbb{N}$, these heuristics construct a decision tree of size $s^{\tilde{O}((\log s)/\varepsilon^2)}$ that achieves error $\le \mathsf{opt}_s + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}_s$ denotes the error of the optimal size-$s$ decision tree for $f$. Previously such a guarantee was not known to be achievable by any algorithm, even one that is not based on top-down heuristics. We complement our algorithmic guarantee with a near-matching $s^{\tilde{\Omega}(\log s)}$ lower bound.

paragraphs: This paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for widely used top-down decision-tree learning heuristics. It considers the agnostic setting, where the target need not be represented perfectly by a tree of the comparison size. The relevant goal is therefore to approach the error of the best such tree, allowing some additional error.

For every monotone target function and comparison size s, the authors show that these heuristics produce a tree with error at most opt_s plus epsilon. Here, opt_s is the smallest error achievable by a size-s tree. The constructed tree can be substantially larger: its size has the stated form s raised to a soft-O quantity of (log s)/epsilon².

The guarantee was previously unavailable even for algorithms outside the top-down family. A near-matching size lower bound, of the form s raised to soft-Omega(log s), complements the positive result. Together, the bounds establish meaningful approximation power for familiar heuristics in the monotone agnostic setting while quantifying the substantial tree-size growth associated with that guarantee.
summary.tldr: For monotone targets, top-down tree heuristics can approach the best size-s tree's error, with quantified tree-size growth and a near-matching lower bound.

title: Provable guarantees for decision tree induction: the agnostic setting

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular methodology to tune the hyperparameters of expensive black-box functions. Traditionally, BO focuses on a single task at a time and is not designed to leverage information from related functions, such as tuning performance objectives of the same algorithm across multiple datasets. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to achieve transfer learning across different datasets as well as different objectives. The main idea is to regress the mapping from hyperparameter to objective quantiles with a semi-parametric Gaussian Copula distribution, which provides robustness against different scales or outliers that can occur in different tasks. We introduce two methods to leverage this estimation: a Thompson sampling strategy as well as a Gaussian Copula process using such quantile estimate as a prior. We show that these strategies can combine the estimation of multiple objectives such as latency and accuracy, steering the optimization toward faster predictions for the same level of accuracy. Experiments on an extensive set of hyperparameter tuning tasks demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods for both hyperparameter optimization and neural architecture search.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning often repeats similar searches across datasets, even when earlier searches could provide useful guidance. This paper develops a way to transfer that information across both datasets and performance objectives. The central challenge is that objective values from different tasks can have different scales or contain outliers, making their raw numbers difficult to compare.

The approach learns how hyperparameter settings map to objective quantiles: their relative positions within an objective’s distribution. It models this relationship with a semi-parametric Gaussian Copula distribution. The authors then use the estimate in two ways, through Thompson sampling and as a prior for a Gaussian Copula process. Both strategies make the learned relationship available to subsequent optimization.

The methods can also combine objectives such as prediction latency and accuracy, guiding searches toward faster predictions at a given accuracy level. Across the reported tuning experiments, they significantly improve on state-of-the-art methods for hyperparameter optimization and neural architecture search. The contribution is therefore both a transferable representation of performance and two concrete ways to use it.
summary.tldr: Learning objective quantiles lets hyperparameter searches transfer information across datasets and objectives while accommodating differing scales and outliers.

title: A Quantile-based Approach for Hyperparameter Transfer Learning

abstract: Efficiently computing equilibria for multiplayer games is still an open challenge in computational game theory. This paper focuses on computing Team-Maxmin Equilibria (TMEs), which is an important solution concept for zero-sum multiplayer games where players in a team having the same utility function play against an adversary independently. Existing algorithms are inefficient to compute TMEs in large games, especially when the strategy space is too large to be represented due to limited memory. In two-player games, the Incremental Strategy Generation (ISG) algorithm is an efficient approach to avoid enumerating all pure strategies. However, the study of ISG for computing TMEs is completely unexplored. To fill this gap, we first study the properties of ISG for multiplayer games, showing that ISG converges to a Nash Equilibrium (NE) but may not converge to a TME. Second, we design an ISG variant for TMEs (ISGT) by exploiting that a TME is an NE maximizing the team’s utility and show that ISGT converges to a TME and the impossibility of relaxing conditions in ISGT. Third, to further improve the scalability, we design an ISGT variant (CISGT) by using the strategy space for computing an equilibrium that is close to a TME but is easier to be computed as the initial strategy space of ISGT. Finally, extensive experimental results show that CISGT is orders of magnitude faster than ISGT and the state-of-the-art algorithm to compute TMEs in large games.

summary.tldr: The paper develops convergent incremental methods for team equilibria and an initialization strategy that greatly accelerates computation in large games.

title: Converging to Team-Maxmin Equilibria in Zero-Sum Multiplayer Games

abstract: In this paper we study a multi-arm bandit problem in which the quality of each arm is measured by the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) at some level alpha of the reward distribution. While existing works in this setting mainly focus on Upper Confidence Bound algorithms, we introduce a new Thompson Sampling approach for CVaR bandits on bounded rewards that is flexible enough to solve a variety of problems grounded on physical resources. Building on a recent work by Riou & Honda (2020), we introduce B-CVTS for continuous bounded rewards and M-CVTS for multinomial distributions. On the theoretical side, we provide a non-trivial extension of their analysis that enables to theoretically bound their CVaR regret minimization performance. Strikingly, our results show that these strategies are the first to provably achieve asymptotic optimality in CVaR bandits, matching the corresponding asymptotic lower bounds for this setting. Further, we illustrate empirically the benefit of Thompson Sampling approaches both in a realistic environment simulating a use-case in agriculture and on various synthetic examples.

The criterion focuses attention on the relevant tail of the reward distribution rather than evaluating options solely by their average rewards. The setting assumes bounded rewards and is motivated by decisions involving physical resources.

The authors introduce Thompson Sampling methods for this objective, extending a line of work that had mainly emphasized upper confidence bounds. summary.tldr: Two Thompson Sampling methods achieve asymptotically optimal regret for bounded-reward bandits evaluated using CVaR.

title: Optimal Thompson Sampling strategies for support-aware CVaR bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of learning useful robotic skills from previously collected offline data without access to manually specified rewards or additional online exploration, a setting that is becoming increasingly important for scaling robot learning by reusing past robotic data. In particular, we propose the objective of learning a functional understanding of the environment by learning to reach any goal state in a given dataset. We employ goal-conditioned Q-learning with hindsight relabeling and develop several techniques that enable training in a particularly challenging offline setting. We find that our method can operate on high-dimensional camera images and learn a variety of skills on real robots that generalize to previously unseen scenes and objects. We also show that our method can learn to reach long-horizon goals across multiple episodes through goal chaining, and learn rich representations that can help with downstream tasks through pre-training or auxiliary objectives.

paragraphs: This paper studies how robots can learn useful skills from data that has already been collected, without manually designed rewards or further exploration during training. It frames understanding an environment in practical terms: learn how to reach goal states represented in the dataset. This turns past experience into material for learning a range of behaviors.

The method combines goal-conditioned Q-learning with hindsight relabeling, which reinterprets recorded experience in terms of goals it achieved. The authors also develop techniques specifically for the difficult offline setting. Their objective connects learning directly to what a robot can accomplish, while making it possible to reuse data without assigning a separate reward to every desired skill.

The reported results show learning from camera images on real robots, with skills generalizing to unseen objects and scenes. Goal chaining supports longer-horizon goals by connecting experience across multiple episodes. The learned representations can also help downstream tasks through pretraining or auxiliary objectives, giving the offline data value beyond the initially learned goal-reaching behaviors.
summary.tldr: Robots learn goal-reaching skills and useful representations from existing data without manually specified rewards or additional exploration.

title: Actionable Models: Unsupervised Offline Reinforcement Learning of Robotic Skills

abstract: The success of minimax learning problems of generative adversarial networks (GANs) has been observed to depend on the minimax optimization algorithm used for their training. This dependence is commonly attributed to the convergence speed and robustness properties of the underlying optimization algorithm. In this paper, we show that the optimization algorithm also plays a key role in the generalization performance of the trained minimax model. To this end, we analyze the generalization properties of standard gradient descent ascent (GDA) and proximal point method (PPM) algorithms through the lens of algorithmic stability as defined by Bousquet & Elisseeff, 2002 under both convex-concave and nonconvex-nonconcave minimax settings. While the GDA algorithm is not guaranteed to have a vanishing excess risk in convex-concave problems, we show the PPM algorithm enjoys a bounded excess risk in the same setup. For nonconvex-nonconcave problems, we compare the generalization performance of stochastic GDA and GDmax algorithms where the latter fully solves the maximization subproblem at every iteration. Our generalization analysis suggests the superiority of GDA provided that the minimization and maximization subproblems are solved simultaneously with similar learning rates. We discuss several numerical results indicating the role of optimization algorithms in the generalization of learned minimax models.

paragraphs: Minimax models, including generative adversarial networks, involve competing minimization and maximization objectives. Their training algorithm can affect more than convergence speed. This paper studies how that choice also influences generalization, using algorithmic stability to examine how learning behavior changes when the training data changes.

For convex-concave problems, the authors compare gradient descent ascent with the proximal point method. Gradient descent ascent is not guaranteed to achieve vanishing excess risk, while the proximal point method has a bounded excess-risk guarantee in the same setting. The distinction concerns the strength of the available guarantees; a bounded result should not automatically be read as a claim that excess risk vanishes.

For nonconvex-nonconcave problems, the comparison is between stochastic gradient descent ascent and GDmax, which fully solves the maximization problem at every iteration. The analysis suggests an advantage for gradient descent ascent when both sides update simultaneously with similar learning rates. Numerical results illustrate the role of optimization choices in generalization, supporting the paper’s emphasis on the training procedure as part of statistical performance.
summary.tldr: Stability analysis links minimax optimization choices to generalization and suggests benefits from simultaneous gradient updates with similar learning rates.

title: Train simultaneously, generalize better: Stability of gradient-based minimax learners

abstract: A wide range of optimization problems arising in machine learning can be solved by gradient descent algorithms, and a central question in this area is how to efficiently compress a large-scale dataset so as to reduce the computational complexity. Coreset is a popular data compression technique that has been extensively studied before. However, most of existing coreset methods are problem-dependent and cannot be used as a general tool for a broader range of applications. A key obstacle is that they often rely on the pseudo-dimension and total sensitivity bound that can be very high or hard to obtain. In this paper, based on the “locality” property of gradient descent algorithms, we propose a new framework, termed “sequential coreset”, which effectively avoids these obstacles. Moreover, our method is particularly suitable for sparse optimization whence the coreset size can be further reduced to be only poly-logarithmically dependent on the dimension. In practice, the experimental results suggest that our method can save a large amount of running time compared with the baseline algorithms.

A coreset addresses this by compressing the dataset into a smaller representation. The paper targets a difficulty with making this idea broadly useful: existing coreset constructions often depend on mathematical quantities that can be large or difficult to calculate for a particular problem.

The proposed sequential coreset framework instead builds on the locality of gradient descent. The key idea is to exploit the local character of the optimization process when designing the compression. This provides a route around reliance on pseudo-dimension and total sensitivity bounds, which are obstacles for many earlier methods.

The framework is especially suitable for sparse optimization, where its coreset size can depend only polylogarithmically on dimension. That makes the dependence on dimension particularly mild in this setting. Experiments suggest substantial running-time savings relative to the evaluated baseline algorithms, supporting the practical value of compression designed around how optimization proceeds.
summary.tldr: Sequential coresets exploit gradient descent’s locality to compress training data, with particularly favorable size dependence for sparse optimization.

title: A Novel Sequential Coreset Method for Gradient Descent Algorithms

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are considered as intellectual property of their corresponding owners and thus are in urgent need of ownership protection, due to the massive amount of time and resources invested in designing, tuning and training them. In this paper, we propose a novel watermark-based ownership protection method by using the residuals of important parameters. Different from other watermark-based ownership protection methods that rely on some specific neural network architectures and during verification require external data source, namely ownership indicators, our method does not explicitly use ownership indicators for verification to defeat various attacks against DNN watermarks. Specifically, we greedily select a few and important model parameters for embedding so that the impairment caused by the changed parameters can be reduced and the robustness against different attacks can be improved as the selected parameters can well preserve the model information. Also, without the external data sources for verification, the adversary can hardly cast doubts on ownership verification by forging counterfeit watermarks. The extensive experiments show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in five tasks.

This paper proposes embedding a watermark through residuals of important model parameters. Its verification process does not explicitly rely on external ownership indicators, which other watermarking approaches use as evidence of ownership.

The authors argue that this choice reduces the impairment caused by changing parameters while improving robustness against attacks, because the selected parameters preserve model information well. Parameter selection therefore serves both the model’s predictive behavior and the persistence of its ownership signal.

Extensive experiments across five tasks show better performance than previous state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines selective embedding with a verification design intended to strengthen ownership protection. The robustness claim concerns resistance to the attacks studied and does not establish that watermark forgery or removal is impossible.
summary.tldr: Greedily embedding watermarks in important parameter residuals improves ownership protection without explicitly using external verification indicators.

title: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks with Greedy Residuals

abstract: Text-to-image generation has traditionally focused on finding better modeling assumptions for training on a fixed dataset. These assumptions might involve complex architectures, auxiliary losses, or side information such as object part labels or segmentation masks supplied during training. We describe a simple approach for this task based on a transformer that autoregressively models the text and image tokens as a single stream of data. With sufficient data and scale, our approach is competitive with previous domain-specific models when evaluated in a zero-shot fashion.

paragraphs: Text-to-image generation connects a written description with a corresponding image. The paper examines a simple modeling approach in a field where progress had often centered on specialized architectures, additional training losses, or extra annotations such as object-part labels and segmentation masks. It shifts attention toward a shared representation of text and images.

The proposed transformer treats text tokens and image tokens as one stream. It models that stream autoregressively, predicting successive tokens from preceding ones. This places the relationship between language and visual content inside a single sequential modeling task, making the joint token stream the central organizing choice of the approach.

The authors report that, with sufficient training data and scale, this approach is competitive with earlier domain-specific models under zero-shot evaluation. The condition on data and scale is part of the finding. The result supports the idea that a comparatively simple joint modeling formulation can achieve competitive text-to-image performance when developed at sufficient scale, broadening the set of approaches available for the task.
summary.tldr: With sufficient data and scale, a transformer modeling text and image tokens together achieves competitive zero-shot text-to-image generation.

title: Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: We present a detailed study of estimation errors in terms of surrogate loss estimation errors. We refer to such guarantees as H-consistency bounds, since they account for the hypothesis set H adopted. These guarantees are significantly stronger than H-calibration or H-consistency. They are also more informative than similar excess error bounds derived in the literature, when H is the family of all measurable functions. We prove general theorems providing such guarantees, for both the distribution-dependent and distribution-independent settings. We show that our bounds are tight, modulo a convexity assumption. We also show that previous excess error bounds can be recovered as special cases of our general results. We then present a series of explicit bounds in the case of the zero-one loss, with multiple choices of the surrogate loss and for both the family of linear functions and neural networks with one hidden-layer. We further prove more favorable distribution-dependent guarantees in that case. We also present a series of explicit bounds in the case of the adversarial loss, with surrogate losses based on the supremum of the $\rho$-margin, hinge or sigmoid loss and for the same two general hypothesis sets. Here too, we prove several enhancements of these guarantees under natural distributional assumptions. Finally, we report the results of simulations illustrating our bounds and their tightness.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss instead of the error measure ultimately of interest. This paper studies how error in the surrogate objective translates into error for the target objective while accounting for the hypothesis class H. Keeping that class explicit makes the guarantees relevant to the functions a learner can actually use.

The authors develop general H-consistency bounds both with and without dependence on the data distribution. These quantitative guarantees are stronger than H-calibration or H-consistency alone, and recover earlier excess-error bounds as special cases. They show tightness subject to a convexity assumption, clarifying when the bounds accurately capture the relationship between the two objectives.

The paper then derives explicit results for classification error using several surrogate losses, for linear functions and neural networks with one hidden layer. It also treats adversarial losses using surrogates built from margin, hinge, or sigmoid losses. Distributional assumptions yield stronger guarantees in several cases. Simulations illustrate the bounds and their tightness, connecting the general theory to concrete hypothesis classes and learning objectives.
summary.tldr: H-consistency bounds quantify how surrogate-loss errors translate into target errors for specified hypothesis classes.

title: H-Consistency Bounds for Surrogate Loss Minimizers

abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods solve ill-posed inverse problems through iterative proximal algorithms by replacing a proximal operator by a denoising operation. When applied with deep neural network denoisers, these methods have shown state-of-the-art visual performance for image restoration problems. However, their theoretical convergence analysis is still incomplete. Most of the existing convergence results consider nonexpansive denoisers, which is non-realistic, or limit their analysis to strongly convex data-fidelity terms in the inverse problem to solve. Recently, it was proposed to train the denoiser as a gradient descent step on a functional parameterized by a deep neural network. Using such a denoiser guarantees the convergence of the PnP version of the Half-Quadratic-Splitting (PnP-HQS) iterative algorithm. In this paper, we show that this gradient denoiser can actually correspond to the proximal operator of another scalar function. Given this new result, we exploit the convergence theory of proximal algorithms in the nonconvex setting to obtain convergence results for PnP-PGD (Proximal Gradient Descent) and PnP-ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers). When built on top of a smooth gradient denoiser, we show that PnP-PGD and PnP-ADMM are convergent and target stationary points of an explicit functional. These convergence results are confirmed with numerical experiments on deblurring, super-resolution and inpainting.

summary.tldr: Interpreting a smooth gradient denoiser as a proximal operator yields convergence guarantees for two plug-and-play methods toward stationary points.

title: Proximal Denoiser for Convergent Plug-and-Play Optimization with Nonconvex Regularization

abstract: Past work has shown that large language models are susceptible to privacy attacks, where adversaries generate sequences from a trained model and detect which sequences are memorized from the training set. In this work, we show that the success of these attacks is largely due to duplication in commonly used web-scraped training sets. We first show that the rate at which language models regenerate training sequences is superlinearly related to a sequence’s count in the training set. For instance, a sequence that is present 10 times in the training data is on average generated 1000x more often than a sequence that is present only once. We next show that existing methods for detecting memorized sequences have near-chance accuracy on non-duplicated training sequences. Finally, we find that after applying methods to deduplicate training data, language models are considerably more secure against these types of privacy attacks. Taken together, our results motivate an increased focus on deduplication in privacy-sensitive applications and a reevaluation of the practicality of existing privacy attacks.

paragraphs: Some privacy attacks on language models generate text and then try to identify passages memorized from training. This paper investigates how repeated material in web-scraped training data contributes to those attacks. The authors find that duplication accounts for a large part of the success of the attacks they examine.

The relationship between repetition and regeneration is stronger than proportional. A sequence appearing ten times in training is, on average, generated one thousand times as often as a sequence appearing once. The authors also find that existing methods for detecting memorized sequences perform near chance on training sequences that were not duplicated. These observations connect attack effectiveness to both how frequently text reappears and how well attackers can recognize it.

Removing duplicate training material makes the evaluated language models considerably more secure against these types of attacks. The findings support deduplication as a practical priority for privacy-sensitive applications and motivate reconsidering how effective existing attacks are under different data preparation choices. The demonstrated improvement concerns the studied attacks rather than a general guarantee of privacy.
summary.tldr: Repeated training text strongly increases regeneration and privacy-attack success, while deduplication substantially reduces the studied risks.

title: Deduplicating Training Data Mitigates Privacy Risks in Language Models

abstract: We study crowdsourced PAC learning of threshold function, where the labels are gathered from a pool of annotators some of whom may behave adversarially. This is yet a challenging problem and until recently has computationally and query efficient PAC learning algorithm been established by Awasthi et al. (2017). In this paper, we show that by leveraging the more easily acquired pairwise comparison queries, it is possible to exponentially reduce the label complexity while retaining the overall query complexity and runtime. Our main algorithmic contributions are a comparison-equipped labeling scheme that can faithfully recover the true labels of a small set of instances, and a label-efficient filtering process that in conjunction with the small labeled set can reliably infer the true labels of a large instance set.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a threshold function from a crowd of annotators, some of whom may respond adversarially. The objective is PAC learning: obtaining a sufficiently accurate predictor with high probability. In this setting, the learner must manage unreliable responses while keeping both the annotation effort and computation efficient.

The central idea is to supplement direct label requests with pairwise comparisons, which the abstract describes as easier to acquire. The authors develop a comparison-assisted procedure that reliably recovers the true labels of a small group of examples. They then introduce a label-efficient filtering process that uses this small labeled group to infer true labels for a much larger collection.

The resulting approach can exponentially reduce the number of label queries while preserving overall query complexity and runtime. The distinction between labels and total queries is essential: the improvement concerns how much direct labeling is needed, while comparisons remain part of the information gathered. The result applies to the studied threshold-learning problem with potentially adversarial annotators.
summary.tldr: Pairwise comparisons can exponentially reduce direct label requirements for crowdsourced threshold learning while preserving total query complexity and runtime.

title: Efficient PAC Learning from the Crowd with Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: In deep learning, mixture-of-experts (MoE) activates one or few experts (sub-networks) on a per-sample or per-token basis, resulting in significant computation reduction. The recently proposed patch-level routing in MoE (pMoE) divides each input into $n$ patches (or tokens) and sends $l$ patches ($l\ll n$) to each expert through prioritized routing. pMoE has demonstrated great empirical success in reducing training and inference costs while maintaining test accuracy. However, the theoretical explanation of pMoE and the general MoE remains elusive. Focusing on a supervised classification task using a mixture of two-layer convolutional neural networks (CNNs), we show for the first time that pMoE provably reduces the required number of training samples to achieve desirable generalization (referred to as the sample complexity) by a factor in the polynomial order of $n/l$, and outperforms its single-expert counterpart of the same or even larger capacity. The advantage results from the discriminative routing property, which is justified in both theory and practice that pMoE routers can filter label-irrelevant patches and route similar class-discriminative patches to the same expert. Our experimental results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA support our theoretical findings on pMoE’s generalization and show that pMoE can avoid learning spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Patch-level mixture-of-experts models divide an input into n patches and route only a smaller number, l, to each expert. This can reduce computation while preserving accuracy. The paper investigates a further question: whether selectively routing patches can reduce the number of training examples needed for good generalization, giving theoretical support to observed empirical success.

For a supervised classification task using mixtures of two-layer convolutional networks, the authors prove a sample-complexity improvement by a factor polynomial in n/l. In the studied setting, the model outperforms a single expert with equal or even greater capacity. The explanation is discriminative routing: routers filter out patches irrelevant to the label and send similar, class-informative patches to the same expert.

Theory and practical evidence support this routing property. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA also support the generalization findings and show that the method can avoid learning spurious correlations. The result ties a particular routing behavior to sample efficiency within the analyzed CNN setting, adding a statistical benefit to the computational motivation for expert models.
summary.tldr: For the studied two-layer CNN setting, patch routing provably reduces sample complexity by directing class-relevant patches to specialized experts.

title: Patch-level Routing in Mixture-of-Experts is Provably Sample-efficient for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Spherical CNNs generalize CNNs to functions on the sphere, by using spherical convolutions as the main linear operation. The most accurate and efficient way to compute spherical convolutions is in the spectral domain (via the convolution theorem), which is still costlier than the usual planar convolutions. For this reason, applications of spherical CNNs have so far been limited to small problems that can be approached with low model capacity. In this work, we show how spherical CNNs can be scaled for much larger problems. To achieve this, we make critical improvements including novel variants of common model components, an implementation of core operations to exploit hardware accelerator characteristics, and application-specific input representations that exploit the properties of our model. Experiments show our larger spherical CNNs reach state-of-the-art on several targets of the QM9 molecular benchmark, which was previously dominated by equivariant graph neural networks, and achieve competitive performance on multiple weather forecasting tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/google-research/spherical-cnn.

paragraphs: Spherical convolutional neural networks extend convolution to signals defined on a sphere. Computing these convolutions in the spectral domain offers accuracy and efficiency, but still costs more than ordinary planar convolution. This expense has restricted applications to smaller problems and models with limited capacity.

The paper tackles scaling through several connected changes. It introduces variants of familiar model components, implements core operations to take advantage of hardware accelerators, and designs input representations suited to particular applications and the model's properties. Together, these improvements allow larger spherical networks to address more demanding problems.

Experiments show leading performance on several prediction targets in the QM9 molecular benchmark, a setting previously dominated by equivariant graph neural networks. The larger models also achieve competitive results on multiple weather forecasting tasks. These findings demonstrate that spherical convolution can be useful beyond the small-scale settings imposed by its computational cost. The contribution combines model design, implementation, and input representation to make that increased scale effective in the reported applications.
summary.tldr: Model, implementation, and representation improvements scale spherical CNNs to strong molecular prediction and competitive weather forecasting results.

title: Scaling Spherical CNNs

abstract: Aiming at promoting the safe real-world deployment of Reinforcement Learning (RL), research on safe RL has made significant progress in recent years. However, most existing works in the literature still focus on the online setting where risky violations of the safety budget are likely to be incurred during training. Besides, in many realworld applications, the learned policy is required to respond to dynamically determined safety budgets (i.e., constraint threshold) in real time. In this paper, we target at the above real-time budget constraint problem under the offline setting, and propose Trajectory-based REal-time Budget Inference (TREBI) as a novel solution that approaches this problem from the perspective of trajectory distribution. Theoretically, we prove an error bound of the estimation on the episodic reward and cost under the offline setting and thus provide a performance guarantee for TREBI. Empirical results on a wide range of simulation tasks and a real-world large-scale advertising application demonstrate the capability of TREBI in solving real-time budget constraint problems under offline settings.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must balance reward with constraints on cost. Online training can violate those constraints while a policy learns, and practical deployments may require the policy to respond immediately when the permitted safety budget changes. This paper addresses both concerns by studying real-time budget constraints in an offline setting.

The proposed TREBI method approaches the problem through distributions over trajectories. This makes sequences of behavior the basis for handling a dynamically specified budget. Its focus is on adapting to the constraint threshold supplied in real time while operating within the offline reinforcement-learning setting, where training does not depend on collecting risky online experience.

The authors derive an error bound for estimates of episodic reward and cost, providing a performance guarantee for TREBI. Evaluations across simulation tasks and a large-scale real-world advertising application demonstrate its ability to handle changing budget constraints. The theoretical and empirical results support budget-responsive decision-making, with the guarantee specifically grounded in the analysis of offline reward and cost estimation.
summary.tldr: TREBI uses trajectory distributions to handle changing safety budgets in offline reinforcement learning.

title: Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning with Real-Time Budget Constraints

abstract: 2D human pose estimation predicts keypoint locations and the corresponding confidence. Calibration-wise, the confidence should be aligned with the pose accuracy. Yet existing pose estimation methods tend to estimate confidence with heuristics such as the maximum value of heatmaps. This work shows, through theoretical analysis and empirical verification, a calibration gap in current pose estimation frameworks. Our derivations directly lead to closed-form adjustments in the confidence based on additionally inferred instance size and visibility. Given the black-box nature of deep neural networks, however, it is not possible to close the gap with only closed-form adjustments. We go one step further and propose a Calibrated ConfidenceNet (CCNet) to explicitly learn network-specific adjustments with a confidence prediction branch. The proposed CCNet, as a lightweight post-hoc addition, improves the calibration of standard off-the-shelf pose estimation frameworks.

paragraphs: A human pose estimator predicts body-keypoint locations and confidence values. For confidence to be useful, it should reflect how accurate those predictions are. This paper shows through theory and experiments that common confidence heuristics, such as taking a heatmap's maximum value, leave a gap between reported confidence and pose accuracy.

The theoretical analysis leads to explicit confidence adjustments using additionally inferred instance size and visibility. These factors supply information that a simple heatmap-based confidence can miss. However, the authors find that such closed-form adjustments alone cannot eliminate the calibration gap because they cannot fully account for the behavior of a black-box neural network.

To address the remaining mismatch, the authors introduce Calibrated ConfidenceNet, or CCNet. It adds a confidence-prediction branch that learns adjustments specific to the underlying network. As a lightweight component applied after the original model is available, CCNet improves calibration in standard off-the-shelf pose estimators. The stated improvement concerns making confidence more faithful to prediction accuracy.
summary.tldr: CCNet improves pose-estimation confidence calibration by combining analytically motivated adjustments with learned network-specific corrections.

title: On the Calibration of Human Pose Estimation

abstract: In this work, we introduce the Prototypical Transformer (ProtoFormer), a general and unified framework that approaches various motion tasks from a prototype perspective. ProtoFormer seamlessly integrates prototype learning with Transformer by thoughtfully considering motion dynamics, introducing two innovative designs. First, Cross-Attention Prototyping discovers prototypes based on signature motion patterns, providing transparency in understanding motion scenes. Second, Latent Synchronization guides feature representation learning via prototypes, effectively mitigating the problem of motion uncertainty. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance on popular motion tasks such as optical flow and scene depth. Furthermore, it exhibits generality across various downstream tasks, including object tracking and video stabilization.

paragraphs: Motion understanding involves learning representations that can support several related tasks. ProtoFormer approaches this through prototypes: representative motion patterns that organize how a model interprets a scene. The paper combines prototype learning with a Transformer in a unified framework, with its design explicitly taking motion dynamics into account.

Two components implement the approach. Cross-Attention Prototyping discovers prototypes associated with characteristic motion patterns, providing a more transparent basis for understanding motion scenes. Latent Synchronization then uses those prototypes to guide feature learning and reduce motion uncertainty. The prototypes thus serve both as an organizing representation and as guidance for learning the features used by the model.

The reported experiments show competitive performance on optical flow and scene depth, along with applicability to object tracking and video stabilization. These results support the framework's generality across several motion-related tasks. The stated finding is that prototype-guided representations can work across this range of applications, with competitive task performance rather than a claim of uniformly surpassing every alternative.
summary.tldr: ProtoFormer uses learned motion prototypes to guide Transformer representations and achieve competitive results across several motion-related tasks.

title: Prototypical Transformer As Unified Motion Learners

abstract: Counterfactual estimation from observations represents a critical endeavor in numerous application fields, such as healthcare and finance, with the primary challenge being the mitigation of treatment bias. The balancing strategy aimed at reducing covariate disparities between different treatment groups serves as a universal solution. However, when it comes to the time series data, the effectiveness of balancing strategies remains an open question, with a thorough analysis of the robustness and applicability of balancing strategies still lacking. This paper revisits counterfactual estimation in the temporal setting and provides a brief overview of recent advancements in balancing strategies. More importantly, we conduct a critical empirical examination for the effectiveness of the balancing strategies within the realm of temporal counterfactual estimation in various settings on multiple datasets. Our findings could be of significant interest to researchers and practitioners and call for a reexamination of the balancing strategy in time series settings.

paragraphs: Counterfactual estimation asks what might have happened under a different treatment or decision, using observations of what actually occurred. A central difficulty is treatment bias: groups receiving different treatments can differ in other relevant characteristics. Balancing strategies try to reduce these differences so that comparisons between treatment groups are more informative.

This paper examines whether that strategy works effectively when observations form time series. The authors revisit counterfactual estimation in this temporal setting and summarize recent balancing approaches. Their main contribution is an empirical investigation across multiple datasets and settings, focused on the effectiveness, robustness, and applicability of balancing rather than introducing a new estimation method.

The findings lead the authors to call for reconsidering how balancing is used with time-series data. That conclusion questions the transfer of a broadly used strategy into temporal problems; it does not establish that balancing always fails. The practical significance is that reducing differences between treatment groups deserves direct evaluation in temporal estimation, rather than being treated as sufficient evidence that the counterfactual estimates will improve.
summary.tldr: An empirical study across datasets calls for reexamining the effectiveness of balancing strategies for time-series counterfactual estimation.

title: An Empirical Examination of Balancing Strategy for Counterfactual Estimation on Time Series

abstract: We present a novel perspective on goal-conditioned reinforcement learning by framing it within the context of denoising diffusion models. Analogous to the diffusion process, where Gaussian noise is used to create random trajectories that walk away from the data manifold, we construct trajectories that move away from potential goal states. We then learn a goal-conditioned policy to reverse these deviations, analogous to the score function. This approach, which we call Merlin, can reach specified goals from arbitrary initial states without learning a separate value function. In contrast to recent works utilizing diffusion models in offline RL, Merlin stands out as the first method to perform diffusion in the state space, requiring only one "denoising" iteration per environment step. We experimentally validate our approach in various offline goal-reaching tasks, demonstrating substantial performance enhancements compared to state-of-the-art methods while improving computational efficiency over other diffusion-based RL methods by an order of magnitude. Our results suggest that this perspective on diffusion for RL is a simple and scalable approach for sequential decision making.

paragraphs: Merlin approaches goal-conditioned reinforcement learning through the logic of denoising diffusion. Instead of beginning only with trajectories toward a target, it constructs trajectories that move away from potential goal states. A goal-conditioned policy then learns to reverse these departures, connecting the task of reaching a goal with undoing a process that moves away from it.

The diffusion process operates in state space, and the learned policy plays a role analogous to a score function. Merlin can reach specified goals from arbitrary initial states without training a separate value function. Its interaction procedure requires only one denoising iteration per environment step, making the relationship between diffusion and sequential action selection especially direct.

Experiments on several offline goal-reaching tasks report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Compared with other diffusion-based reinforcement learning approaches, Merlin also improves computational efficiency by an order of magnitude. These findings support the authors' suggestion that state-space diffusion offers a simple, scalable perspective on sequential decision making. The empirical gains concern the evaluated offline goal-reaching tasks, while broader scalability is presented as a promising implication.
summary.tldr: Merlin learns to reverse trajectories away from goals, enabling state-space diffusion policies with one denoising iteration per environment step.

title: Learning to Reach Goals via Diffusion

abstract: In deep learning, classification tasks are formalized as optimization problems often solved via the minimization of the cross-entropy. However, recent advancements in the design of objective functions allow the usage of the $f$-divergence to generalize the formulation of the optimization problem for classification. We adopt a Bayesian perspective and formulate the classification task as a maximum a posteriori probability problem. We propose a class of objective functions based on the variational representation of the $f$-divergence. Furthermore, driven by the challenge of improving the state-of-the-art approach, we propose a bottom-up method that leads us to the formulation of an objective function corresponding to a novel $f$-divergence referred to as shifted log (SL). We theoretically analyze the objective functions proposed and numerically test them in three application scenarios: toy examples, image datasets, and signal detection/decoding problems. The analyzed scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and that the SL divergence achieves the highest classification accuracy in almost all the considered cases.

paragraphs: Classification models are commonly trained by minimizing cross-entropy, but this paper explores a broader family of objectives based on f-divergences. The authors take a Bayesian perspective, expressing classification as a maximum a posteriori probability problem. This provides the starting point for deriving alternative objectives rather than treating cross-entropy as the default formulation.

They use a variational representation of f-divergence to construct a class of training objectives. They also take a bottom-up approach to developing an additional objective associated with a new divergence called shifted log, or SL. The contribution therefore includes both a general formulation and a particular member designed to improve classification performance.

The paper analyzes the proposed objectives theoretically and evaluates them on toy examples, image datasets, and signal detection or decoding problems. Across these settings, the results support the approach, with SL achieving the highest classification accuracy in almost all considered cases. This is evidence that the choice of divergence can materially affect classification outcomes within the tested applications.
summary.tldr: The paper derives classification objectives from f-divergences and introduces shifted log divergence, which achieves the highest accuracy in almost all evaluated cases.

title: $f$-Divergence Based Classification: Beyond the Use of Cross-Entropy

abstract: Spectral Kernel Networks (SKNs) emerge as a promising approach in machine learning, melding solid theoretical foundations of spectral kernels with the representation power of hierarchical architectures. At its core, the spectral density function plays a pivotal role by revealing essential patterns in data distributions, thereby offering deep insights into the underlying framework in real-world tasks. Nevertheless, prevailing designs of spectral density often overlook the intricate interactions within data structures. This phenomenon consequently neglects expanses of the hypothesis space, thus curtailing the performance of SKNs. This paper addresses the issues through a novel approach, the Copula-Nested Spectral Kernel Network (CokeNet). Concretely, we first redefine the spectral density with the form of copulas to enhance the diversity of spectral densities. Next, the specific expression of the copula module is designed to allow the excavation of complex dependence structures. Finally, the unified kernel network is proposed by integrating the corresponding spectral kernel and the copula module. Through rigorous theoretical analysis and experimental verification, CokeNet demonstrates superior performance and significant advancements over SOTA algorithms in the field.
