paragraphs: Spectral Kernel Networks combine spectral kernels with hierarchical representations. Their spectral density helps determine the patterns the resulting model can capture. The paper argues that existing density designs overlook complex dependencies in data, leaving portions of the possible function space unexplored and restricting the networks’ performance.

CokeNet changes the spectral density using copulas, mathematical constructions for representing dependence. The purpose is to make the available spectral densities more diverse and allow richer interactions to enter the model. The authors design a copula module specifically to capture complex dependence structures, then integrate it with the corresponding spectral kernel in a unified network.

This approach places dependency modeling inside the construction of the kernel network itself. Its significance is that the choice of spectral density becomes a route to expanding what the architecture can represent. The authors support CokeNet with theoretical analysis and experimental verification, reporting superior performance over state-of-the-art algorithms. The stated findings support the proposed use of copulas to enrich these networks, without specifying a numerical improvement in the abstract.
summary.tldr: CokeNet uses copulas to enrich spectral kernel networks with more expressive models of dependence.

title: Copula-Nested Spectral Kernel Network

abstract: Policy gradient methods have enabled deep reinforcement learning (RL) to approach challenging continuous control problems, even when the underlying systems involve highly nonlinear dynamics that generate complex non-smooth optimization landscapes. We develop a rigorous framework for understanding how policy gradient methods mollify non-smooth optimization landscapes to enable effective policy search, as well as the downside of it: while making the objective function smoother and easier to optimize, the stochastic objective deviates further from the original problem. We demonstrate the equivalence between policy gradient methods and solving backward heat equations. Following the ill-posedness of backward heat equations from PDE theory, we present a fundamental challenge to the use of policy gradient under stochasticity. Moreover, we make the connection between this limitation and the uncertainty principle in harmonic analysis to understand the effects of exploration with stochastic policies in RL. We also provide experimental results to illustrate both the positive and negative aspects of mollification effects in practice.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods can tackle continuous-control problems even when nonlinear dynamics create rough, nonsmooth optimization landscapes. This paper develops a mathematical explanation of how stochastic policies smooth those landscapes. The smoothing, called mollification, can make the objective easier to optimize and thereby help policy search.

The same mechanism has a cost: the stochastic objective moves further away from the original problem as smoothing increases. The authors establish an equivalence between policy gradient methods and solving backward heat equations. Because those equations are ill-posed in partial differential equation theory, the connection exposes a fundamental challenge for policy gradient methods operating under stochasticity.

The paper further relates this limitation to the uncertainty principle in harmonic analysis, using that connection to interpret exploration with stochastic policies. Experiments illustrate both the helpful and harmful effects of smoothing. The result is a framework for understanding a tradeoff within exploration: randomness can improve the optimization landscape while also changing the objective being optimized, so easier optimization does not by itself establish closer agreement with the original problem.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how stochastic policy gradients smooth difficult objectives while introducing a fundamental tradeoff between optimization ease and fidelity to the original problem.

title: Mollification Effects of Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: We propose a novel algorithmic framework for distributional reinforcement learning, based on learning finite-dimensional mean embeddings of return distributions. The framework reveals a wide variety of new algorithms for dynamic programming and temporal-difference algorithms that rely on the sketch Bellman operator, which updates mean embeddings with simple linear-algebraic computations. We provide asymptotic convergence theory, and examine the empirical performance of the algorithms on a suite of tabular tasks. Further, we show that this approach can be straightforwardly combined with deep reinforcement learning.

We provide asymptotic convergence theory, and examine the empirical performance of the algorithms on a suite of tabular tasks. paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the distribution of returns associated with behavior. This paper proposes learning finite-dimensional mean embeddings of those distributions. The resulting representation provides a compact object on which learning algorithms can operate, making the choice of distribution representation a central part of the method.

The framework introduces a sketch Bellman operator that updates these embeddings through simple linear algebra. This operator supports a variety of algorithms for dynamic programming and temporal-difference learning. The contribution therefore extends beyond a single update rule: it supplies a shared way to construct algorithms around the same representation and computational operation.

The authors provide asymptotic convergence theory and examine empirical behavior on tabular tasks. They also show that the approach can be combined straightforwardly with deep reinforcement learning. These results connect the proposed representation to both theoretical analysis and practical learning settings. The convergence claim concerns asymptotic behavior, while the reported experiments explore how the algorithms perform on the tabular problems considered.
summary.tldr: Finite-dimensional mean embeddings turn distributional Bellman updates into linear-algebraic operations, supporting a family of reinforcement learning algorithms.

title: Distributional Bellman Operators over Mean Embeddings

abstract: In image processing, solving inverse problems is the task of finding plausible reconstructions of an image that was corrupted by some (usually known) degradation operator. Commonly, this process is done using a generative image model that can guide the reconstruction towards solutions that appear natural. The success of diffusion models over the last few years has made them a leading candidate for this task. However, the sequential nature of diffusion models makes this conditional sampling process challenging. Furthermore, since diffusion models are often defined in the latent space of an autoencoder, the encoder-decoder transformations introduce additional difficulties. To address these challenges, we suggest a novel sampling method based on sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) in the latent space of diffusion models. We name our method LD-SMC. We define a generative model for the data using additional auxiliary observations and perform posterior inference with SMC sampling based on a backward diffusion process. Empirical evaluations on ImageNet and FFHQ show the benefits of LD-SMC over competing methods in various inverse problem tasks and especially in challenging inpainting tasks.

paragraphs: An image inverse problem asks which plausible original images could have produced a corrupted observation. A generative model can guide reconstruction toward natural-looking solutions, but conditioning a diffusion model on an observation is challenging because generation proceeds sequentially. When diffusion takes place in an autoencoder's latent space, the transformations between latent representations and images introduce further difficulties.

LD-SMC addresses these issues with sequential Monte Carlo sampling in latent space. The authors define a generative model that includes additional auxiliary observations, then perform posterior inference using a backward diffusion process. This formulation places the reconstruction task within a sampling procedure that accounts for observations while following the model's sequential generation structure.

Evaluations on ImageNet and FFHQ show benefits over competing methods across several inverse problems, with especially strong findings for challenging inpainting tasks. The practical significance is a method for obtaining plausible reconstructions while handling the extra complications of latent diffusion. The evidence supports the proposed inference procedure on the evaluated reconstruction tasks, particularly where missing image content makes conditioning difficult.
summary.tldr: LD-SMC combines latent diffusion with sequential Monte Carlo inference to improve image reconstruction, especially on challenging inpainting tasks.

title: Inverse Problem Sampling in Latent Space Using Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: Fast and accurate generation of molecular conformers is desired for downstream computational chemistry and drug discovery tasks. Currently, training and sampling state-of-the-art diffusion or flow-based models for conformer generation require significant computational resources. In this work, we build upon flow-matching and propose two mechanisms for accelerating training and inference of generative models for 3D molecular conformer generation. For fast training, we introduce the SO(3)-Averaged Flow training objective, which leads to faster convergence to better generation quality compared to conditional optimal transport flow or Kabsch-aligned flow. We demonstrate that models trained using SO(3)-Averaged Flow can reach state-of-the-art conformer generation quality. For fast inference, we show that the reflow and distillation methods of flow-based models enable few-steps or even one-step molecular conformer generation with high quality. The training techniques proposed in this work show a path towards highly efficient molecular conformer generation with flow-based models.

paragraphs: Generating three-dimensional molecular conformers accurately and quickly is useful for computational chemistry and drug discovery. Existing diffusion and flow-based generators can require substantial computation both during training and when producing samples. This paper addresses those two costs separately within a flow-matching approach.

For training, the authors introduce an SO(3)-Averaged Flow objective. They report that it converges faster and reaches better generation quality than conditional optimal transport flow or Kabsch-aligned flow. Models trained with the new objective can reach state-of-the-art conformer generation quality, making training efficiency compatible with strong output quality in the reported results.

For inference, the paper applies reflow and distillation methods to enable generation in only a few steps, or even one step, while retaining high quality. This tackles the repeated computation involved in sampling separately from the cost of learning the model. Together, the two mechanisms show a path toward more efficient flow-based conformer generation across both stages of use.
summary.tldr: An SO(3)-Averaged Flow objective accelerates conformer-model training, while reflow and distillation enable high-quality few-step or one-step generation.

title: Efficient Molecular Conformer Generation with SO(3)-Averaged Flow Matching and Reflow

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited impressive performance and surprising emergent properties. However, their effectiveness remains limited by the fixed context window of the transformer architecture, posing challenges for long-context modeling. Among these challenges, length generalization — the ability to generalize to sequences longer than those seen during training — is a classical and fundamental problem. In this work, we propose a fresh perspective on length generalization, shifting the focus from the conventional emphasis on input features such as positional encodings or data structures to the output distribution of the model. Specifically, through case studies on synthetic tasks, we highlight the critical role of long-short alignment — the consistency of output distributions across sequences of varying lengths. Extending this insight to natural language tasks, we propose a metric called Long-Short Misalignment to quantify this phenomenon, uncovering a strong correlation between the metric and length generalization performance. Building on these findings, we develop a regularization term that promotes long-short alignment during training. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, offering new insights for achieving more effective long-context modeling in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/LongShortAlignment.

paragraphs: Length generalization is the ability to handle sequences longer than those encountered during training. This paper approaches the problem through a language model’s output distributions. It asks whether consistency between outputs on shorter and longer sequences can help explain why some models extend to greater lengths more effectively.

Synthetic task studies highlight long-short alignment: consistency of output distributions across sequence lengths. The authors then introduce Long-Short Misalignment, a metric for measuring this behavior in natural language tasks. They find a strong correlation between the metric and length generalization performance, making output behavior a useful signal for studying the problem.

Building on this observation, the paper develops a training regularizer that encourages alignment across lengths. Extensive experiments support the approach’s effectiveness for long-context modeling. The work thus connects a diagnostic observation with a training intervention: measure how output distributions diverge across lengths, then encourage greater consistency. The reported correlation motivates this strategy, while the experiments provide evidence for the intervention itself.
summary.tldr: Aligning output distributions across short and long sequences provides a useful diagnostic and an effective training regularizer for length generalization.

title: Long-Short Alignment for Effective Long-Context Modeling in LLMs

abstract: Traditional robust methods in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often struggle against coordinated adversarial attacks in cooperative scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose the Wolfpack Adversarial Attack framework, inspired by wolf hunting strategies, which targets an initial agent and its assisting agents to disrupt cooperation. Additionally, we introduce the Wolfpack-Adversarial Learning for MARL (WALL) framework, which trains robust MARL policies to defend against the proposed Wolfpack attack by fostering system-wide collaboration. Experimental results underscore the devastating impact of the Wolfpack attack and the significant robustness improvements achieved by WALL. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunwoolee0504/WALL.

Our code is available at https://github.com/sunwoolee0504/WALL.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent systems depend on agents supporting one another, which creates opportunities for coordinated attacks. This paper investigates attacks directed at that cooperative behavior. The authors argue that traditional robustness methods in multi-agent reinforcement learning often struggle when adversaries coordinate their interference across a team.

The proposed Wolfpack attack first targets an agent and also targets the agents that assist it. Inspired by wolf hunting strategies, this structure aims to disrupt cooperation through linked pressure on the initial target and its support. The paper pairs this attack with Wolfpack-Adversarial Learning for MARL, or WALL, which trains policies to defend against it by encouraging collaboration across the system.

Experiments show a severe impact from the Wolfpack attack and substantial robustness improvements from WALL. The attack and defense therefore serve complementary purposes: one exposes weaknesses in cooperative behavior, and the other trains collaboration to withstand the proposed threat. The findings support treating robustness as a property of the interacting team, with the reported defense gains established against the evaluated Wolfpack attack.
summary.tldr: Wolfpack attacks an agent and its helpers, while WALL trains team-wide collaboration to improve robustness against that attack.

title: Wolfpack Adversarial Attack for Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The real world naturally has dimensions of time and space. Therefore, estimating the counterfactual outcomes with spatial-temporal attributes is a crucial problem. However, previous methods are based on classical statistical models, which still have limitations in performance and generalization. This paper proposes a novel framework for estimating counterfactual outcomes with spatial-temporal attributes using the Transformer, exhibiting stronger estimation ability. Under mild assumptions, the proposed estimator within this framework is consistent and asymptotically normal. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct simulation experiments and real data experiments. Simulation experiments show that our estimator has a stronger estimation capability than baseline methods. Real data experiments provide a valuable conclusion to the causal effect of conflicts on forest loss in Colombia. The source code is available at this URL.

paragraphs: Counterfactual outcome estimation asks what an outcome would have been under a different circumstance. When observations vary across locations and over time, an estimator must account for both spatial and temporal attributes. This paper proposes a Transformer-based framework for that problem, addressing performance and generalization limitations associated with earlier classical statistical approaches.

The contribution combines a learned estimation framework with theoretical guarantees. Under assumptions described by the authors as mild, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Consistency concerns approaching the target as data increase, while asymptotic normality characterizes the limiting form of estimation error. These properties are conditional on the stated assumptions rather than automatic consequences of using a Transformer.

Simulation experiments report stronger estimation ability than baseline methods. The authors also apply the framework to real data concerning the causal effect of conflict on forest loss in Colombia. This application connects the estimator to a concrete spatial-temporal causal question. The abstract reports a valuable conclusion from that analysis without specifying the effect’s direction or size.
summary.tldr: A Transformer framework improves spatial-temporal counterfactual estimation in simulations and has consistency and asymptotic normality under stated assumptions.

title: Transformer-Based Spatial-Temporal Counterfactual Outcomes Estimation

abstract: Quantizing model weights is critical for reducing the communication and inference costs of large models. However, quantizing models – especially to low precisions like int4 or int2 – requires a trade-off in model quality; int2, in particular, is known to severely degrade model quality. Consequently, practitioners are often forced to maintain multiple models with different quantization levels or serve a single model that best satisfies the quality-latency trade-off. On the other hand, integer data types, such as int8, inherently possess a nested (Matryoshka) structure where smaller bit-width integers, like int4 or int2, are nested within the most significant bits. Leveraging this insight, in this paper, we propose Matryoshka Quantization (MatQuant), a novel multi-scale quantization technique that alleviates the aforementioned challenge. This technique allows us to train and maintain a single quantized model but serve it with the precision demanded by the deployment. Furthermore, leveraging MatQuant’s co-training and co-distillation, int2 precision models extracted by MatQuant outperform standard int2 quantization by up to 4% and 7% with OmniQuant and QAT as base algorithms respectively. Finally, we demonstrate that by using an extra bit to represent outliers, a model with an effective precision of 2.05-bit improves further by 6% with OmniQuant as the base algorithm.

paragraphs: Matryoshka Quantization addresses the need to deploy a model at different numerical precisions. Lower precision reduces communication and inference costs, but can damage quality, especially at two bits. This often leaves practitioners maintaining several quantized models or selecting a single compromise between quality and latency.

The method uses the nested structure of integer representations: the most significant bits of a larger integer can provide a smaller-bit representation. MatQuant trains a single quantized model that can then be served at the precision a deployment requires. Its co-training and co-distillation also improve the quality of the lowest-precision versions extracted from that shared model.

The authors report that extracted two-bit models outperform standard two-bit quantization by up to 4% with OmniQuant and 7% with quantization-aware training as the base algorithm. They further report a 6% improvement using OmniQuant when an extra bit represents outliers, producing an effective precision of 2.05 bits. These results show that jointly training nested precision levels can support deployment flexibility while improving the reported low-precision quality.
summary.tldr: MatQuant trains one model for multiple nested precision levels and improves the quality of its extracted two-bit versions.

title: Matryoshka Quantization

abstract: We address the problem of convex optimization with dueling feedback, where the goal is to minimize a convex function given a weaker form of dueling feedback. Each query consists of two points and the dueling feedback returns a (noisy) single-bit binary comparison of the function values of the two queried points. The translation of the function values to the single comparison bit is through a transfer function. This problem has been addressed previously for some restricted classes of transfer functions, but here we consider a very general transfer function class which includes all functions that admit a series expansion about the origin. Our main contribution is an efficient algorithm with convergence rate of $O(\epsilon^{-4p})$ for smooth convex functions, and an optimal rate of $\widetilde O(\epsilon^{-2p})$ when the objective is both smooth and strongly convex, where $p$ is the minimal degree (with a non-zero coefficient) in the transfer’s series expansion about the origin.

The algorithm cannot directly observe their objective values; it receives a single bit indicating their relative quality. A transfer function controls how differences in objective values become this limited feedback, making its behavior central to the optimization problem.

Earlier approaches handled restricted families of transfer functions. The authors develop an efficient algorithm for a much broader class, including all transfer functions that admit a series expansion around zero. Their guarantees depend on p, the smallest degree with a nonzero coefficient in that expansion. This connects convergence to how the comparison mechanism behaves when objective values are close.

For smooth convex objectives, the stated convergence rate is O(ε^(-4p)). When the objective is also strongly convex, the rate improves to Õ(ε^(-2p)), which the authors establish as optimal. The results show how both the objective’s structure and the comparison mechanism determine the difficulty of reaching a desired accuracy using only dueling feedback.
summary.tldr: An algorithm optimizes smooth convex functions from noisy comparisons across a broad transfer-function class, with an optimal rate under strong convexity.

title: Dueling Convex Optimization with General Preferences

abstract: We introduce adaptive learn-then-test (aLTT), an efficient hyperparameter selection procedure that provides finite-sample statistical guarantees on the population risk of AI models. Unlike the existing learn-then-test (LTT) technique, which relies on conventional p-value-based multiple hypothesis testing (MHT), aLTT implements sequential data-dependent MHT with early termination by leveraging e-processes. As a result, aLTT can reduce the number of testing rounds, making it particularly well-suited for scenarios in which testing is costly or presents safety risks. Apart from maintaining statistical validity, in applications such as online policy selection for offline reinforcement learning and prompt engineering, aLTT is shown to achieve the same performance as LTT while requiring only a fraction of the testing rounds.

paragraphs: Selecting a model configuration involves more than finding a promising score: the chosen configuration may also need a statistical guarantee about its population risk. Adaptive learn-then-test, or aLTT, addresses this selection problem while trying to reduce the amount of testing required. Its guarantees apply with a finite number of observations.

Existing learn-then-test uses multiple hypothesis testing based on conventional p-values. The proposed method instead uses e-processes to support sequential, data-dependent testing with early termination. This allows the testing procedure to respond to accumulating evidence and stop early while preserving statistical validity. The central contribution is therefore a way to make testing adaptive without giving up the stated risk guarantees.

The paper demonstrates the approach in online policy selection for offline reinforcement learning and in prompt engineering. In these applications, aLTT reaches the same performance as LTT using only a fraction of the testing rounds. That reduction is particularly relevant when each additional test is expensive or exposes a system to safety risks, because the selection procedure itself consumes resources.
summary.tldr: Adaptive learn-then-test preserves finite-sample risk guarantees while reducing testing rounds through sequential testing and early stopping.

title: Adaptive Learn-then-Test: Statistically Valid and Efficient Hyperparameter Selection

abstract: The performance of models trained by Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is sensitive to perturbations in observations, lowering their trustworthiness in complex environments. Adversarial training is a valuable approach to enhance their performance robustness. However, existing methods often overfit to adversarial perturbations of observations and fail to incorporate prior information about the policy adopted by their protagonist agent, i.e., the primary one being trained. To address this important issue, this paper introduces Adversarial Training with Stochastic Adversary (ATSA), where the proposed adversary is trained online alongside the protagonist agent. The former consists of Stochastic Director (SDor) and SDor-guided generaTor (STor). SDor performs policy perturbations by minimizing the expected team reward of protagonists and maximizing the entropy of its policy, while STor generates adversarial perturbations of observations by following SDor’s guidance. We prove that SDor’s soft policy converges to a global optimum according to factorized maximum-entropy MARL and leads to the optimal adversary. This paper also introduces an SDor-STor loss function to quantify the difference between a) perturbations in the agent’s policy and b) those advised by SDor. We evaluate our ATSA on StarCraft II tasks and autonomous driving scenarios, demonstrating that a) it is robust against diverse perturbations of observations while maintaining outstanding performance in perturbation-free environments, and b) it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

Experiments on StarCraft II and autonomous-driving scenarios report robustness to diverse observation perturbations, strong performance without perturbations, and improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the coordinated director-generator design.
summary.tldr: ATSA jointly trains a stochastic policy-level director and observation-perturbation generator to improve multi-agent robustness.

title: Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Adversary

abstract: The measurement tasks involved in evaluating generative AI (GenAI) systems lack sufficient scientific rigor, leading to what has been described as "a tangle of sloppy tests [and] apples-to-oranges comparisons" (Roose, 2024). In this position paper, we argue that the ML community would benefit from learning from and drawing on the social sciences when developing and using measurement instruments for evaluating GenAI systems. Specifically, our position is that evaluating GenAI systems is a social science measurement challenge. We present a four-level framework, grounded in measurement theory from the social sciences, for measuring concepts related to the capabilities, behaviors, and impacts of GenAI systems. This framework has two important implications: First, it can broaden the expertise involved in evaluating GenAI systems by enabling stakeholders with different perspectives to participate in conceptual debates. Second, it brings rigor to both conceptual and operational debates by offering a set of lenses for interrogating validity.

paragraphs: Evaluating generative AI requires deciding what concepts such as capability, behavior, and impact mean, then choosing how to measure them. This position paper argues that current evaluation practices lack sufficient scientific rigor. It proposes drawing on social science measurement theory to improve both the questions evaluators ask and the instruments they use.

The authors present a four-level framework for measuring concepts relevant to generative AI systems. The framework connects conceptual debates with operational ones: researchers must examine the meaning of a target concept as well as how an evaluation represents it. Its central concern is validity, or whether a measurement supports the interpretation being placed on it.

The authors identify two benefits of this approach. It can broaden participation by making room for stakeholders with different perspectives to debate the concepts being measured. It also provides structured ways to scrutinize evaluation choices. The contribution is a framework for making evaluations more defensible and interpretable, rather than treating agreement on a test procedure as sufficient agreement about what its results mean.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a social science measurement framework to clarify what generative AI evaluations measure and whether their interpretations are valid.

title: Position: Evaluating Generative AI Systems Is a Social Science Measurement Challenge

abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) is a central computational tool in physics, chemistry, and biology, enabling quantitative prediction of experimental observables as expectations over high-dimensional molecular distributions such as Boltzmann distributions and transition densities. However, conventional MD is fundamentally limited by the high computational cost required to generate independent samples. Generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) has recently emerged as an alternative, learning surrogates of molecular distributions either from data or through interaction with energy models. While these methods enable efficient sampling, their transferability across molecular systems is often limited. In this work, we show that incorporating auxiliary sources of information can improve the data efficiency and generalization of transferable implicit transfer operators (TITO) for molecular dynamics. We find that coarse-grained TITO models are substantially more data-efficient than Boltzmann Emulators, and that incorporating protein language model (pLM) embeddings further improves out-of-distribution generalization. Our approach, PLaTITO, achieves state-of-the-art performance on equilibrium sampling benchmarks for out-of-distribution protein systems, including fast-folding proteins. We further study the impact of additional conditioning signals such as structural embeddings, temperature, and large-language-model-derived embeddings on model performance.

Generative models offer learned surrogates that sample efficiently, yet transferring those models between molecular systems remains difficult. This paper investigates whether auxiliary information can improve that transfer for transferable implicit transfer operators, or TITO.

The authors find that coarse-grained TITO models use data substantially more efficiently than Boltzmann Emulators. summary.tldr: PLaTITO adds protein language model embeddings to generative molecular dynamics, improving generalization to unseen protein systems.

title: Protein Language Model Embeddings Improve Generalization of Implicit Transfer Operators

abstract: The goal of this paper is to improve the performance and reliability of vision-language-action (VLA) models through iterative online interaction. Since collecting policy rollouts in the real world is expensive, we investigate whether a learned simulator—specifically, an action-conditioned video generation model—can be used to generate additional rollout data. Unfortunately, existing world models lack the physical fidelity necessary for policy improvement: they are predominantly trained on demonstration datasets that lack coverage of many different physical interactions (particularly failure cases) and struggle to accurately model small yet critical physical details in contact-rich object manipulation. We propose a simple iterative improvement algorithm that uses real-world roll-out data to improve the fidelity of the world model, which can then, in turn, be used to generate supplemental synthetic data for improving the VLA model. In our experiments on a real robot, we use this approach to improve the performance of a state-of-the-art VLA model on multiple downstream tasks. We achieve a 39.2% absolute success rate improvement over the base policy and 11.6% improvement from training with the generated synthetic rollouts. Videos can be found at this anonymous website: https://sites.google.com/view/vla-w.

paragraphs: Improving a robot policy through real-world trials is expensive, making simulated rollout data attractive. VLAW studies an action-conditioned video model as a learned simulator. The difficulty is physical fidelity: models trained mainly on demonstrations have limited coverage of failures and can miss small contact details that matter for manipulation.

The proposed algorithm alternates improvement of the simulator and the vision-language-action policy. Real-world rollouts improve the world model's fidelity, after which that model generates supplemental synthetic rollouts for policy training. This connects real experience to both parts of the system, allowing a better simulator to contribute additional training data for the robot.

The authors report a 39.2-percentage-point absolute success-rate improvement over the base policy and an 11.6% improvement from training with generated synthetic rollouts. The findings support iterative co-improvement in the tested setting, with real-world data addressing simulator weaknesses before its generated experience is used to improve the policy.
summary.tldr: VLAW alternates real-world refinement of a video world model with robot-policy training on supplemental synthetic rollouts.

title: VLAW: Iterative Co-Improvement of Vision-Language-Action Policy and World Model

abstract: Autonomous driving requires safe planning, but most learning-based planners lack explicit self-correction ability: once an unsafe action is proposed, there is no mechanism to correct it. Thus, we propose CorrectionPlanner, an autoregressive planner with self-correction that contains a propose, evaluate, and correct loop in the motion-token generation process. At each planning step, the policy proposes an action, namely a motion token, and a learned collision critic predicts whether it will induce a collision within a short horizon. If the critic predicts a collision, we retain the sequence of historical unsafe motion tokens as a self-correction trace, generate the next motion token conditioned on it, and repeat this process until the safe motion token is proposed or the safety criterion is met. This self-correction trace, consisting of all the unsafe motion tokens, represents the planner’s correction process in motion-token space. We train the planner with imitation learning followed by model-based reinforcement learning using rollouts from a pretrained world model that realistically models agents’ reactive behaviors. Closed-loop evaluations show that CorrectionPlanner reduces the collision rate by over $20%$ on Waymax and obtains state-of-the-art planning scores on nuPlan.

paragraphs: A driving planner needs a way to revise an action that appears unsafe before committing to it. CorrectionPlanner builds this ability into autoregressive motion generation. Each planning step includes a loop that proposes a motion token, evaluates its collision risk, and generates a correction when needed.

A learned collision critic predicts whether a proposed token will lead to a collision over a short horizon. When it predicts a collision, the planner retains that unsafe token in a correction trace. Subsequent proposals are conditioned on the accumulated trace, so the generation process explicitly uses its previous rejected attempts. The loop continues until a safe token is proposed or the safety criterion is met.

These results support explicit revision during planning, while the safety evaluation itself relies on a learned, short-horizon collision predictor.
summary.tldr: CorrectionPlanner improves driving plans through a learned collision-checking loop that conditions revised actions on earlier unsafe proposals.

title: CorrectionPlanner: Self-Correction Planner with Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Driving

abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, existing group-based RLVR methods often suffer from severe sample inefficiency. This inefficiency stems from reliance on point estimation of rewards from a small number of rollouts, leading to high estimation variance, variance collapse, and ineffective utilization of generated responses. In this work, we reformulate RLVR from a statistical estimation perspective by modeling rewards as samples drawn from a policy-induced distribution and casting advantage computation as the problem of estimating the reward distribution from finite data. Building on this view, we propose Discounted Beta–Bernoulli (DBB) reward estimation, which leverages historical reward statistics for the non-stationary distribution. Although biased, the resulting estimator exhibits reduced and stable variance and theoretically avoids variance collapse. Under mild non-stationarity, it also achieves a lower mean squared error than standard point estimation, as we characterize analytically and verify empirically. Across six in-distribution and three out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks, GRPO with DBB consistently outperforms naive GRPO and strong recent baselines, including the replay-based RePO and the variance-collapse-aware GRESO and DAPO. Relative to GRPO, it achieves average Acc@8 improvements of 3.43/2.32 points in-distribution and 10.05/8.34 points out-of-distribution on the 1.7B and 8B models, respectively, without additional computational cost or memory usage.

Group-based methods estimate learning signals from small sets of generated responses, which can make reward estimates noisy or cause their estimated variance to collapse. This paper treats the problem as estimating a changing reward distribution from limited observations.

The analysis shows that it avoids variance collapse and, under mild non-stationarity, has lower mean squared error than standard point estimation.

For the 1.7B and 8B models, average Acc@8 gains over GRPO are 3.43 and 2.32 points in-distribution, and 10.05 and 8.34 points out-of-distribution. The reported improvements require no additional computation or memory. These results connect better statistical estimation of rewards with more effective use of generated training responses.
summary.tldr: Discounted Beta–Bernoulli reward estimation improves GRPO by using historical outcomes to stabilize learning signals from small response groups.

title: Discounted Beta–Bernoulli Reward Estimation for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) with multimodal large language models has shown strong potential, yet most existing methods still depend on large-scale annotations or expert-designed priors, limiting their ability to acquire anomaly knowledge with as little human intervention as possible. To address this, we propose Linguistic Relative Policy Optimization (LRPO), which distills group-relative semantic advantages from multiple reasoning trajectories into a linguistically expressed anomaly experience prior, and adapts the model by injecting this prior into the context to steer its output distribution without any parameter updates. LRPO builds two complementary experience representations: general experience captures transferable anomaly preferences across scenarios, while scenario experience models context-dependent anomaly rules for targeted refinement. To further improve the learned experience, we introduce an anomaly alignment reward that guides trajectory optimization to match human risk preferences and reinforce temporally grounded reasoning. Extensive experiments on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, and UBNormal demonstrate that LRPO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods under tuning-free settings.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can reason about unusual events in video, but many approaches rely on extensive annotations or expert-written priors. LRPO aims to acquire useful anomaly experience with less human intervention. It compares multiple reasoning trajectories and distills their relative semantic advantages into a prior expressed in language, which is then placed in the model’s context.

This contextual prior steers the output distribution without updating model parameters. LRPO separates its experience into two complementary forms: general experience captures anomaly preferences that transfer across scenarios, while scenario experience captures rules that depend on the particular setting. This division lets the contextual guidance combine broadly useful judgments with more targeted refinements.

Experiments on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, and UBNormal report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods under tuning-free settings. The findings support language-based experience as a mechanism for adapting anomaly reasoning through context, with reward-guided refinement helping shape what that experience contains.
summary.tldr: LRPO improves video anomaly reasoning without parameter updates by distilling comparative reasoning experience into contextual language guidance.

title: Linguistic Relative Policy Optimization for Video Anomaly Reasoning

abstract: Federated learning (FL) across multiple HPC facilities faces stochastic admission delays from batch schedulers that dominate wall-clock time. Synchronous FL suffers from severe stragglers, while asynchronous FL accumulates stale updates when queues spike. We propose FedQueue, a queue-aware FL protocol that incorporates scheduler delays directly into training and aggregation, which (i) predicts per-facility queue delays online to budget local work, (ii) applies cutoff-based admission that buffers late arrivals to bound staleness, and (iii) performs staleness-aware aggregation to stabilize heterogeneous local workloads. We prove the convergence for non-convex objectives at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{R})$ under bounded staleness, and show that the admission controls yield bounded staleness with high probability under queue-prediction error. Real-world cross-facility deployment of FedQueue shows 20.5% improvement over baseline algorithms. Controlled queue simulations demonstrate robust improvement over the baselines; in particular, up to 60% reduction in time to reach a target accuracy level under high queue variance and non-IID partitions.

We prove the convergence for non-convex objectives at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{R})$ under bounded staleness, and show that the admission controls yield bounded staleness with high probability under queue-prediction error. paragraphs: Federated learning across high-performance computing facilities must contend with batch queues before training jobs can run. These unpredictable admission delays can dominate elapsed training time. Synchronous approaches wait for slow facilities, while asynchronous approaches risk incorporating updates that have become stale during long queue waits.

FedQueue makes queue behavior part of the training protocol. It predicts each facility’s delay online to determine how much local work to assign. Cutoff-based admission buffers late arrivals to control staleness, and aggregation accounts for update age while accommodating different local workloads. Together, these mechanisms connect scheduling decisions with how model updates are produced and combined.

For nonconvex objectives, the paper proves an O(1/√R) convergence rate under bounded staleness. It also shows that its admission controls bound staleness with high probability under queue-prediction error. A real deployment reports a 20.5% improvement over baseline algorithms. Controlled simulations show up to 60% less time to reach target accuracy when queue variance is high and data partitions are non-IID.
summary.tldr: FedQueue incorporates HPC queue predictions and update staleness into federated training to improve convergence efficiency and elapsed training time.

title: FedQueue: Queue-Aware Federated Learning for Cross-Facility HPC Training

abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive models have emerged as a unifying paradigm across modalities such as text and images, but their extension to 3D molecule generation remains underexplored. The gap stems from two fundamental challenges: (1) how to tokenize molecules into a canonical 1D sequence of tokens that is invariant to both SE(3) transformations and atom index permutations, and (2) how to design an architecture capable of modeling hybrid atom-based tokens that couple discrete atom types with continuous 3D coordinates. To address these challenges, we introduce InertialAR. It first performs generation-oriented canonical tokenization by aligning each molecule to a canonical inertial frame and reordering atoms, thereby converting arbitrary 3D structures into a unique, SE(3)- and permutation-invariant sequence of tokens for autoregressive generation. Built upon this canonical tokenization, we propose geometric positional encoding (GeoPE), which endows Transformer attention with 3D geometric awareness. Finally, InertialAR utilizes a hierarchical autoregressive paradigm to decode the next atom, consecutively predicting the atom type and 3D coordinates via Diffusion Loss. Experimentally, InertialAR achieves state-of-the-art performance on 8 of the 10 evaluation metrics for unconditional generation across QM9, GEOM-Drugs, and B3LYP. Moreover, it significantly outperforms baselines in controllable generation for targeted chemical functionality, attaining state-of-the-art results across all 5 metrics. Code is available at github.com/HaoruiLi46/InertialAR.

abstract: Existing benchmarks for computational materials discovery primarily evaluate static predictive tasks or isolated computational sub-tasks. While valuable, these evaluations neglect the inherently iterative and adaptive nature of scientific discovery. We introduce MAterials Discovery Environments (MADE), a novel framework for benchmarking end-to-end autonomous materials discovery pipelines. MADE simulates closed loop discovery campaigns in which an agent or algorithm proposes, evaluates, and refines candidate materials under a constrained oracle budget, capturing the sequential and resource-limited nature of real discovery workflows. We formalize discovery as a search for thermodynamically stable compounds relative to a given convex hull, and evaluate efficacy and efficiency via comparison to baseline algorithms. The framework is flexible; users can compose discovery agents from interchangeable components such as generative models, filters, and planners, enabling the study of arbitrary workflows ranging from fixed pipelines to agentic systems. We demonstrate this by conducting systematic experiments across a diverse range of systems and algorithms, finding that adaptive planning becomes more important to discovery efficiency as the search space scales.

paragraphs: Materials discovery involves repeatedly proposing candidates, evaluating them, and deciding what to try next. MADE evaluates that entire process. It addresses a gap in benchmarks centered on static predictions or separate computational tasks, which do not capture how a discovery system adapts its search as evidence accumulates.

The framework simulates discovery campaigns with a limited budget for oracle evaluations. The objective is to find thermodynamically stable compounds relative to a specified convex hull, making the stability reference part of the task definition. Discovery systems can be assembled from interchangeable generators, filters, and planners. This supports comparisons between fixed pipelines and agents that change their decisions during a campaign.

The authors compare efficacy and efficiency against baseline algorithms across diverse systems and methods. Their experiments find that adaptive planning becomes more important for discovery efficiency as the search space grows. The finding emphasizes the value of choosing subsequent evaluations in response to earlier results. MADE provides a common setting for studying that sequential decision process under explicit resource constraints.
summary.tldr: MADE benchmarks iterative materials discovery under limited evaluation budgets and finds adaptive planning increasingly valuable as search spaces grow.

title: MADE: Benchmark Environments for Closed-Loop Materials Discovery

abstract: Domain-specific large language models (LLMs), typically developed by fine-tuning a pre-trained general-purpose LLM on specialized datasets, represent a significant advancement in applied AI. A common strategy in LLM fine-tuning is curriculum learning, which pre-orders training samples based on metrics like difficulty to improve learning efficiency compared to a random sampling strategy. However, most existing methods for LLM fine-tuning rely on a static curriculum, designed prior to training, which lacks adaptability to the model’s evolving needs during fine-tuning. To address this, we propose EDCO, a novel framework based on two key concepts: inference entropy and dynamic curriculum orchestration. Inspired by recent findings that maintaining high answer entropy benefits long-term reasoning gains, EDCO prioritizes samples with high inference entropy in a continuously adapted curriculum. EDCO integrates three core components: an efficient entropy estimator that uses prefix tokens to approximate full-sequence entropy, an entropy-based curriculum generator that selects data points with the highest inference entropy, and an LLM trainer that optimizes the model on the selected curriculum. Comprehensive experiments in communication, medicine and law domains, EDCO outperforms traditional curriculum strategies for fine-tuning Qwen3-4B and Llama3.2-3B models under supervised and reinforcement learning settings. Furthermore, the proposed efficient entropy estimation reduces computational time by 83.5% while maintaining high accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/GTS-AIData/EDCO.

paragraphs: A training curriculum determines which examples a model encounters as it learns. Many fine-tuning curricula fix that ordering before training, even though the model's needs change as its capabilities develop. EDCO addresses this mismatch by continually adapting sample selection using inference entropy, a measure of uncertainty in the model's possible outputs.

The framework has three connected components. An efficient estimator approximates full-answer entropy from prefix tokens. A curriculum generator prioritizes examples with high estimated entropy, and a trainer updates the model using the selected data. This repeated process allows the curriculum to reflect the model's evolving uncertainty rather than depend entirely on an initial assessment.

Experiments cover communication, medicine, and law with Qwen3-4B and Llama3.2-3B, under both supervised and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. EDCO outperforms traditional curriculum strategies in these evaluations. The entropy estimator reduces computational time by 83.5% while retaining high accuracy. That efficiency result concerns entropy estimation, and matters because repeated estimates are central to keeping the curriculum responsive during training.
summary.tldr: EDCO continually selects high-uncertainty training examples using an efficient entropy estimate to improve domain-specific language-model fine-tuning.

title: EDCO: Dynamic Curriculum Orchestration for Domain-specific Large Language Model Fine-tuning

abstract: Multi-agent LLM debates are increasingly used in domains such as policy, politics, and city planning, where ground truth is often unavailable. Yet existing evaluations rely heavily on outcome-based proxies such as consensus, majority vote, or LLM-as-judge scores, which can miss failures like sycophancy, domination, and premature convergence. We introduce a diagnostic framework that evaluates both debate outcomes and the deliberative process using interpretable metrics for engagement, responsiveness, influence asymmetry, balance, stability, and agent utility. Across real-world debate settings and validation benchmarks, our process-level diagnostics align more closely with human judgments and reveal interaction failures that standard outcome-only measures overlook. These results show that reliable evaluation of multi-agent debates requires measuring not only what answer agents reach, but how they reach it.

paragraphs: When language models debate policy or planning questions, there may be no single correct answer against which to score them. Evaluations often substitute agreement, majority voting, or another model's judgment. This paper argues that those outcome measures can overlook problems in the discussion itself, including excessive agreement, domination by one participant, and settling on a conclusion too early.

The authors introduce a framework that examines both the final outcome and the process used to reach it. Its interpretable measures cover engagement, responsiveness, unequal influence, balance, stability, and agent utility. Together, these dimensions provide a way to inspect whether a debate involved substantive interaction, rather than treating the final consensus as sufficient evidence of quality.

Across real-world debate settings and validation benchmarks, the process diagnostics agree more closely with human judgments and expose failures missed by outcome-only evaluations. The contribution is an evaluation method: it makes weaknesses in collective deliberation more visible and supports assessing how agents reach their answers.
summary.tldr: Process-level diagnostics reveal failures in multi-agent debates that consensus and final-answer scores can miss.

title: A Diagnostic Study of Multi-Agent LLMs for Real-World Debates

abstract: The online construction of vectorized high-definition (HD) maps is a cornerstone of modern autonomous driving systems. State-of-the-art approaches, particularly those based on the DETR framework, formulate this as an instance detection problem. However, their reliance on independent, learnable object queries results in a predominantly local query perspective, neglecting the inherent global representation within HD maps. In this work, we propose MapGR (Global Representation learning for HD Map construction), an architecture designed to learn and utilize global representations from queries. Our method introduces two synergistic modules: a Global Representation Learning (GRL) module, which encourages the distribution of all queries to better align with the global map through a carefully designed holistic segmentation task, and a Global Representation Guidance (GRG) module, which endows each individual query with explicit, global-level contextual information to facilitate its optimization. Evaluations on the nuScenes and Argoverse2 datasets validate the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating substantial improvements in mean Average Precision (mAP) compared to leading baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/skyshoumeng/MapGR.

paragraphs: Online construction of vectorized high-definition maps is an important component of autonomous driving. Many leading methods treat map construction as detecting separate instances using learned object queries. The paper argues that this encourages a local perspective, leaving the map’s overall structure insufficiently represented in the queries used to construct it.

MapGR introduces two complementary modules. Global Representation Learning uses a holistic segmentation task to encourage the collection of queries to align with the complete map. Global Representation Guidance then supplies individual queries with explicit global context to help optimize them. One module develops a shared view of the map, while the other makes that view available to each local prediction.

These results support the value of combining instance-level detection with map-wide representation learning. The contribution is a mechanism for making queries reflect both their individual targets and the broader spatial structure they collectively describe.
summary.tldr: MapGR improves vectorized map construction by teaching object queries to learn and use global map context.

title: Learning Global Representation from Queries for Vectorized HD Map Construction

abstract: In standard causal attention, each token’s query, key, and value (QKV) are static and encode only preceding context. We introduce CAuSal aTtention with Lookahead kEys (CASTLE), an attention mechanism that continually updates each token’s keys as the context unfolds. We term these updated keys lookahead keys because they belong to earlier positions yet integrate information from tokens that appear later relative to those positions, while strictly preserving the autoregressive property. Although the mechanism appears sequential, we derive a mathematical equivalence that avoids explicitly materializing lookahead keys at each position and enables efficient parallel training. On language modeling benchmarks, CASTLE consistently outperforms standard causal attention across model scales, reducing validation perplexity and improving average performance on a range of downstream tasks.

We term these updated keys lookahead keys because they belong to earlier positions yet integrate information from tokens that appear later relative to those positions, while strictly preserving the autoregressive property. paragraphs: CASTLE changes how causal attention represents earlier tokens as a sequence develops. Standard causal attention gives each token fixed queries, keys, and values based on its preceding context. Keys determine how later queries access those representations, so a fixed key cannot incorporate context that arrives after its original token.

The proposed mechanism continually updates earlier tokens’ keys using the context that has since become available. These are called lookahead keys because they include information later than the positions they represent. The mechanism nevertheless preserves autoregressive generation: looking ahead relative to an earlier token does not mean accessing future information beyond the current prediction point.

Updating keys repeatedly might appear to require sequential training. The authors derive an equivalent mathematical formulation that avoids explicitly constructing every updated key and allows efficient parallel training. Across the evaluated model scales, CASTLE reduces validation perplexity and improves average downstream task performance relative to standard causal attention. The findings support updating how past information is accessed as a useful attention design.
summary.tldr: CASTLE updates earlier tokens’ attention keys with newly available context while preserving autoregressive generation and efficient parallel training.

title: Causal Attention with Lookahead Keys

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often introduce errors when generating image captions, resulting in misaligned image-text pairs. Our work focuses on a class of captioning errors that we refer to as systematic misalignments, where a recurring error in MLLM-generated captions is closely associated with the presence of a specific visual feature in the paired image. Given a vision-language dataset with MLLM-generated captions, our aim in this work is to detect such errors, a task we refer to as systematic misalignment detection. As our first key contribution, we present Symbal, which utilizes a structured, dual-stage setup with off-the-shelf foundation models to identify systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language. As our second key contribution, we introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate automated methods on our proposed task. SymbalBench consists of 1.7 million image-text pairs from two domains (natural and medical images), organized into 420 vision-language datasets with annotated systematic misalignments. Symbal exhibits strong performance on this benchmark, correctly identifying systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets, a nearly 4x improvement over the closest baseline. We supplement our evaluations on SymbalBench with real-world evaluations, showing that (1) Symbal can accurately surface systematic misalignments in captions generated by four MLLMs and (2) Symbal is a powerful tool for auditing off-the-shelf image-caption datasets. Ultimately, our novel task, method, and benchmark can aid users with auditing MLLM-generated captions and identifying critical errors, without requiring access to the underlying MLLM. Code is available at https://github.com/Stanford-AIMI/Symbal.

title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions

abstract: Foundation flow-matching (FM) models promise universal priors for solving inverse problems (IPs); yet today, they trail behind domain-specific and even untrained priors. How can we unlock their potential? We introduce FMPlug, a plug-in framework that redefines how foundation FMs are used in IPs. FMPlug combines an instance-guided, time-dependent warm-start strategy with sharp Gaussianity regularization, adding problem-specific guidance while preserving the Gaussian structures. For evaluation, we consider both simple image restoration tasks and scientific IPs with a few similar samples—where the prohibitive cost of data collection and model training hinders the development of domain-specific generative models. Our superior experimental results confirm the effectiveness of FMPlug. Overall, FMPlug paves the way for making foundation FM models practical, reusable priors for IPs, especially scientific ones with few similar samples.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover an underlying object or signal from observations, and generative priors help guide that recovery. Foundation flow-matching models promise reusable priors, yet the paper reports that current uses trail domain-specific and even untrained alternatives. FMPlug addresses how to use a foundation model effectively for a particular inverse-problem instance.

The framework combines an instance-guided warm start that varies with time and a sharp Gaussianity regularizer. The warm start supplies problem-specific guidance, while the regularizer preserves Gaussian structure. Their combination aims to adapt the reconstruction process to the current problem while retaining structures important to using the foundation flow-matching prior.

Evaluation covers simple image restoration and scientific inverse problems with only a few similar samples. The latter setting matters because collecting specialized data and training a domain-specific generator can be prohibitively expensive. The authors report superior experimental results, supporting FMPlug as a way to make existing foundation models more practical and reusable for these tasks. The findings concern the evaluated settings, with particular motivation from scientific applications where similar examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: FMPlug combines instance-guided initialization and Gaussianity regularization to improve foundation flow-matching priors for inverse problems.

title: Saving Foundation Flow-Matching Priors for Inverse Problems

abstract: Recent approaches for video generation with camera control often create anchor videos (i.e., rendered videos that approximate desired camera motions) to guide diffusion models as a structured prior, by rendering from estimated point clouds following camera trajectories. However, errors in point cloud and camera trajectory estimation often lead to inaccurate anchor videos with higher training cost and low efficiency, as the model is forced to compensate for rendering misalignments. To address these limitations, we introduce EPiC, an efficient and precise camera control learning framework that constructs well-aligned training anchor videos without the need for camera pose or point cloud estimation. Concretely, we create highly precise anchor videos by masking source videos based on first-frame visibility, which ensures strong alignment, eliminates the need for camera/point cloud estimation, and thus can be readily applied to any in-the-wild video. Furthermore, we introduce Anchor-ControlNet, a lightweight module that integrates anchor video guidance in visible regions to pretrained video diffusion models, with less than 1% of additional parameters. EPiC achieves efficient training with substantially fewer parameters, training steps, and less data, and generalizes robustly to anchor videos made with point clouds at test time, enabling precise 3D-informed camera control. EPiC achieves SoTA performance on RealEstate10K and MiraData for I2V camera control task. Notably, EPiC also exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to video-to-video (V2V) scenarios.

paragraphs: Camera-controlled video generation often uses an anchor video to show the desired camera motion. Rendering these anchors from estimated point clouds and camera trajectories can introduce misalignment, forcing the generator to compensate during training. EPiC changes how training anchors are constructed so that guidance aligns closely with the source video.

The framework masks source videos according to what is visible in their first frame. This produces training anchors without estimating camera poses or point clouds. A lightweight Anchor-ControlNet then feeds guidance from visible regions into a pretrained video diffusion model, adding less than 1% to its parameter count. The design reduces the burden of learning from inaccurate rendered guidance.

The authors report efficient training with fewer parameters, steps, and data, plus state-of-the-art image-to-video camera control on RealEstate10K and MiraData. At test time, the model generalizes to anchors rendered from point clouds, enabling 3D-informed control despite the different training construction. It also shows strong zero-shot generalization to video-to-video scenarios, extending the reported usefulness beyond its image-to-video evaluation.
summary.tldr: EPiC learns efficient camera control from precisely aligned masked-video anchors and transfers to point-cloud guidance at test time.

title: EPiC: Efficient Video Camera Control Learning with Precise Anchor-Video Guidance

abstract: Structural Causal Models (SCM) are a powerful framework for describing complicated dynamics across the natural sciences. A particularly elegant way of interpreting SCMs is via do-Shapley values, a game-theoretic method of quantifying the average effect of $d$ variables across exponentially many interventions. Like Shapley values, computing do-Shapley values generally requires evaluating exponentially many terms. The foundation of our work is a reformulation of do-Shapley values in terms of the irreducible sets of the underlying SCM. Leveraging this insight, we can exactly compute do-Shapley values in time linear in the number of irreducible sets $r$, which itself can range from $d$ to $2^d$ depending on the graph structure of the SCM. Since $r$ is unknown a priori, we complement the exact algorithm with an estimator that, like general Shapley value estimators, can be run with any query budget. As the query budget approaches $r$, our estimators can produce more accurate estimates than prior methods by several orders of magnitude, and, when the budget reaches $r$, return the Shapley values up to machine precision. Beyond computational speed, we also reduce the identification burden: we prove that non-parametric identifiability of do-Shapley values requires only the identification of interventional effects for the $d$ singleton coalitions, rather than all classes.

Depending on graph structure, r can range from the number of variables to an exponential in that number, so the speedup is structure-dependent. Because r is initially unknown, the authors also provide estimators that accept any query budget. As the budget approaches r, these can outperform previous estimators by several orders of magnitude in accuracy; at r, they recover values to machine precision.

The paper also reduces what must be identified from causal information. It proves that identifying interventional effects for singleton coalitions is sufficient for nonparametric identification of do-Shapley values. Together, the results reduce both computation and the intervention-identification burden by exploiting causal structure.
summary.tldr: A reformulation using irreducible causal sets enables structure-dependent exact do-Shapley computation and reduces the required identification of intervention effects.

title: Exactly Computing do-Shapley Values

abstract: Time series forecasting has long relied on dense endogenous observations, yet in many real-world scenarios, such data is scarce or even absent. Existing approaches attempt to compensate with exogenous variables, but their reliance on incomplete endogenous histories makes them brittle under data scarcity. In this work, we introduce sparse endogenous forecasting as a new setting, where exogenous sequences and only sparse endogenous observations are available. To tackle this problem, we propose TimeSeed, a lightweight architecture that redefines sparse forecasting as a context reconstruction task. By jointly exploiting the stability of exogenous sequences and the limited but informative endogenous signals, TimeSeed reconstructs robust historical representations and transforms forecasting into a tractable sequence-based prediction problem. Remarkably, TimeSeed achieves this with a purely linear architecture using only 0.19M parameters, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art deep models on seven real-world benchmarks, with an average improvement of 13.01% in MSE and 7.54% in MAE. These results establish sparse endogenous forecasting as a practical and promising paradigm, opening a new direction for time series analysis under extreme data scarcity. Code is available at this repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Alistair-7.

paragraphs: Forecasting often assumes a dense history of the variable being predicted. In practice, observations of that target variable can be sparse even when external time-varying inputs are available. This paper formalizes sparse endogenous forecasting, where those external sequences must be combined with only limited observations of the target itself.

TimeSeed approaches the problem by reconstructing historical context. It jointly uses the stability of exogenous sequences and the information carried by sparse endogenous observations to build robust historical representations. Forecasting then operates on those reconstructed representations as a sequence-prediction problem. The architecture is entirely linear and contains 0.19 million parameters, making the reconstruction strategy central to its approach.

Across seven real-world benchmarks, TimeSeed consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art deep models, with average improvements of 13.01% in mean squared error and 7.54% in mean absolute error. These findings support context reconstruction as an effective way to use external sequences when target histories are scarce, and show that a small linear architecture can perform strongly in this setting.
summary.tldr: TimeSeed reconstructs forecasting context from external sequences and sparse target observations, outperforming compared deep models with a small linear architecture.

title: TimeSeed: Effective Time Series Forecasting with Sparse Endogenous Variables

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong complex reasoning capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, their reasoning patterns remain too complicated to analyze. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpretability, existing approaches predominantly operate at the token level, creating a granularity mismatch when capturing more critical step-level information, such as reasoning direction and semantic transitions. In this work, we propose step-level sparse autoencoder (SSAE), which serves as an analytical tool to disentangle different aspects of LLMs’ reasoning steps into sparse features. Specifically, by precisely controlling the sparsity of a step feature conditioned on its context, we form an information bottleneck in step reconstruction, which splits incremental information from background information and disentangles it into several sparsely activated dimensions. Experiments on multiple base models and reasoning tasks show the effectiveness of the extracted features. By linear probing, we can easily predict surface-level information, such as generation length and first token distribution, as well as more complicated properties, such as the correctness and logicality of the step. These observations indicate that LLMs should already at least partly know about these properties during generation, which provides the foundation for the self-verification ability of LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/SSAE.

paragraphs: The Step-Level Sparse Autoencoder examines language-model reasoning at the level of complete reasoning steps. The paper argues that token-level analysis can miss properties such as a step’s direction or its transition in meaning. SSAE instead seeks sparse features that separate different aspects of a step and expose what it contributes beyond the preceding context.

The method controls the sparsity of a step representation conditioned on that context. This creates an information bottleneck during reconstruction, separating incremental information from background information and distributing it across a small number of activated dimensions. The resulting features provide an analytical representation intended to match the scale at which reasoning develops.

Across multiple base models and reasoning tasks, simple linear probes can predict both surface properties, such as generation length and first-token distribution, and more complex properties, including correctness and logicality. The authors interpret this as evidence that models already possess at least partial information about these qualities during generation. That supports a potential foundation for self-verification, without establishing that models reliably act on this information themselves.
summary.tldr: SSAE extracts sparse reasoning-step features that predict properties including correctness and logicality, suggesting partial internal information relevant to self-verification.

title: Step-Level Sparse Autoencoder for Reasoning Process Interpretation

abstract: LLM-based deep research agents are largely built on the ReAct framework. This linear design makes it difficult to revisit earlier states, branch into alternative search directions, or maintain global awareness under long contexts, often leading to local optima, redundant exploration, and inefficient search. We propose Re-TRAC, an agentic framework that performs cross-trajectory exploration by generating a structured state representation after each trajectory to summarize evidence, uncertainties, failures, and future plans, and conditioning subsequent trajectories on this state representation. This enables iterative reflection and globally informed planning, reframing research as a progressive process. Empirical results show that Re-TRAC consistently outperforms ReAct by 15–20% on BrowseComp with frontier LLMs. For smaller models, we introduce Re-TRAC-aware supervised fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art performance at comparable scales. Notably, Re-TRAC shows a monotonic reduction in tool calls and token usage across rounds, indicating progressively targeted exploration driven by cross-trajectory reflection rather than redundant search.
